a: It is hardly dammed or straightened
It flows only through national parks
It carries water only in spring
It is closed to all ships
60533.e: Only one large dam was built on the lower Vistula, in 1970 at Włocławek. Other planned dams were never built, so there are still many sandbanks and floodplains.
60533.m: The lower Vistula is hardly dammed and therefore very natural.

a: An artificial outlet channel straight to the Baltic Sea
A bridge over the mouth of the Vistula
A tunnel under the Vistula in Gdańsk
A canal between the Vistula and the Oder
60534.e: After severe floods caused by ice jams, a new short route to the sea was dug near Świbno. Since then the main stream has flowed into the sea there.
60534.m: The Vistula cut takes the river to the sea by a short route.

60535.q: Which place at the mouth of the Vistula in Gdańsk is known because the Second World War began there on 1 September 1939?
60535.e: On the morning of 1 September 1939 the German training ship Schleswig-Holstein fired on the Polish ammunition depot at Westerplatte. It lies on the Dead Vistula, an old branch of the river mouth.
60535.m: The Second World War began at Westerplatte in 1939.

60536.q: Which two large Polish cities both lie on the Vistula?
60536.e: The Vistula flows from the Beskids via Kraków and Warsaw to Gdańsk. Wrocław and Szczecin lie on the Oder, Poznań on the Warta.
60536.m: Kraków, Warsaw and Gdańsk lie on the Vistula.

60537.e: The Dnieper rises in the Valdai Hills west of Moscow. The sources of the Volga are also there.
60537.m: The Dnieper begins in the Valdai Hills.

60538.q: What does the city name Zaporizhzhia originally mean?
60538.e: The Zaporozhian Cossacks lived below the former Dnieper rapids. The rapids disappeared into a reservoir in the 20th century.

60539.q: Which sea does the Dnieper flow into?
60539.e: Together with the Southern Bug, the Dnieper flows into the Black Sea through a wide, lagoon-like estuary called a liman.
60539.m: The Dnieper flows into the Black Sea.

60540.q: Which community lived on the rapids of the lower Dnieper from the 16th century?
60540.e: On the island of Khortytsia and nearby, the Zaporozhian Cossacks built their fortified camps, the Sich. They are seen as an important root of Ukrainian history.
60540.m: The Zaporozhian Cossacks lived on the lower Dnieper.

60542.q: On which tributary of the Dnieper did Napoleon's army suffer heavy losses during the retreat in 1812?
60542.e: Tens of thousands of soldiers died crossing the Berezina in November 1812. Swiss regiments also fought there, which the Beresinalied (Berezina song) recalls.
60542.m: At the Berezina, Napoleon's Russian campaign ended in disaster.

60543.q: Which Russian city lies on the upper Dnieper?
60543.e: Smolensk is one of the oldest cities in Russia and lies on the still young Dnieper. Tver, on the other hand, lies on the Volga.
60543.m: Smolensk lies on the upper Dnieper.

60544.q: What happened to the Dnieper in Ukraine in the 20th century?
a: It was dammed into a chain of reservoirs
It was moved into an underground canal
It was diverted to the Volga
60544.e: Large dams turned the Dnieper into a chain of reservoirs, the largest being the Kremenchuk Reservoir. They provide electricity and water for irrigation.
60544.m: The Dnieper in Ukraine is dammed almost all the way.

60545.q: Which canal carried water from the lower Dnieper to the Crimean peninsula?
60545.e: The canal was built from 1961 and supplied the dry Crimea with water for farming and towns. It branched off at Nova Kakhovka.
60545.m: The North Crimean Canal brought Dnieper water to Crimea.

60546.q: On which mountain does the Po rise?
60546.e: The Po rises on Monte Viso in the Cottian Alps near the French border. At about 650 km it is the longest river in Italy.
60546.m: The Po begins on Monte Viso.

60547.q: How was the Po Valley formed?
a: An arm of the sea was filled with debris from the Alps and Apennines.
A volcano collapsed and left a hollow.
A huge glacial lake drained completely.
Sea level fell sharply in Roman times.
60547.e: Between the Alps and the Apennines lay a hollow that was once covered by the sea. Over millions of years rivers deposited thick sediments and filled it up.
60547.m: The Po Valley is a sea basin filled with river debris.

60548.q: Why does the Po Valley often have some of the worst air quality in Europe in winter?
a: Temperature inversions trap exhaust fumes between the Alps and the Apennines.
The foehn blows Saharan dust into the plain.
The many rice fields release soot.
Sea winds bring salt from the coast.
60548.e: The plain is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and in winter cold air often lies under warmer air. Pollutants from traffic, industry and heating then cannot escape.
60548.m: During an inversion, exhaust fumes collect in the Po Valley.

60549.q: Which city is the largest in the Po Valley?
60549.e: With over 1.3 million inhabitants, Milan is the largest city in the plain and the centre of a huge built-up area. The Po Valley is the economic heart of Italy.
60549.m: Milan is the largest city in the Po Valley.

60550.q: Why does the Po in its lower course partly lie higher than the surrounding land?
a: It deposits debris and is enclosed by high embankments
The sea pushes its water upwards
Glaciers fill its bed with ice
60550.e: The Po deposits a lot of sediment in its embanked riverbed, which therefore gets higher and higher. If the embankments break, as in 1951 in the Polesine, large areas are flooded.
60550.m: The embanked Po partly flows above the level of the land around it.

60551.q: What is the area called where the Po splits into many branches as it flows into the sea, which is a nature park?
60551.e: The Po Delta keeps growing out into the sea through sediment. Its lagoons and reed beds are important habitats for water birds.
60551.m: Before reaching the sea, the Po splits into a large delta.

60552.q: Which crop is grown on irrigated fields in the western Po Valley, more than anywhere else in Europe?
60552.e: In Piedmont and Lombardy the fields are flooded through canals such as the Canale Cavour with water from the Po and Alpine rivers. Italy is the largest rice producer in Europe.
60552.m: The Po Valley is the largest rice-growing area in Europe.

60553.q: Which river flows through Lake Como and then into the Po?
60553.e: The Adda comes from the Valtellina, flows through Lake Como and joins the Po near Cremona. The Mincio, on the other hand, drains Lake Garda.
60553.m: The Adda links Lake Como with the Po.

60554.q: Which river links Lake Ladoga with the Baltic Sea?
60554.e: The Neva is only about 74 kilometres long but carries a great deal of water. St Petersburg lies at its mouth on the Baltic Sea.
60554.m: The Neva flows from Lake Ladoga through St Petersburg into the Baltic.

60555.q: What was the supply route across frozen Lake Ladoga during the siege of Leningrad called?
60555.e: In winter lorries drove across the ice, and in summer ships sailed. During the siege from 1941 to 1944 this route was the only link into the city.
60555.m: The Road of Life led across Lake Ladoga to Leningrad.

60556.q: On which island in Lake Ladoga is there a famous Russian Orthodox monastery?
60556.e: Valaam Monastery lies on the island of the same name in the north of Lake Ladoga. In the Winter War in 1940 the monks were evacuated to Finland.
60556.m: A famous monastery stands on the island of Valaam.

60557.q: Which mammal lives as a subspecies of its own only in the fresh water of Lake Ladoga?
60557.e: The Ladoga ringed seal is a leftover from the time after the Ice Age when the lake was connected to the sea. It is endemic and endangered.
60557.m: A subspecies of ringed seal of its own lives in Lake Ladoga.

60558.q: Roughly how deep is Lake Ladoga at its deepest point?
60558.e: The greatest depth of about 230 m is in the rocky north-west. The south of the lake is much shallower.
60558.m: Lake Ladoga is over two hundred metres deep in the north.

60559.q: What makes Lake Ladoga special among Europe's lakes?
a: It is the largest lake in Europe
It is the deepest lake in Europe
It is the saltiest lake in Europe
It is the highest lake in Europe
60559.e: At about 17,700 square kilometres, Lake Ladoga is the largest lake entirely in Europe. It is almost half the size of Switzerland.
60559.m: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe.

60560.q: Why was the Shlisselburg fortress at the outflow of the Neva from Lake Ladoga so important?
a: It controlled the waterway between the lake and the Baltic Sea
It protected gold mines on the lakeshore
It was the tsars' summer residence
It guarded the border with China
60560.e: The fortress (Oreshek) lies on a small island at the outflow of the Neva. Peter the Great captured it from the Swedes in 1702 and so secured the route to the Baltic.
60560.m: Shlisselburg was the key to the route from Lake Ladoga to the Baltic.

60561.q: Roughly how large is the area of Lake Ladoga?
60561.e: Without islands, the lake covers about 17,700 to 17,900 km², depending on the source. That is more than 40 per cent of the area of Switzerland.
60561.m: Lake Ladoga is almost half the size of Switzerland.

60562.q: Why does the Baltic Sea have a much lower salt content than the Atlantic?
a: Many rivers supply fresh water, and exchange with the North Sea is small.
Ice in winter removes all the salt from the water.
Underground springs wash the salt into the ground.
60562.e: The Baltic is a brackish sea, as it receives a lot of fresh water from rivers and rainfall. Salty North Sea water only gets in through shallow, narrow passages.
60562.m: The Baltic is a brackish sea with little salt.

60563.q: Which straits link the Baltic Sea with the Kattegat?
a: Øresund, Great Belt and Little Belt
Skagerrak, Pentland Firth and the Minch
Bothnian Sea, Sea of Åland and Archipelago Sea
60563.e: The three Danish straits lie between Jutland, the Danish islands and Sweden. All the water exchange with the North Sea passes through them.
60563.m: The Øresund and the Belts are the Baltic's gateway to the North Sea.

60564.q: What is the main cause of the oxygen-poor dead zones on the floor of the Baltic Sea?
a: Oil drilling in the central Baltic
Too strong a current on the seabed
60564.e: Nitrogen and phosphorus encourage algal blooms, and breaking these down on the seabed uses up a lot of oxygen. On top of this, the stable layering of the water prevents mixing.
60564.m: Too many nutrients make the Baltic suffocate on its floor.

60565.q: What do the rare major inflows of salt water from the North Sea do in the Baltic Sea?
a: They bring oxygen into the deep basins.
They make the Baltic freeze in winter.
They raise the water level permanently by metres.
They wash all the brackish water out.
60565.e: In certain storm conditions, a lot of salty, oxygen-rich water flows over the sills into the Baltic. Because it is heavy, it sinks and supplies the deep basins with oxygen.
60565.m: Saltwater inflows supply the depths of the Baltic with oxygen.

60566.q: What did the area of today's Baltic Sea look like during the last Ice Age?
a: It was covered by a thick ice sheet
It was a warm inland sea
It was a dry lowland without ice
It was part of the Mediterranean
60566.e: During the last Ice Age a huge ice sheet lay over Scandinavia and the Baltic. Only after it melted did the Baltic Sea form, switching several times between fresh and salt water.
60566.m: The Baltic is a young sea that formed after the Ice Age.

60567.q: Why does the land on the Gulf of Bothnia rise by up to almost 1 cm every year?
a: The Earth's crust is springing back after the ice sheet melted.
Volcanoes are slowly pushing the rock upwards.
The Baltic is evaporating and the level is falling.
Rivers deposit so much sand there.
60567.e: The weight of the Ice Age ice sheet had pressed the crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly rising again, which is called post-glacial rebound.
60567.m: Scandinavia has been slowly rising again since the Ice Age.

60568.q: What is the typical coastal form of Western Pomerania called, with shallow, bay-like waters behind islands and peninsulas?
60568.e: Bodden are shallow, often brackish bays separated from the open sea by spits and islands. One example is the area around Fischland-Darss-Zingst.
60568.m: Bodden shape the landscape on the coast of Western Pomerania.

60570.q: Which intergovernmental commission has worked to protect the Baltic Sea since the 1970s?
60570.e: It is based on the Helsinki Convention of 1974, to which all the coastal states and the EU belong. The OSPAR Commission, on the other hand, is responsible for the north-east Atlantic.
60570.m: HELCOM protects the marine environment of the Baltic.

60571.q: Why are many of the East Frisian Islands slowly moving east?
a: The current removes sand in the west and deposits it in the east.
The Earth's crust is shifting under the North Sea.
The tides push the islands as a whole.
The wind blows dunes out to sea.
60571.e: The East Frisian Islands are sandy barrier islands. Without protective structures their western ends would break away while their eastern ends grew.
60571.m: The East Frisian Islands move east with the sand.

60572.q: Which salt-loving plant is one of the first to colonise the mud at the edge of the salt marshes?
60572.e: Glasswort holds the mud in place and so slowly raises the ground. Marram grass, on the other hand, grows on dry sand dunes.
60572.m: Glasswort is a pioneer plant on the mudflats.

60573.q: What are the brushwood groynes (Lahnungen) off the coast in the Wadden Sea for?
a: They calm the water so that mud settles.
They lead the water into the tidal channels.
They mark safe routes for mudflat walkers.
They serve as resting places for seals.
60573.e: Lahnungen are double rows of wooden posts filled with brushwood. Mud settles in the calm fields between them, and new foreshore is created.
60573.m: Brushwood groynes help create new land on the coast.

60574.q: Which sunken settlement in the North Frisian Wadden Sea is still a well-known legend today?
60574.e: Rungholt was lost in 1362 in a huge storm surge, the Grote Mandrenke. Vineta is a legendary town on the Baltic, Ys one in Brittany.
60574.m: Rungholt sank into the Wadden Sea in 1362.

60575.q: Which introduced shellfish species now forms large reefs in the Wadden Sea?
60575.e: The Pacific oyster was introduced for farming and spread widely from the 1990s. It often pushes out the native blue mussel.
60575.m: The Pacific oyster has spread widely in the Wadden Sea.

60576.q: Why are many shelducks unable to fly for a few weeks in the Wadden Sea in late summer?
a: They are too heavy from eating so much.
They are nesting on the sandbanks.
Their wings are stuck together by salt water.
60576.e: During the moult, shelducks lose their flight feathers and cannot fly for a few weeks. Tens of thousands then gather on remote sandbanks in the Wadden Sea, where they find shelter and food.
60576.m: Many shelducks moult in the Wadden Sea.

60577.q: How has the island of Sylt been linked to the mainland since 1927?
a: By the Hindenburg Dam with the railway
By a tunnel under the mudflats
By a footpath at low tide
60577.e: The dam, about 11 km long, carries only railway tracks. Cars are taken to Sylt on trains.
60577.m: You reach Sylt by train over the Hindenburg Dam.

60578.q: Which wild animal, which also lives in the Wadden Sea, is the largest predator in Germany?
60578.e: Grey seal bulls can grow over 2 m long and weigh about 300 kg. There are large colonies on Heligoland and near Amrum, for example.
60578.m: The grey seal is Germany's largest predator.

60579.q: Which river brings the most water into the Black Sea?
60579.e: The Danube flows into the sea through a large delta in Romania and Ukraine. It drains large parts of Central Europe, including the Grisons via the Inn.
60579.m: The Danube is the largest river flowing into the Black Sea.

60580.q: What does the disputed “flood hypothesis” about the Black Sea say?
a: A freshwater lake was suddenly flooded by the Mediterranean after the Ice Age.
The sea was created by a meteorite impact.
The sea once dried up completely in ancient times.
A flood wave from the Caspian Sea filled the basin.
60580.e: The researchers Ryan and Pitman suggested a rapid flooding about 7500 years ago. Other experts think a gradual rise is more likely.
60580.m: According to one hypothesis, the Black Sea was once suddenly flooded.

60581.q: Roughly how salty is the surface water of the Black Sea?
60581.e: The salt content is about half that of the world's oceans, which have about 35 g per litre. Deeper down the water is a little saltier.
60581.m: The Black Sea is about half as salty as the ocean.

60582.q: Which mountain range runs along Turkey's Black Sea coast?
60582.e: The Pontic Mountains rise steeply behind the northern coast of Anatolia. They catch a lot of rain, so the coast is very green.
60582.m: The Pontic Mountains line Turkey's Black Sea coast.

60583.q: Which ancient region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea was, according to legend, the destination of the Argonauts?
60583.e: The Argonauts searched for the Golden Fleece in Colchis, in today's western Georgia. Taurica, on the other hand, was the name for Crimea.
60583.m: The Argonauts sailed to Colchis on the Black Sea.

60584.q: Roughly how big is the Black Sea compared with Switzerland?
a: A good ten times as big
About a hundred times as big
60584.e: The Black Sea covers about 436,000 km², Switzerland about 41,000 km². That makes a little more than ten times as much.
60584.m: The Black Sea is a good ten times as big as Switzerland.

60585.q: Which introduced animal caused the anchovy fishery in the Black Sea to collapse in the 1980s?
60585.e: The comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi probably arrived in ships' ballast water. It ate huge amounts of plankton and fish larvae.
60585.m: An introduced comb jelly harmed fishing in the Black Sea.

60586.q: Which canal has shortened the shipping route from the Danube to the Black Sea since 1984?
60586.e: The canal runs from Cernavodă straight to the coast near Constanța. This means ships do not have to take the long detour through the delta.
60586.m: The Danube-Black Sea Canal provides a shortcut to the coast.

60587.q: In which year was the first bridge over the Bosphorus opened?
60587.e: The first Bosphorus Bridge was opened for the 50th anniversary of the Republic of Turkey. Today there are three suspension bridges.
60587.m: Since 1973 a bridge has linked Europe and Asia in Istanbul.

60589.q: Why was a third bridge opened far to the north of the Bosphorus in 2016?
a: To keep heavy traffic out of central Istanbul
To stop shipping on the Bosphorus
To link Istanbul with Asia for the first time
Because the old bridges had collapsed
60589.e: The Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge carries a motorway and railway tracks. It is meant to route lorries around the overloaded city centre.
60589.m: The northernmost Bosphorus bridge takes heavy traffic away from the city centre.

60590.q: What is the planned artificial waterway west of the Bosphorus called?
60590.e: The canal is meant to link the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara and relieve the Bosphorus. The project is disputed because of environmental and cost issues.
60590.m: Kanal Istanbul is meant to relieve the Bosphorus.

60591.q: What is the small tower on a rocky islet in the Bosphorus off Üsküdar called?
60591.e: The Maiden's Tower (Kız Kulesi) has stood on a tiny island for centuries. It served as a lighthouse and customs station.
60591.m: The Maiden's Tower stands in the middle of the Bosphorus.

60592.q: Why did the Ottomans build fortresses on both banks at the narrowest point of the Bosphorus?
a: To control the passage of ships
To get salt from the sea
To protect their sultan's palace there
To build a bridge over the strait
60592.e: With Anadolu Hisarı on the Asian side and Rumeli Hisarı on the European side, the Ottomans could close the strait. This helped them in the siege of Constantinople in 1453.
60592.m: The fortresses on the Bosphorus controlled shipping through the strait.

60593.q: According to the common view, how was the Bosphorus formed?
a: As a river valley flooded by the sea
As the crater of a volcano
60593.e: Its winding shape is reminiscent of a river valley that was flooded when sea level rose. Tectonic fault lines also played a part.
60593.m: The Bosphorus is regarded as a drowned river valley.

60594.q: Which famous luxury train ran to Istanbul on the Bosphorus from 1889?
60594.e: The Orient Express ran from Paris to Constantinople, today's Istanbul, and ended at Sirkeci station. On the Asian side, the Baghdad Railway began at Haydarpaşa station.
60594.m: The Orient Express ended in Istanbul on the Bosphorus.

60595.q: Which strait was called the “Cimmerian Bosphorus” in ancient times?
60595.e: As well as the Thracian Bosphorus near Byzantion, there was the Cimmerian Bosphorus between Crimea and Taman. The ancient Bosporan Kingdom lay there.
60595.m: The Cimmerian Bosphorus is today's Kerch Strait.

60596.q: What is the Strait of Dover called in French?
60596.e: The French name the strait after the town of Calais. A département is also named after it.
60596.m: In French the Strait of Dover is called the Pas de Calais.

60597.q: Where on the English Channel has one of the world's first large tidal power stations stood since 1966?
a: On the Seine near Le Havre
60597.e: The power station uses the very high tidal range in Brittany. A dam across the mouth of the Rance contains the turbines.
60597.m: Electricity has been generated from the tides on the Rance since 1966.

60598.q: Which peninsula in Normandy, with the port of Cherbourg, juts far out into the English Channel?
60598.e: The Cotentin Peninsula separates the Bay of the Seine from the Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel. Cherbourg at its tip is an important ferry port.
60598.m: Cherbourg lies at the tip of the Cotentin Peninsula.

60599.q: On which Channel Island are cars banned?
60599.e: On Sark only tractors, bicycles and horse-drawn carriages are used. Until 2008 the island was regarded as the last feudal state in Europe.
60599.m: There are no cars on Sark.

60600.q: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail through the English Channel and fail?
60600.e: The fleet was meant to make an invasion of England possible, but it was defeated off Gravelines and scattered by storms. In 1066, on the other hand, William the Conqueror crossed over.
60600.m: The Spanish Armada failed in the English Channel in 1588.

60601.q: What was the evacuation of over 300,000 Allied soldiers from Dunkirk in 1940 called?
60601.e: Many ships and boats carried the trapped troops across the Channel to England. Overlord, on the other hand, was the landing in Normandy in 1944.
60601.m: Operation Dynamo rescued soldiers from Dunkirk in 1940.

60602.q: How is the heavy shipping traffic in the Strait of Dover regulated?
a: By a traffic separation scheme with separate lanes
By traffic lights on each coast
By allowing passage only by day
By a lock in the middle
60602.e: Ships heading south-west use the English side, and those heading north-east the French side. This avoids collisions.
60602.m: In the Strait of Dover there are separate lanes for ships.

60603.q: Which British territories in the English Channel were occupied by German troops in the Second World War?
60603.e: The Channel Islands were occupied from 1940 to 1945. They were the only British Crown territory in Europe to be occupied.
60603.m: The Channel Islands were under German occupation from 1940 to 1945.

60604.q: Why does the town of Adria, which gave the sea its name, now lie about 20 km from the sea?
a: The Po and Adige have pushed the coast out with sediments.
Sea level has fallen sharply since Roman times.
An earthquake moved the town inland.
The town was rebuilt further inland in the Middle Ages.
60604.e: In ancient times Adria was an important port. Since then the rivers have deposited so much material that the coast has moved far to the east.
60604.m: River sediments have cut the town of Adria off from the sea.

60605.q: Which strait links the Adriatic with the Ionian Sea?
60605.e: The Strait of Otranto lies between Apulia and Albania and is about 70 km wide. Water is exchanged with the Mediterranean through it.
60605.m: The Strait of Otranto is the gateway to the Adriatic.

60606.q: Why is the northern Adriatic particularly shallow and warm in summer?
a: It is a flooded part of the Po Valley, mostly less than 50 m deep.
Warm water flows in from the Red Sea there.
It is separated from the open sea by dams.
60606.e: The northern part lies on the continental shelf and therefore warms up quickly. In the south, by contrast, the Adriatic is over 1200 m deep.
60606.m: The northern Adriatic is shallow and therefore warms up quickly.

60607.q: How were the long chains of islands parallel to the coast off Dalmatia formed?
a: Parallel mountain ridges were partly flooded after the Ice Age
Volcanoes formed a chain of islands
Glaciers pushed moraines out to sea
60607.e: Mountain ridges there run parallel to the coast and were partly flooded after the Ice Age. The ridges now stick out of the sea as long islands. This is called the Dalmatian type of coast.
60607.m: On the Dalmatian coast the islands lie parallel to the mainland.

60608.q: What is the bay between Istria and the Croatian mainland, with the islands of Krk and Cres, called?
60608.e: The port city of Rijeka also lies on the Kvarner Gulf. Krk is linked to the mainland by a bridge.
60608.m: The islands of Krk and Cres lie in the Kvarner Gulf.

60609.q: What is the natural sloshing of the Adriatic's water level called, which together with the sirocco can make floods in Venice worse?
60609.e: In a seiche the water sloshes back and forth in the long Adriatic basin, rather like in a bathtub. If this coincides with high tide and a south wind, the water in Venice rises especially high.
60609.m: A seiche makes the water of the Adriatic slosh back and forth.

60610.q: The Adriatic port of Ancona has a Greek name. What does that tell us about its history?
a: It was founded by Greek settlers
It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire
The Greek alphabet was invented there
60610.e: Greek settlers named the place after the curved headland Ankon, which means “elbow”. Today Ancona is an important ferry port for Croatia and Greece.
60610.m: Ancona was founded by the Greeks.

60611.q: Which Adriatic port was the end point of the Roman Via Appia?
60611.e: The Via Appia ran from Rome via Capua to Brindisi. From there people crossed over to Greece.
60611.m: The Via Appia ended in Brindisi.

60612.q: What is the continuation of the North Atlantic Current that flows north along the Norwegian coast called?
60612.e: Off Scandinavia the North Atlantic Current continues as the Norwegian Current. It carries warm Atlantic water far into the Arctic.
60612.m: The Norwegian Current carries Atlantic warmth north along the coast of Norway.

60613.q: Which ocean current branches south from the North Atlantic Current and flows along Portugal and north-west Africa?
60613.e: Part of the water turns south off Europe and flows as the relatively cool Canary Current off north-west Africa. This closes the subtropical gyre of the North Atlantic.
60613.m: The Canary Current is the cool southern branch that closes the North Atlantic circuit.

60614.q: What mainly drives the North Atlantic Current?
a: Westerly winds and differences in temperature and salt content
The water of Europe's large rivers
60614.e: Westerly winds push the surface water north-east. In addition, cold, salty water sinks in the north and draws warm water after it.
60614.m: Wind and differences in temperature and salt keep the North Atlantic Current going.

60615.q: Why does the west coast of Svalbard stay free of ice longer in winter than the east coast?
a: An offshoot of warm Atlantic water flows north there
Hot volcanic springs warm the sea there
The sun shines longer there in winter
Strong storms prevent any ice forming there
60615.e: The West Spitsbergen Current is the northernmost offshoot of the North Atlantic Current. It brings warmth to the west coast, while the east side is shaped by cold polar water.
60615.m: Warm Atlantic water keeps the west coast of Svalbard free of ice for longer.

60616.q: Why are winters in Reykjavík milder than in Helsinki, even though Reykjavík lies further north?
a: A branch of the North Atlantic Current brings warm water to Iceland's coast
The long summer days store heat into the winter
Greenland protects Iceland from all cold winds
Iceland lies higher above sea level than Finland
60616.e: The Irminger Current, a branch of the North Atlantic Current, flows around the south and west of Iceland. Helsinki, on the other hand, is influenced by the cold continental climate.
60616.m: Warm Atlantic water makes the winters on Iceland's coast mild.

60617.q: What is the cold, salty water mass called that forms when the water of the North Atlantic Current sinks in the far north?
60617.e: In the Nordic Seas and the Labrador Sea the salty water cools, becomes denser and sinks. This forms North Atlantic Deep Water, which flows south at depth.
60617.m: North Atlantic Deep Water is cooled surface water that sinks in the north.

60618.q: Why is it especially often foggy off Newfoundland, where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current?
a: Warm, moist air cools over cold water
Volcanoes release a lot of steam there
The sea is especially low in salt there
60618.e: When moist air moves from the warm water over the cold water of the Labrador Current, it cools below the dew point. This creates advection fog, for which the Grand Banks of Newfoundland are notorious.
60618.m: Fog often forms over the Grand Banks because warm sea air cools over cold water.

60619.q: Why can even palm trees grow outdoors on the north-west coast of Scotland?
a: The North Atlantic Current gives mild, almost frost-free winters
The summers there are hotter than on the Mediterranean
Warm winds from the Sahara reach the coast
The ground is warmed by volcanoes
60619.e: The warm water of the North Atlantic Current greatly softens the winters on Scotland's west coast. That is why plants from all over the world grow in gardens such as Inverewe, even though the coast lies at almost 58 degrees north.
60619.m: The North Atlantic Current makes Scotland's coast surprisingly mild.

60620.q: What is the striking zone south of Greenland called, where the sea has hardly warmed or has even cooled, against the worldwide trend?
60620.e: Many researchers interpret the “Cold Blob” in the subpolar North Atlantic as a possible sign that the Atlantic overturning circulation is weakening. Less warm water then reaches the north.
60620.m: The Cold Blob south of Greenland is seen as a possible warning sign of a weaker Atlantic circulation.

60621.q: Between which mountain ranges is the mistral speeded up in the Rhône Valley as if through a nozzle?
60621.e: The mistral flows through the gap between the foothills of the Alps and the Cévennes on the edge of the Massif Central. The narrowing speeds up the air as if through a nozzle.
60621.m: In the Rhône Valley the mistral is speeded up between the Alps and the Cévennes as if through a nozzle.

60622.q: Which pattern of air pressure typically sets off a mistral?
a: High over the Bay of Biscay, low over the Gulf of Genoa
Low over the Bay of Biscay, high over the Gulf of Genoa
High over Russia, low over Iceland
Low over the Sahara, high over Scandinavia
60622.e: When there is a high over the Bay of Biscay and a low around the Gulf of Genoa, cold air flows from the north to the Mediterranean. A passing cold front often strengthens the mistral further.
60622.m: A high over Biscay and a low near Genoa set the mistral going.

60623.q: In which seasons does the mistral occur most often?
60623.e: The mistral is most frequent and strongest in winter and spring, but it can blow in any season. It often lasts from one to several days.
60623.m: The mistral blows mainly in winter and spring.

60624.q: What does the name “mistral” originally mean in Occitan?
60624.e: The name comes from the Languedoc dialect of Occitan and means “masterly”. It goes back to the Latin “magistralis”.
60624.m: The mistral is named the “masterly” wind.

60625.q: What effect does a strong mistral have on the water temperature in the Gulf of Lion?
a: It falls because cold deep water rises
It rises because warm air heats the sea
It stays the same because the wind blows only over land
It rises because river water is added
60625.e: The offshore wind pushes the warm surface water out to sea. Colder water rises from the depths to replace it, and the sea near the coast cools noticeably.
60625.m: The mistral drives warm surface water away, so cold deep water rises.

60626.q: Because of the mistral, which way do traditional Provençal farmhouses (mas) usually face?
a: With the gable towards the wind
60626.e: The mas turn their backs to the north wind and open towards the south. The north side usually has only a few small windows.
60626.m: Provençal farmhouses face south and turn their backs on the mistral.

60627.q: Which trees did farmers in the Rhône Valley plant in long rows as protection against the mistral?
60627.e: Dense rows of cypresses slow down the wind and protect fields and gardens. They still shape the landscape of Provence today.
60627.m: Cypress hedges protect the fields in the Rhône Valley from the mistral.

60628.q: Why do many church towers in Provence have open wrought-iron frames instead of closed belfries?
a: So that the mistral can blow through freely
So that the bells can be stolen more easily
Because there is no stone in Provence
Because iron has a cooling effect in summer
60628.e: The open wrought-iron frames give the wind little surface to push against. So the tower is put under less strain in a strong mistral.
60628.m: Open iron frames on Provençal towers let the mistral blow through.

60629.q: Which painter complained in letters from Arles that the mistral made painting outdoors difficult?
60629.e: Van Gogh lived in Provence in 1888 and 1889 and often painted outdoors. In his letters he described how the mistral shook his easel.
60629.m: Van Gogh had to battle the mistral while painting in Provence.

60630.q: Why does the bora arrive cold at the coast despite descending, while the foehn becomes warm as it descends?
a: The starting air is so cold that the warming is not enough
The bora keeps rising as it blows
The sea cools the air beforehand
The bora blows only at night without sun
60630.e: The bora also warms up dry-adiabatically as it descends. But the cold air from inland is so cold that it still reaches the Adriatic as a cold wind.
60630.m: The bora stays cold because its starting air is very cold, despite warming as it descends.

60631.q: In which port city are ropes or chains put up along some steep streets to hold on to during a strong bora?
60631.e: In Trieste gusts of the bora often exceed 120 km/h, and in extreme cases reach almost 200 km/h. That is why chains are sometimes put up along the pavements.
60631.m: In Trieste pedestrians hold on to chains during a strong bora.

60632.q: Which Croatian coastal mountain range, about 145 kilometres long, is regarded as one of the strongest bora zones?
60632.e: Velebit separates the continental interior from the coast. Near Senj and Karlobag the bora reaches extreme speeds.
60632.m: At Velebit the bora rushes down to the Adriatic especially violently.

60633.q: What do people in Trieste call the bora when there is high pressure and a clear sky?
60633.e: The “clear bora” occurs with high pressure and a cloudless sky. The “dark bora” (bora scura) comes with low pressure, clouds and often rain or snow.
60633.m: The bora chiara blows with high pressure under a clear sky.

60634.q: Which Greek wind god is the name bora linguistically related to?
60634.e: Bora goes back to the Greek Boreas, the god of the north wind. The Croatian word “bura”, on the other hand, comes from a Slavic word for storm.
60634.m: The name bora is related to Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind.

60635.q: In which season does the bora occur most often?
60635.e: The bora needs very cold air inland behind the mountains. That is why it is most frequent in winter, when it blows in violent gusts.
60635.m: The bora is mainly a winter wind.

60636.q: Why are bridges and coast roads in Croatia often closed during a strong bora?
a: Hurricane-force gusts can blow vehicles over
The bora always brings thick fog
The bora makes the sea rise over the roads
The bora brings heat that melts the road surface
60636.e: Bora gusts often exceed 150 km/h, and 248 km/h was even measured at the Maslenica Bridge. This is life-threatening for lorries, caravans and motorbikes.
60636.m: During a strong bora, bridges and roads on the Adriatic are closed.

60637.q: What do you call a wind like the bora that rushes down from mountains to the coast?
60637.e: In a downslope wind, air flows over a mountain ridge and rushes down the other side. The foehn is also a downslope wind, but it arrives warm.
60637.m: The bora is a cold downslope wind.

60638.q: What is the bora said to have done on the island of Pag during the cold wave of February 2012?
a: Thrown fish out of the sea
60638.e: During the 2012 cold wave the bora on Pag was so strong that, according to reports, it threw fish out of the sea onto land. The island is completely exposed to the bora.
60638.m: On Pag the bora shows its strength especially impressively.

60639.q: What draws the sirocco from North Africa northwards across the Mediterranean?
a: Lows moving east across the Mediterranean
The Azores High over the Atlantic
60639.e: Low-pressure areas moving east suck hot desert air northwards on their front side. The air then flows anticlockwise around the low towards southern Europe.
60639.m: The sirocco is drawn north by lows over the Mediterranean.

60640.q: Why is the sirocco in southern Italy usually damp and humid, even though it comes from the desert?
a: It picks up moisture over the Mediterranean
It brings rain from the Sahara
It forms over the Alpine glaciers
60640.e: In North Africa the sirocco is dry and dusty. On its way across the Mediterranean it picks up a lot of water vapour, so it reaches southern Italy as a warm, damp wind.
60640.m: The sirocco becomes damp over the Mediterranean and arrives humid in southern Europe.

60641.q: What is the sirocco called on the Croatian Adriatic coast?
60641.e: In Croatia the warm, damp south-east wind is called jugo, which means “south”. It often brings high seas and rain.
60641.m: On the Croatian coast the sirocco is called jugo.

60642.q: Which phenomenon in Venice gets worse when the sirocco pushes water into the northern Adriatic?
60642.e: The south-east wind piles the water up northwards in the long, narrow Adriatic. If this coincides with high tide, the lagoon city is flooded.
60642.m: Together with high tide, the sirocco can cause acqua alta in Venice.

60643.q: Which Arabic word does the name sirocco go back to?
60643.e: The name comes from the Arabic “šurūq”, which is related to “aš-šarq” (the east). Seen from Italy, the wind blows from the south-east.
60643.m: The name sirocco comes from an Arabic word for east.

60644.q: What is rain coloured reddish by Saharan sand from the sirocco called in southern Italy?
60644.e: The sirocco carries fine red desert dust with it. When this falls with raindrops, it is called blood rain.
60644.m: Saharan dust in rain colours so-called blood rain reddish.

60645.q: What can sometimes be seen on the snow in the Swiss Alps after sirocco conditions?
60645.e: South winds carry Saharan dust across the Mediterranean as far as the Alps. The dust colours the snow yellowish to reddish and makes it melt faster.
60645.m: After south winds, Saharan dust colours Alpine snow yellowish to reddish.

60646.q: In which seasons does the sirocco blow most often?
60646.e: The sirocco is most frequent in spring and autumn. That is when low-pressure areas most often move across the Mediterranean and suck hot desert air northwards.
60646.m: The sirocco blows most often in spring and autumn.

60647.q: What does the Egyptian name “khamsin” for a hot, dusty desert wind mean?
60647.e: Khamsin means “fifty” in Arabic. The name refers to the period of about fifty days in spring when this wind can occur in Egypt.
60647.m: The khamsin is named after the roughly fifty days in which it can blow.

60648.q: From which original vegetation did the maquis in the Mediterranean mostly develop?
60648.e: Slash-and-burn clearing, grazing and logging have destroyed the evergreen forests of holm oak since ancient times. In their place grew the evergreen scrub of the maquis.
60648.m: The maquis mostly replaces cleared holm oak forests.

60649.q: What is the low, open rocky heath that develops from the maquis through even heavier overuse called in France?
60649.e: With intensive grazing and soil erosion, the maquis turns into a low, often stony heath. In France it is called garrigue.
60649.m: The garrigue is a more degraded, lower form of the maquis.

60650.q: Which herbs typically grow wild in the low rocky heath of the Mediterranean?
60650.e: The rocky heath is called garrigue in France and phrygana in Greece. Its plants contain fragrant essential oils that protect them from drying out and from being eaten by animals.
60650.m: Thyme, rosemary and lavender scent the Mediterranean rocky heath.

60651.q: How have many maquis plants adapted to frequent fires?
a: They sprout again from the rootstock after the fire
They have especially thick, wet leaves
They grow only in damp gorges
60651.e: Many shrubs such as tree heath sprout again from the rootstock after a fire. The seeds of rock roses even germinate especially well after a fire.
60651.m: Many maquis plants survive fires and sprout again afterwards.

60652.q: What is the shrub vegetation similar to the maquis in California's Mediterranean climate called?
60652.e: Like the Mediterranean, California has dry summers and wet winters. Chaparral, an evergreen scrub with hard leaves, grows there.
60652.m: The chaparral is California's counterpart to the maquis.

60653.q: Why do maquis, chaparral and fynbos look similar, even though they share hardly any species?
a: Because of convergent evolution under a similar climate
Because all the species come from the same continent
Because they grow on the same rock
60653.e: Similar climates with dry summers have produced similar adaptations independently of one another. This is called convergent evolution.
60653.m: The same climate makes similar-looking plants develop on different continents.

60654.q: Which maquis shrub bears red, round fruits that look like strawberries?
60654.e: The strawberry tree is a typical woody plant of the maquis. Its red, warty fruits are edible and ripen in autumn and winter.
60654.m: The strawberry tree is a typical maquis shrub.

60655.q: What were the French resistance fighters who hid in the scrubland during the Second World War called?
60655.e: The French word for this scrub is “maquis”. Because fighters of the Résistance often hid in this scrubland, they were called maquisards.
60655.m: The maquisards of the Résistance are named after the French word for maquis scrub.

60656.q: How tall do the evergreen shrubs of the maquis usually grow?
60656.e: The shrubs of the maquis usually reach 1 to 3 metres. Scrub woodland that has developed from overused oak forests can grow 3 to 5 metres high.
60656.m: The maquis is dense scrub usually one to three metres high.

60657.q: Which Köppen climate type applies to the whole of Ireland?
60657.e: Cfb stands for a temperate climate that is wet all year with warm but not hot summers. It is the typical oceanic climate of Western Europe.
60657.m: Ireland has an oceanic climate of Köppen type Cfb.

60658.q: Roughly how much rain falls on Valentia Island on the west coast compared with Dublin?
60658.e: Valentia gets about 1400 mm a year, Dublin only about 714 mm. The moist westerly winds drop their rain first on the west coast.
60658.m: Ireland's west coast is almost twice as wet as Dublin.

60659.q: Why is Dublin drier than the west coast of Ireland?
a: It lies in the lee of the westerly winds and the mountains
It is closer to the equator
A desert wind dries out the east coast
The Irish Sea is frozen there
60659.e: The rain-bearing winds usually come from the Atlantic in the west. By the time they reach the east coast, they have already lost much of their moisture over mountains and hills.
60659.m: Ireland's east coast lies in the rain shadow of the westerly winds.

60660.q: Which Canadian place lies at almost the same latitude as Dublin but has a January average far below minus 10 degrees?
60660.e: Goose Bay in Labrador lies, like Dublin, at about 53 degrees north. Without a warm ocean current and with cold continental air, the winters there are much harsher.
60660.m: The same latitude does not mean the same climate, as Dublin and Goose Bay show.

60661.q: Which plant, originally from South America, grows wild in long hedges in Kerry and West Cork?
60661.e: Fuchsia thrives in the mild, damp and almost frost-free winters of south-west Ireland. It lines many roads there with red flowers.
60661.m: Fuchsia hedges in south-west Ireland show how mild the winters are.

60662.q: Which type of bog covers large areas of western Ireland because of the high rainfall?
60662.e: Blanket bogs form where it rains so often that peat spreads over the whole landscape like a blanket. They need a very wet, cool climate.
60662.m: Blanket bogs form only in very rainy climates such as western Ireland.

60663.q: Which former hurricane hit Ireland with severe storm-force gusts in October 2017?
60663.e: Ophelia had become a strong hurricane unusually far east in the Atlantic. As a storm it hit Ireland on 16 October 2017 and caused deaths.
60663.m: Ex-hurricane Ophelia hit Ireland with full force in 2017.

60664.q: Why are very low winter temperatures extremely rare in Ireland?
a: The surrounding sea has a balancing effect
Ireland lies at the latitude of North Africa
The island is almost completely forested
Hot springs warm the whole island
60664.e: The sea stores heat and releases it in winter. That is why Ireland's record low is only -19.1 °C, measured in 1881 at Markree Castle in County Sligo.
60664.m: Thanks to the sea, Ireland hardly ever gets extremely cold.

60665.q: Why do summers in Ireland rarely get very hot?
a: The cool Atlantic and frequent westerly winds dampen the heat
Ireland lies north of the Arctic Circle
High mountains keep the warm air away
Constant east winds from Siberia cool the island
60665.e: The air over Ireland usually comes from the Atlantic and is rather cool and damp in summer. That is why the heat record is only 33.3 °C, measured in 1887 at Kilkenny Castle.
60665.m: The Atlantic keeps Irish summers mild.

60666.q: Which Köppen climate type applies to Moscow?
60666.e: Dfb stands for a cold temperate climate that is wet all year with warm summers and cold winters. It is typical of the interior of Eastern Europe.
60666.m: Moscow has a continental climate of Köppen type Dfb.

60667.q: Roughly how big is the difference in Moscow between the average of the coldest and the warmest month?
60667.e: January in Moscow averages about -6 °C, and July about 19 °C. An annual range of about 25 degrees is typically continental.
60667.m: In the continental climate of Eastern Europe, summer and winter are far apart.

60668.q: Which winter high-pressure area often brings Eastern Europe icy cold air from the east?
60668.e: In winter the air over the Asian mainland cools sharply and the Siberian High forms. Its western edge steers icy east winds towards Eastern Europe.
60668.m: The Siberian High sends icy air to Eastern Europe in winter.

60669.q: In which season does most rain fall in the continental climate of Eastern Europe?
60669.e: In summer the land heats up strongly, the air rises, and showers and thunderstorms form. In winter, by contrast, the cold air is dry.
60669.m: In a continental climate it rains most in summer.

60670.q: What is the time in spring and autumn called in Russia when roads and fields sink into mud?
60670.e: When the snow melts and in the rainy autumn, unpaved roads turn soft. The rasputitsa often made travel and military campaigns almost impossible.
60670.m: The rasputitsa is the mud season in Russia.

60671.q: What is the transition zone between broadleaf forest and grassy steppe in Ukraine and southern Russia called?
60671.e: In the forest steppe, islands of forest alternate with grassland. Towards the south it gets drier, and the forest gives way to open steppe.
60671.m: The forest steppe forms the transition from forest to steppe.

60672.q: Which vegetation belt lies north of the mixed forest in Russia?
60672.e: With shorter summers and longer, colder winters, conifers dominate north of the mixed forest. This boreal coniferous forest is called the taiga.
60672.m: North of the mixed forest in Russia the taiga begins.

60673.q: What natural vegetation originally covered large parts of southern Ukraine?
60673.e: In the dry, continental south of Ukraine there is not enough rain for dense forests. Grassy steppe originally grew there, most of which is now farmland.
60673.m: Southern Ukraine was originally a steppe region.

60674.q: Why is the growing season in Eastern Europe shorter than in Western Europe at the same latitude?
a: The winters are longer and colder
The summers are cooler and wetter
The sun is lower in the sky there
60674.e: Without the softening influence of the Atlantic, frosty periods last longer in the east. So plants can grow for fewer months of the year.
60674.m: Long, cold winters shorten the growing season in Eastern Europe.

60675.q: Where was the European heat record of 48.8 degrees measured on 11 August 2021?
60675.e: A station at Floridia near Syracuse measured 48.8 °C. The World Meteorological Organization recognised the value as the European record.
60675.m: The European heat record of 48.8 degrees was measured in Sicily in 2021.

60676.q: According to common estimates, how many deaths did the 2003 heatwave cause in Europe?
60676.e: Studies estimate the number of extra deaths at more than 70,000. Older people in Italy, France and Spain were especially affected.
60676.m: The 2003 heatwave cost over 70,000 people their lives in Europe.

60677.q: Where was the Swiss heat record of 41.5 degrees measured during the 2003 heatwave (as of 2026)?
60677.e: Grono in the Mesolcina valley (Grisons) reached 41.5 °C on 11 August 2003. This is still the highest value ever measured in Switzerland (as of 2026).
60677.m: The Swiss heat record of 41.5 degrees comes from Grono.

60678.q: Which weather pattern often causes long-lasting heatwaves in southern Europe?
a: A blocking high, as in an omega block
A series of fast-moving Atlantic lows
A stable Icelandic low over Spain
60678.e: A blocking high stays in place for days and steers lows around it. Sinking air warms up, and the sun heats the ground further.
60678.m: Blocking highs hold heatwaves in place for days.

60679.q: From what minimum temperature do meteorologists speak of a tropical night?
60679.e: A tropical night is when the temperature does not fall below 20 °C at night. Many such nights are a strain on health because the body cannot recover.
60679.m: In a tropical night it stays at least 20 degrees warm.

60680.q: Which sight in Athens was closed to visitors in the afternoon in July 2023 because of extreme heat?
60680.e: With temperatures above 40 °C, the Greek authorities closed the Acropolis during the hottest hours. This was to protect visitors and staff.
60680.m: Because of extreme heat, even the Acropolis was closed at times in 2023.

60681.q: Why do big cities such as Athens cool down less on hot nights than the surrounding countryside?
a: Because of the urban heat island effect
Because they are near the Arctic Circle
Because there are more forests there
Because of the cooling sea breeze
60681.e: Asphalt, concrete and dense buildings store heat during the day and release it at night. There is also a lack of vegetation that cools through evaporation.
60681.m: Cities form heat islands that hardly cool down at night.

60682.q: Why are heat records in Spain usually measured inland, for example near Córdoba, and not on the coast?
a: Because the sea dampens the heat on the coast
Because the interior is closer to the equator
Because it rains more often inland in summer
Because a foehn from the Pyrenees blows there all the time
60682.e: Water warms up more slowly than land and evens out temperatures. Inland this influence is missing. So in 2021 La Rambla near Córdoba measured 47.6 °C, the Spanish record.
60682.m: In Spain it gets hottest far from the sea.

60683.q: Which region of Portugal is regarded as particularly hot and dry?
60683.e: The Alentejo in the south of the interior has very hot, dry summers. Amareleja measured 47.3 °C on 1 August 2003.
60683.m: The Alentejo is one of the hottest regions in Europe.

60684.q: On which Greek island did thousands of holidaymakers have to be evacuated in July 2023 because of forest fires during a heatwave?
60684.e: After days of heat, large forest fires spread on Rhodes. Thousands of tourists had to leave their hotels, and some were taken to safety by boat.
60684.m: Heat and drought caused devastating forest fires on Rhodes in 2023.

60685.q: According to a 2022 study, which high-pressure area has expanded more than at any time in 1200 years, drying out the Iberian Peninsula?
60685.e: An expanded Azores High steers the winter rain lows away to the north. The study in “Nature Geoscience” linked this development with climate change.
60685.m: An expanded Azores High keeps the winter rain away from the Iberian Peninsula.

60686.q: What sometimes appears in Spanish reservoirs during extreme drought?
60686.e: Many reservoirs were created in the 20th century and flooded villages. In the drought years of 2019 and 2022, for example, the Dolmen of Guadalperal, the “Spanish Stonehenge”, reappeared.
60686.m: In droughts, sunken buildings emerge from Spain's reservoirs.

60687.q: Which building became almost completely visible in the Catalan reservoir of Sau during the 2023 drought?
60687.e: The church of Sant Romà de Sau stood in a village that the reservoir flooded in the 1960s. With the water level low, it was almost completely dry in 2023.
60687.m: The church in the Sau reservoir became a symbol of the drought in Catalonia.

60688.q: Which Spanish region declared a state of emergency because of drought in February 2024, which also affected Barcelona?
60688.e: The reservoirs in Catalonia had fallen to historically low levels. With the drought emergency, water use in and around Barcelona was restricted.
60688.m: Catalonia had to declare a state of emergency because of drought in 2024.

60689.q: Which wetland in Andalusia is suffering from falling groundwater, partly because of wells for strawberry farming?
60689.e: Doñana National Park is one of the most important wetlands in Europe. Drought and partly illegal water extraction for farming are making many lagoons dry up.
60689.m: Doñana is drying out through drought and overuse of groundwater.

60690.q: What is the canal system called that carries water from the Tagus to the dry south-east of Spain?
60690.e: Since 1979, water from the upper Tagus has been carried into the Segura basin to Murcia and Alicante. In drought years the transfer is politically very controversial.
60690.m: The Tagus-Segura transfer brings water to Spain's dry south-east.

60691.q: With which technique do Spanish coastal cities such as Barcelona try to secure their water supply during drought?
60691.e: Desalination plants produce drinking water from seawater, usually by reverse osmosis. They supply water regardless of rain, but need a lot of energy.
60691.m: Seawater desalination makes coastal cities less dependent on rain.

60692.q: Which product became much more expensive worldwide in 2023, mainly because of drought and heat in Spain?
60692.e: Spain is the world's largest producer of olive oil. After two years of drought the harvest collapsed, and prices rose to record levels.
60692.m: Drought in Spain made olive oil prices rise sharply in 2023.

60693.q: Why do Spain and Portugal need an agreement about rivers such as the Tagus and Douro?
a: The rivers rise in Spain and then flow through Portugal
The rivers form the border with France
Portugal supplies Spain with drinking water by ship
Spain has no rivers of its own
60693.e: The Tagus, Douro and Guadiana rise in Spain and then reach Portugal. The Albufeira Convention of 1998 sets out how much water Spain must let through, even in drought years.
60693.m: Spain and Portugal share large rivers and regulate their water by agreement.

60694.q: Which gas in the upper atmosphere produces the common green aurora?
60694.e: Excited oxygen atoms give off light with a wavelength of 557.7 nanometres. This green is the most common colour of the aurora.
60694.m: Green auroras come from excited oxygen.

60695.q: Why do red auroras appear mainly at very great heights?
a: The air there is so thin that excited oxygen can give off red light
The oxygen there is warmer and glows
60695.e: For red light, an oxygen atom must stay excited for a long time. Only in very thin air does it avoid colliding with other particles during this time.
60695.m: Red auroras form in the very thin air of the uppermost atmosphere.

60696.q: What is the ring-shaped area around the magnetic pole where auroras are most frequent called?
60696.e: The auroral oval lies roughly between 65 and 75 degrees magnetic latitude. When solar activity is strong, it expands southwards.
60696.m: Auroras occur mainly in the auroral oval around the magnetic pole.

60697.q: Which index do aurora forecasts use to give the strength of geomagnetic activity?
60697.e: The Kp index runs from 0 to 9 and measures disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field. The higher the value, the further south auroras can be seen.
60697.m: A high Kp index shows that auroras may be visible far to the south.

60698.q: In which month in 2024 were auroras clearly visible over Switzerland too, after an extreme solar storm?
60698.e: On 10 and 11 May 2024 a very strong geomagnetic storm hit the Earth. Auroras could be seen as far as southern and central Europe, including Switzerland.
60698.m: In May 2024 auroras even lit up the sky over Switzerland.

60699.q: Roughly how long does a sunspot cycle last, which affects how often auroras occur?
60699.e: Solar activity varies in a cycle of about 11 years. Around the maximum there are more solar storms and therefore more auroras.
60699.m: Auroras become more frequent at the maximum of the roughly eleven-year solar cycle.

60700.q: What could a solar storm like the one in 1859 mainly damage today?
60700.e: The solar storm of 1859 disrupted telegraph lines worldwide. Today strong currents would mainly endanger power grids, satellites and radio links.
60700.m: Strong solar storms threaten power grids and satellites.

60701.q: Which place in Swedish Lapland is known among aurora fans for an often cloud-free “blue hole”?
60701.e: Abisko lies in the rain shadow of the mountains by Lake Torneträsk. That is why the sky there is often clear, even when there are clouds all around.
60701.m: Thanks to its often clear sky, Abisko is an aurora hotspot.

60702.q: Why can you hardly see auroras in northern Scandinavia in summer?
a: Because it does not get properly dark at night
Because the sun sends out no particles in summer
Because the Earth's magnetic field is weaker in summer
Because auroras only form when there is frost
60702.e: Auroras happen all year round. But in summer the sky in the far north is too bright to see them because of the midnight sun.
60702.m: You can only see auroras when the sky is dark.

60703.q: Roughly at what latitude is the Arctic Circle?
60703.e: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66 degrees 34 minutes north. North of it, the sun does not set at least once a year.
60703.m: North of the Arctic Circle at about 66.6 degrees there is the midnight sun.

60704.q: Why can the midnight sun also be seen a little south of the Arctic Circle?
a: Because of the refraction of light in the atmosphere
Because of reflection from sea ice
Because of the Earth's orbit around the sun
60704.e: The atmosphere bends light near the horizon, and the sun's disc has a certain size. That is why the sun stays visible up to about 80 to 100 kilometres south of the Arctic Circle.
60704.m: Because of refraction, the midnight sun reaches a little south of the Arctic Circle.

a: The tilt of the Earth's axis of about 23.4 degrees
The flattening of the Earth at the poles
60705.e: Because the Earth's axis is tilted, the northern hemisphere faces the sun in summer. Near the pole the sun then stays above the horizon around the clock.
60705.m: The midnight sun is caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis.

60706.q: Roughly for how long does the sun not set in Longyearbyen on Svalbard in summer?
60706.e: Longyearbyen lies at about 78 degrees north. The midnight sun lasts there from about mid-April to the end of August.
60706.m: The closer to the pole, the longer the midnight sun lasts.

60707.q: Near which Finnish town does the Arctic Circle run right through the well-known Santa Claus Village?
60707.e: Rovaniemi is the capital of Lapland. On the northern edge of the town the Arctic Circle line is marked and is a popular spot for photos.
60707.m: Near Rovaniemi you can walk across the Arctic Circle.

60708.q: Which part of Iceland lies north of the Arctic Circle?
a: Only part of the small island of Grímsey
The whole northern half of the island
About a third of the country
60708.e: Iceland's main island lies entirely south of the Arctic Circle. Only Grímsey, about 40 kilometres off the north coast, is crossed by the Arctic Circle.
60708.m: Only the island of Grímsey lies partly north of the Arctic Circle in Iceland.

60709.q: What are the bright summer nights called in St Petersburg, where there is no midnight sun?
60709.e: St Petersburg lies at about 60 degrees north, south of the Arctic Circle. The sun sets briefly, but it does not get properly dark.
60709.m: In St Petersburg there are White Nights in summer instead of the midnight sun.

60710.q: Why is the Arctic Circle slowly shifting?
a: Because the tilt of the Earth's axis is changing slightly
Because the Earth is rotating more and more slowly
Because the polar ice is melting
60710.e: The tilt of the Earth's axis varies over thousands of years and is currently slowly decreasing. As a result, the Arctic Circle moves about 14.5 metres north every year.
60710.m: The Arctic Circle moves because the tilt of the Earth's axis changes.

60711.q: Which European capital lies furthest north?
60711.e: Reykjavík lies at about 64 degrees north, a good two degrees south of the Arctic Circle. There is no midnight sun there, but in June it hardly gets dark at night.
60711.m: Reykjavík is the northernmost capital in Europe.

60712.q: Between which two lithospheric plates does Iceland lie?
60712.e: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates are drifting apart. As a result the island gets about 2 centimetres wider every year.
60712.m: Iceland is slowly being torn apart by two plates drifting away from each other.

60713.q: Which combination explains Iceland's particularly strong volcanic activity?
60713.e: Under Iceland a spreading mid-ocean ridge meets a hot mantle plume (hotspot). This combination supplies especially large amounts of magma, which is why Iceland rises above sea level.
60713.m: Iceland owes its existence to a hotspot right on an ocean ridge.

60714.q: Roughly what share of homes in Iceland are heated with geothermal heat?
60714.e: About nine out of ten households in Iceland are heated through district heating networks fed by geothermal energy. Reykjavík also gets its heating water from hot springs and boreholes.
60714.m: Almost all homes in Iceland are heated with geothermal energy.

60715.q: Roughly how is Iceland's electricity generated?
60715.e: Iceland generates practically all its electricity from renewable sources: about seven tenths from the hydropower of glacial rivers and almost a third from geothermal energy. A lot of electricity goes to energy-hungry aluminium smelters.
60715.m: Iceland's electricity comes almost entirely from hydropower and geothermal energy.

60716.q: Where does the water of the famous “Blue Lagoon” on the Reykjanes peninsula come from?
a: From the Svartsengi geothermal power station
60716.e: The Blue Lagoon is fed by the salty, mineral-rich waste water of the neighbouring Svartsengi geothermal power station. The milky blue colour comes from dissolved silica.
60716.m: The Blue Lagoon is a by-product of using geothermal energy.

60717.q: Which spouting spring in Haukadalur gave all the geysers in the world their name?
60717.e: The “Great Geysir” in Haukadalur has been known since the Middle Ages; its name comes from the Icelandic verb “geysa” (to gush). Today it is mostly quiet, while neighbouring Strokkur erupts every few minutes.
60717.m: The word geyser comes from Icelandic.

60718.q: What was the consequence of the eruption of the Laki fissure in 1783 and 1784?
a: A famine in which about a fifth of Icelanders died
The formation of the island of Surtsey
The destruction of the capital, Reykjavík
The melting of the Vatnajökull glacier
60718.e: The Laki fissure eruption released huge amounts of fluorine and sulphur gases; grazing animals died, and in the famine that followed (Móðuharðindin) about a fifth to a quarter of the population died. The sulphur haze also affected the weather across Europe.
60718.m: The Laki eruption caused the worst famine in Icelandic history.

60719.q: Which island formed from 1963 through an undersea eruption off the south coast of Iceland?
60719.e: Surtsey grew out of the sea from 1963 to 1967 and has since been an open-air laboratory for how plants and animals colonise new land. Since 2008 the island has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site and closed to visitors.
60719.m: Surtsey shows how life conquers a brand-new island.

60720.q: How did helpers on Heimaey in 1973 try to keep the lava of the Eldfell volcano away from the harbour?
a: They cooled the lava with pumped seawater
They blew up the crater with dynamite
60720.e: Powerful pumps sprayed millions of tonnes of seawater onto the lava front until it solidified. As a result the important fishing harbour was saved and was even better protected.
60720.m: On Heimaey lava was slowed down with water on a scale never seen before.

60721.q: Which ancient towns were buried in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
60721.e: The eruption buried Pompeii under pumice and ash and Herculaneum under pyroclastic deposits; Stabiae was also hit. The excavations give a unique insight into Roman everyday life.
60721.m: Vesuvius preserved Pompeii for almost two thousand years.

60722.q: Who is the “Plinian” type of eruption named after?
60722.e: Pliny the Younger described the eruption of AD 79 in two letters to Tacitus, including the pine-tree-shaped eruption column. Highly explosive eruptions with a tall ash column are named after him today.
60722.m: An eyewitness account gave the Plinian eruption its name.

60723.q: Which Roman scholar and fleet commander died at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
60723.e: Pliny the Elder, author of the “Natural History”, set out with the fleet from Misenum to rescue people and observe the eruption. He died on the coast near Stabiae.
60723.m: Pliny the Elder paid for his curiosity about Vesuvius with his life.

60724.q: Which type of volcano is Vesuvius?
60724.e: Vesuvius is built up from alternating layers of lava and ash, which is typical of a stratovolcano. Its thick, gas-rich magma often leads to explosive eruptions.
60724.m: Stratovolcanoes like Vesuvius usually erupt explosively.

60725.q: What is the older, semicircular crater rim that surrounds today's cone of Vesuvius to the north called?
60725.e: Monte Somma is the remains of an older, collapsed volcano, in whose caldera the younger cone of Vesuvius grew. That is why volcanoes of this shape are called Somma volcanoes.
60725.m: Vesuvius is a volcano inside the crater of an older volcano.

60726.q: What killed most of the victims in Herculaneum during the eruption of AD 79?
60726.e: Herculaneum was reached by glowing avalanches of gas, ash and rock that raced down the slope at high speed. The people on the beach died from the extreme heat within a very short time.
60726.m: Pyroclastic flows are the deadliest danger from explosive volcanoes.

60727.q: Which observatory, founded in 1841, is regarded as the oldest volcano observatory in the world?
60727.e: The Osservatorio Vesuviano was founded in 1841 under the King of the Two Sicilies on the slope of Vesuvius. Today, as part of the Italian institute INGV, it monitors the volcanoes around Naples.
60727.m: Systematic volcano monitoring began on Vesuvius.

60728.q: Why is Vesuvius regarded as one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world?
a: Because hundreds of thousands of people live in its danger zone
Because it erupts several times every year
Because it is the highest volcano in Europe
Because its lava is particularly runny
60728.e: Vesuvius tends to erupt explosively, and several hundred thousand people live in the “zona rossa” around the volcano. There is an evacuation plan for an emergency, which needs days of warning.
60728.m: With Vesuvius, the dense population makes the risk so great.

60729.q: Which Neapolitan song of 1880 was written for the funicular railway that then ran up Vesuvius?
60729.e: “Funiculì, funiculà” by Luigi Denza and Peppino Turco advertised the funicular to the summit of Vesuvius, opened in 1880. The railway was later destroyed by eruptions, but the song stayed world-famous.
60729.m: An advertising song for a mountain railway became a world hit.

60730.q: Which nickname is given to Stromboli because of its constant glowing eruptions?
60730.e: Because Stromboli has thrown out glowing lumps of lava every few minutes, almost without stopping, for centuries, its eruptions guided sailors at night. That is where the name “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean” comes from.
60730.m: Stromboli has lit the way for sailors since ancient times.

60731.q: What is typical of a “Strombolian” eruption?
a: Regular small explosions that throw out lumps of lava
An ash column many kilometres high
Very runny lava flowing out calmly
An eruption completely under glacier ice
60731.e: In Strombolian activity, large gas bubbles burst at the surface of the magma column and fling glowing cinders and bombs some tens to hundreds of metres high. The explosions are usually moderate and repeat at short intervals.
60731.m: Strombolian eruptions are small, rhythmic explosions.

60732.q: Which group of islands does Stromboli belong to?
60732.e: Stromboli is the north-easternmost of the Lipari or Aeolian Islands north of Sicily. The island group has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000 because of its importance for volcanology.
60732.m: Stromboli and Vulcano belong to the Lipari Islands.

60733.q: What is the steep channel on the north-west slope of Stromboli called, down which lava and rubble plunge into the sea?
60733.e: The Sciara del Fuoco (“slide of fire”) is the scar of a large landslide. Material thrown out rolls down this channel into the sea, which is why the villages lie on the other side of the island.
60733.m: Material from Stromboli slides into the sea down the Sciara del Fuoco.

60734.q: What set off a tsunami on Stromboli in December 2002?
a: A landslide on the Sciara del Fuoco
An earthquake in the Strait of Messina
The collapse of Etna's summit crater
A meteorite impact in the Tyrrhenian Sea
60734.e: During an eruption, millions of cubic metres of rock slid from the Sciara del Fuoco into the sea. The waves damaged houses on the coast of Stromboli and could be felt as far as other islands.
60734.m: Landslides on volcanic islands can also set off tsunamis.

60735.q: How high does Stromboli rise above sea level?
60735.e: The summit of Stromboli lies about 924 metres above sea level. But most of the volcanic cone is under water, because the sea there is well over a thousand metres deep.
60735.m: Only the tip of Stromboli can be seen above water.

60736.q: Which actress played the leading role in Roberto Rossellini's 1950 film “Stromboli”?
60736.e: Rossellini shot “Stromboli” on the volcanic island itself, with a real eruption as a backdrop. The Swedish actress Ingrid Bergman played the lead, and the film made the island known internationally.
60736.m: Ingrid Bergman made the island of Stromboli world-famous in 1950.

60737.q: What is the small rock off the north-east coast of Stromboli, regarded as the remains of an older vent, called?
60737.e: Strombolicchio is a steep rock tower of solidified magma, the remains of an older eruption centre. Erosion has worn away the softer rock around it, and a lighthouse now stands on the rock.
60737.m: Strombolicchio is the exposed vent of an older volcano.

60738.q: In which novel by Jules Verne do the heroes return to the Earth's surface through an eruption of Stromboli?
a: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
Around the World in Eighty Days
60738.e: In “Journey to the Centre of the Earth”, Professor Lidenbrock and his companions climb down into the Icelandic volcano Snæfellsjökull. At the end they are thrown out of Stromboli on a raft by an eruption.
60738.m: In Jules Verne, the journey leads from Iceland to Stromboli.

60739.q: Roughly when did the great “Minoan” eruption of Santorini take place?
60739.e: The Minoan eruption in the late Bronze Age was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last few thousand years; depending on the method, it is dated between about 1650 and 1550 BC. It tore open today's caldera.
60739.m: Santorini exploded violently in the Bronze Age.

60740.q: What is the large collapsed basin filled by the sea that shapes the look of Santorini called?
60740.e: After the magma chamber was emptied in large eruptions, the roof collapsed and the sea flooded in. The steep caldera walls now carry the villages of Fira and Oia.
60740.m: A caldera forms when a volcano collapses into its empty magma chamber.

60741.q: Which Bronze Age settlement on Santorini was buried under volcanic ash and well preserved?
60741.e: Akrotiri was a thriving town with houses several storeys high and famous wall paintings. Because the inhabitants apparently fled in time, hardly any skeletons have been found there.
60741.m: Akrotiri is often called the Pompeii of the Aegean.

60742.q: What are the young volcanic islands in the middle of the Santorini caldera called?
60742.e: Nea Kameni and Palea Kameni have grown in the caldera through eruptions since ancient times; the last eruption on Nea Kameni was in 1950. They show that the volcano is still active.
60742.m: The Kameni islands are the young, active part of the Santorini volcano.

60743.q: Which Greek island group does Santorini belong to?
60743.e: Santorini is the southernmost larger island of the Cyclades in the Aegean. Geologically it belongs to the South Aegean Volcanic Arc.
60743.m: Santorini is a Cycladic island with a volcanic past.

60744.q: Which geological process causes the volcanic activity of Santorini?
a: Subduction of the African plate under the Aegean plate
Drifting apart at a mid-ocean ridge
A hotspot under the ocean crust
Collision of two continental plates without magma
60744.e: South of Crete the African plate dives under the Aegean plate. Deep down, melts form that rise in the South Aegean Volcanic Arc at Methana, Milos, Santorini and Nisyros.

60745.q: Which myth is the destruction of Santorini in the Bronze Age often linked with?
60745.e: Some researchers think that memories of the downfall of the Minoan world found their way into Plato's story of the sunken Atlantis. However, this link has not been proved.
60745.m: Santorini is seen as a possible origin of the Atlantis legend.

60746.q: What is Santorini officially called in Greek?
60746.e: The name Santorini goes back to the Venetian name “Santa Irini”. The Greek name Thira (ancient Thera) refers to the main island and the municipality.
60746.m: In Greek Santorini is called Thira.

60747.q: What worried the inhabitants of Santorini at the beginning of 2025?
a: A swarm of thousands of earthquakes
A new lava flow through Fira
A tsunami from the Black Sea
60747.e: From the end of January 2025, thousands of earthquakes were recorded between Santorini and Amorgos. Many people temporarily left the island, and the authorities declared a state of emergency.
60747.m: Earthquake swarms show that the Earth beneath Santorini is at work.

60748.q: How high is Teide on Tenerife, the highest mountain in Spain?
60748.e: Pico del Teide reaches 3715 metres above sea level and, measured from the seabed, is over 7000 metres high. Teide National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60748.m: Spain's highest mountain is a volcano on Tenerife.

60749.q: Which Canary Island had a volcanic eruption lasting almost three months in 2021, which destroyed over a thousand buildings?
60749.e: The eruption on the Cumbre Vieja (Tajogaite volcano) lasted from September to December 2021, about 85 days. Lava flows buried houses, roads and banana plantations.
60749.m: La Palma had the longest eruption in its history in 2021.

60750.q: According to the most common explanation, how were the Canary Islands formed?
a: Over a hotspot in the Atlantic
At a subduction zone off Africa
By the collision of Africa and Europe
As broken-off pieces of the Atlas Mountains
60750.e: The islands are volcanic in origin and are usually explained by a hotspot (mantle plume). The eastern islands of Fuerteventura and Lanzarote are the oldest, the western ones, La Palma and El Hierro, the youngest.
60750.m: The Canaries get older and older from west to east.

60751.q: On which island did volcanoes erupt from 1730 to 1736, whose lava fields now form Timanfaya National Park?
60751.e: The eruptions, which lasted six years, covered about a quarter of Lanzarote with lava and ash. In Timanfaya National Park the ground in some places is still so hot that you can grill food on it.
60751.m: Lanzarote bears the marks of a six-year eruption.

60752.q: Off which Canary Island did an undersea volcano erupt in 2011 and 2012?
60752.e: Off the south coast of El Hierro near La Restinga, the undersea volcano Tagoro formed. The sea changed colour, and many fish died because of the gases.
60752.m: Volcanoes can also erupt under water off the Canaries.

60753.q: What does the name “Canary Islands” go back to?
60753.e: Pliny the Elder reported an “Insula Canaria”, named after large dogs (Latin “canis”). The canary bird was only named after the islands later.
60753.m: The Canaries are named after dogs, and the bird after the islands.

60754.q: What is the large reflecting telescope on the Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma called?
60754.e: The Gran Telescopio Canarias, with a mirror more than ten metres across, is one of the largest optical telescopes in the world. Clear, calm air above the trade wind clouds makes La Palma ideal for astronomy.
60754.m: One of the largest telescopes in the world stands on La Palma.

60755.q: What are the original inhabitants of Tenerife called, who lived there before the Spanish conquest in the 15th century?
