60755.e: The Guanches were probably descended from North African Berber peoples and lived without metal tools. After the conquest by Castile, completed in 1496, their culture and language were largely lost.
60755.m: The Guanches were the first inhabitants of Tenerife.

60756.q: Which artist shaped the landscape of Lanzarote by fitting buildings into the lava fields?
60756.e: César Manrique campaigned for a gentle way of building that suits the landscape and designed places such as the Jameos del Agua in a lava tube. Thanks to his work there are hardly any tall buildings on Lanzarote.
60756.m: César Manrique combined art and volcanic landscape on Lanzarote.

60757.q: Which country do the Azores belong to?
60757.e: The Azores are an autonomous region of Portugal in the middle of the North Atlantic, about 1400 kilometres west of Lisbon. This means they are part of the EU.
60757.m: The Azores are an autonomous part of Portugal.

60758.q: Why were the Azores important for shipping from the 16th to the 19th century?
a: As a stopover for ships between Europe, America and Asia
As the site of Europe's largest shipyards
As the only port with coal for steamships
As a store for African gold kept in ice
60758.e: In the middle of the Atlantic, ships could take on water and supplies in the Azores. That is why the port town of Angra do Heroísmo on Terceira is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60758.m: The Azores were a resting place for ocean shipping.

60759.q: Which three lithospheric plates meet near the Azores?
a: North American, Eurasian and African plates
Pacific, North American and Cocos plates
South American, African and Antarctic plates
60759.e: At the Azores triple junction the North American, Eurasian and African plates meet. This explains the volcanic activity and frequent earthquakes on the islands.
60759.m: Three of the Earth's plates touch near the Azores.

60760.q: How high is the volcano Pico, the highest mountain in Portugal?
60760.e: Pico on the island of the same name reaches 2351 metres and is a young stratovolcano. It is clearly higher than the highest mountain on the Portuguese mainland, the Serra da Estrela.
60760.m: Portugal's highest mountain stands in the middle of the Atlantic.

60761.q: Which pressure system, important for the weather in Switzerland, is named after the islands?
60761.e: The Azores High is a subtropical high-pressure area over the Atlantic. When it extends as far as Central Europe in summer, it often brings Switzerland stable, warm weather.
60761.m: The Azores High gives Switzerland many a fine summer.

60762.q: What happened off the Azores island of Faial in 1957 and 1958?
a: A volcanic eruption made new land grow out of the sea
A tsunami washed the whole island clear
A meteorite struck off the coast
Half of the island sank into the sea
60762.e: The eruption of Capelinhos enlarged Faial and covered villages with ash. Afterwards the USA allowed thousands of the people affected to immigrate.

60763.q: What is the Sete Cidades caldera on São Miguel known for?
a: For two connected lakes in blue and green
For the highest geyser in Europe
60763.e: In the large caldera lie the Lagoa Azul and the Lagoa Verde, separated only by a narrow bridge. The different colours come from depth, algae and the reflection of light.
60763.m: In Sete Cidades a blue lake and a green lake lie side by side.

60764.q: What is special about the “Cozido das Furnas” on São Miguel?
a: The stew cooks for hours in hot volcanic ground
It is served with lava poured over it
It is made only of seaweed
It is chilled in glacier ice
60764.e: In Furnas, pots of meat and vegetables are buried in holes in the ground near hot fumaroles. The volcanic heat cooks the stew over several hours.
60764.m: In Furnas the volcano cooks lunch.

60765.q: Which cultural landscape in the Azores has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004?
a: The vineyards on the island of Pico
60765.e: On Pico, vines grow in small plots protected from wind and salt by walls of black lava rock. This network of stone walls became World Heritage in 2004.
60765.m: On Pico, wine grows between walls of lava.

60766.q: Which country do the Faroe Islands belong to?
60766.e: The Faroe Islands are a largely self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark with their own parliament. They celebrate their national festival, Ólavsøka, every year at the end of July in Tórshavn.
60766.m: The Faroe Islands belong to Denmark but largely govern themselves.

60767.q: Which language is Faroese most closely related to?
60767.e: Faroese and Icelandic belong to the West Norse languages and both come from the Old Norse of the Viking Age. Both have kept many old forms.
60767.m: Faroese and Icelandic are close relatives.

60768.q: Why does the lake Sørvágsvatn on the Faroe Islands look in many photos as if it were floating high above the sea?
a: Because of an optical illusion caused by the viewing angle
Because it lies on a plateau 500 metres high
Because its water is lighter than seawater
60768.e: Sørvágsvatn lies only about 30 metres above sea level, but from a certain angle the cliffs below it look much higher. It is the largest lake in the Faroe Islands.
60768.m: Sørvágsvatn fakes a huge height above the sea.

60769.q: What rock are the Faroe Islands mainly made of?
60769.e: The islands consist of layers of flood basalts that poured out about 55 to 60 million years ago when the North Atlantic opened. Glaciers later shaped the steep fjords and cliffs.
60769.m: The Faroe Islands are built from lava layers lying on top of each other.

60770.q: Which seabird with a colourful beak breeds in large colonies on the Faroe Islands, for example on the island of Mykines?
60770.e: Puffins dig their nesting burrows into the grassy slopes of the cliffs. On Mykines you can watch them up close in summer.
60770.m: Many puffins breed on the Faroe Islands in summer.

60771.q: What is the relationship of the Faroe Islands to the European Union?
a: They are not part of the EU, even though Denmark is a member
They are an EU member in their own right
They are fully part of the EU through Denmark
They are part of the Schengen Area with the EU customs union
60771.e: In 1973 the Faroe Islands decided against joining the European Community, mainly because of fishing rights. Fishing is still their most important industry.
60771.m: The Faroe Islands stayed outside the EU because of their fish.

60772.q: What is special about the Eysturoy Tunnel on the Faroe Islands, opened in 2020?
a: A road surface made of glass
60772.e: The undersea tunnel links Streymoy with Eysturoy and has a roundabout with three branches about 70 metres below sea level. The tunnel walls there are lit with art.
60772.m: On the Faroe Islands you drive round a roundabout under the sea.

60773.q: Why is the climate of the Faroe Islands mild in winter despite their northern location?
a: Because of the warm North Atlantic Current
Because of the foehn from the mountains
Because they are close to the Arctic Circle
60773.e: The North Atlantic Current, a continuation of the Gulf Stream, brings warm water into the North Atlantic. That is why the harbours hardly ever freeze and the winters are mild, but windy and damp.
60773.m: The North Atlantic Current warms the Faroe Islands.

60774.q: What is the parliament of the Faroe Islands called, which is one of the oldest parliaments in Europe?
60774.e: The Løgting goes back to a Viking Age assembly (thing) that met on the Tinganes peninsula in Tórshavn. The Althing is Iceland's parliament, the Storting Norway's.
60774.m: With the Løgting, the Faroe Islands have an ancient parliament.

60775.q: What does the Svalbard Treaty of 1920 allow all the states that signed it?
a: Economic activity such as mining on equal terms
Dividing the islands into their own zones
60775.e: The treaty gives Norway sovereignty over Svalbard but guarantees all signatory states equal rights for fishing, hunting and mining. At the same time, military use is restricted.
60775.m: Svalbard belongs to Norway but is open economically to many states.

60776.q: What is the main settlement on Svalbard called?
60776.e: Longyearbyen was founded in 1906 as a mining settlement by the American John Munro Longyear. Today about 2500 people live there, and it is the centre for administration, research and tourism.
60776.m: Longyearbyen is the main settlement on Svalbard.

60777.q: Which facility stores seeds from all over the world inside a mountain near Longyearbyen?
60777.e: The seed vault, opened in 2008, keeps backup copies of seeds from gene banks all over the world. The permafrost keeps the chambers cold even during a power cut.
60777.m: Svalbard guards a vault for the world's seeds.

60778.q: Which settlement on Svalbard is run by a Russian mining company?
60778.e: Barentsburg is run by a Russian state company that mines coal there. This is possible because of the Svalbard Treaty, which allows mining for all signatory states.
60778.m: In Barentsburg, Russians work on Norwegian soil.

60779.q: Which seafarer sighted Spitsbergen in 1596 and gave the island its name?
60779.e: The Dutchman Willem Barentsz called the island “Spitsbergen” because of its pointed mountain peaks. Svalbard is the Norwegian name of the whole archipelago.
60779.m: Spitsbergen is named after its pointed mountains.

60780.q: Why do people on Svalbard usually carry a rifle or go with armed guides outside the settlements?
60780.e: About 3000 polar bears live in the Barents Sea region, which includes Svalbard. Anyone leaving the settlements must protect themselves against encounters, but the polar bears themselves are strictly protected.
60780.m: On Svalbard, outside the settlements you are in polar bear country.

60781.q: Which settlement on Svalbard is today mainly an international research station?
60781.e: Ny-Ålesund used to be a mining settlement and is now home to research stations of many countries. In 1926 Roald Amundsen set off from here for the North Pole in the airship “Norge”.
60781.m: Ny-Ålesund is a village of polar research.

60782.q: Roughly what share of the land area of Svalbard is covered by glaciers?
60782.e: About three fifths of the archipelago lies under ice. Because the Arctic is warming fast, the glaciers are retreating noticeably.
60782.m: More than half of Svalbard is covered by glaciers.

60783.q: Strictly speaking, what does the name Spitsbergen refer to?
a: The largest island of the Svalbard archipelago
The whole archipelago including Bear Island
60783.e: Svalbard refers to the whole group of islands, Spitsbergen to its largest island. In German, however, Spitzbergen is often used for the whole archipelago too.
60783.m: Spitsbergen is the main island of Svalbard.

60784.q: Which city did the lava flow of the great Etna eruption of 1669 reach?
60784.e: The lava flow of 1669 ran as far as the city walls of Catania, partly entered the city and reached the sea. The city still lies at the foot of the volcano today.
60784.m: Catania has lived in the shadow of Etna for centuries.

60785.q: What makes Etna special among Europe's volcanoes?
a: It is the highest active volcano in Europe
It is the only extinct volcano in Italy
It lies completely below sea level
It is the oldest volcano in the world
60785.e: Etna is over 3300 metres high and erupts very often. Its eruptions have been recorded for over 2500 years, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2013.
60785.m: Etna is Europe's highest active volcano.

60786.q: What is the large horseshoe-shaped hollow on the eastern flank of Etna called?
60786.e: The Valle del Bove measures about 5 by 8 kilometres and was probably formed by flank landslides and collapses. Many more recent lava flows run into this hollow.
60786.m: The Valle del Bove is a huge scar on Etna.

60787.q: Where in Sicily is one of the most important groups of Greek temples outside Greece?
60787.e: In the “Valley of the Temples” near Agrigento stand several Doric temples from the 5th century BC, including the well-preserved Temple of Concordia. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60787.m: In Agrigento, temples bear witness to Sicily's Greek past.

60788.q: Which symbol with three legs and a Medusa head appears on the flag of Sicily?
60788.e: The Trinacria stands for the triangular shape of the island with its three capes. The Greek name Trinakria means roughly “the three-pointed one”.
60788.m: The Trinacria shows the three corners of Sicily.

60789.q: Which natural disaster destroyed the cities of Messina and Reggio Calabria in 1908?
a: A storm surge without an earthquake
60789.e: The earthquake of 28 December 1908 and the tsunami that followed killed tens of thousands of people. It is regarded as one of the worst natural disasters in Europe in the 20th century.
60789.m: Messina was destroyed by an earthquake and a tidal wave in 1908.

60790.q: What is the town of Bronte on the western slope of Etna especially known for?
60790.e: Pistachios thrive on the fertile lava soils around Bronte and are sold with a protected designation of origin. Volcanic soils are often very fertile because of their minerals.
60790.m: The famous Bronte pistachios grow on lava on Etna.

60791.q: What happened in 1831 to the island of Ferdinandea off the south coast of Sicily?
a: It appeared through an eruption and soon disappeared again
It sank for ever in an earthquake
It was turned into a fortress
It was joined to the mainland
60791.e: In 1831 an undersea volcano created a small island, which several states claimed. After a few months the sea washed the loose material away again.
60791.m: Ferdinandea was an island that existed for only a few months.

60792.q: According to Greek legend, whose forge lay beneath Etna?
60792.e: According to legend, the smith god Hephaestus (Roman Vulcan) worked with the Cyclopes beneath Etna. The word “volcano” comes from the Roman name.
60792.m: The word volcano goes back to a smith god.

60793.q: Which long-distance trail crosses Corsica and is regarded as one of the most demanding in Europe?
60793.e: The GR 20 runs for about 180 kilometres from Calenzana in the north to Conca in the south across the island's mountains. It has many steep and exposed sections.
60793.m: The GR 20 is the famous mountain trail through Corsica.

60794.q: Who led the independent Corsican Republic from 1755?
60794.e: Pasquale Paoli gave Corsica a constitution that was modern for its time. The republic ended in 1769 with the French conquest.
60794.m: Pasquale Paoli briefly led Corsica to independence.

60795.q: Which later French emperor was born in Ajaccio in 1769?
60795.e: Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio in 1769, one year after Corsica passed to France. His mother tongue was Corsican or Italian.
60795.m: Napoleon was a Corsican from Ajaccio.

60796.q: What French nickname does Corsica have?
60796.e: “Île de Beauté” means “island of beauty” and refers to the combination of high mountains, maquis and sea. The Île des Pins is in New Caledonia.
60796.m: Corsica is called the island of beauty.

60797.q: Geologically, how did the Corsica-Sardinia block form?
a: It broke away from the southern French mainland and rotated to the south-east
It grew out of the sea as a volcanic island
It was split off from the African plate
60797.e: About 30 to 15 million years ago the block broke away from the coast of Provence and Catalonia and rotated anticlockwise. This opened up the Ligurian-Provençal Basin.
60797.m: Corsica and Sardinia were once a piece of southern France.

60798.q: What are the tower-like Bronze Age stone buildings typical of Sardinia called?
60798.e: There are thousands of Bronze Age nuraghi in Sardinia. The site of Su Nuraxi near Barumini has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
60798.m: The nuraghi are the landmarks of Sardinia.

60799.q: Which volcanic rock was mined on Monte Arci in Sardinia in the Neolithic and traded far and wide?
60799.e: Obsidian is natural volcanic glass that could be made into very sharp blades. Obsidian from Monte Arci was traded as far as southern France and northern Italy.
60799.m: The volcanic glass obsidian made Sardinia a trading place early on.

60800.q: Why do researchers often call the mountain region of Ogliastra in Sardinia a “Blue Zone”?
a: Because particularly many people there live to a very old age
Because the sea there is especially blue
Because blue minerals are mined there
Because the region is a closed military zone
60800.e: Researchers use the term “Blue Zones” for regions with a striking number of people who live to 100. In parts of Sardinia, particularly many men reach a very old age.
60800.m: Sardinia is known for its many people over 100.

60801.q: What is the highest mountain massif in Sardinia called?
60801.e: The Gennargentu contains Sardinia's highest peak, Punta La Marmora (about 1834 metres). The area is part of the Barbagia uplands.
60801.m: The Gennargentu is the roof of Sardinia.

60802.q: Which language is regarded as a Romance language of its own in Sardinia?
60802.e: Sardinian is a separate Romance language that has stayed especially close to Latin in some respects. A Catalan dialect is also spoken in Alghero.
60802.m: Sardinian is a Romance language of its own, like Romansh.

60803.q: How were the six-sided basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland formed?
a: By a lava layer slowly cooling and shrinking
By crystals growing in salt lakes
60803.e: About 50 to 60 million years ago basalt lava flowed out there. As it cooled, it contracted and cracked into mostly six-sided columns.
60803.m: Basalt columns form when lava shrinks as it cools.

60804.q: Which hill in the middle of Edinburgh is the remains of an extinct volcano?
60804.e: Arthur's Seat in Holyrood Park is part of a volcano about 350 million years old. Edinburgh's Castle Rock is also a volcanic plug.

60805.q: Which group of islands forms the northernmost part of Scotland and the United Kingdom?
60805.e: The Shetland Islands lie about 170 kilometres north of the Scottish mainland, north-east of Orkney. Their main town is Lerwick.
60805.m: The Shetland Islands are the northernmost part of the United Kingdom.

60806.q: How did Great Britain become an island after the last Ice Age?
a: Rising sea level flooded the land bridge of Doggerland
A continental plate tore Great Britain away from the mainland
A volcanic eruption blasted the English Channel open
Rivers dug out the Channel in a few years
60806.e: After the ice sheets melted, sea level rose sharply. The land bridge of Doggerland in what is now the North Sea was flooded about 8000 years ago.
60806.m: Great Britain has only been an island for about 8000 years.

60807.q: During which event did the volcanic rocks of the Isle of Skye in Scotland form about 60 million years ago?
a: When the Alps were folded up
60807.e: As Europe and North America drifted apart, a lot of magma rose up. This formed the Cuillin on Skye, Fingal's Cave and the Giant's Causeway.
60807.m: The volcanic rocks of Skye formed when the North Atlantic opened.

60808.q: What status does the Isle of Man have?
a: A Crown Dependency of the British Crown, but not part of the United Kingdom
Part of the Republic of Ireland
60808.e: The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Tynwald, and its own laws. The United Kingdom is responsible for foreign policy and defence.
60808.m: The Isle of Man belongs to the Crown but not to the United Kingdom.

60809.q: On which group of islands is the Neolithic village of Skara Brae?
60809.e: Skara Brae was inhabited about 5000 years ago and uncovered by a storm in the 19th century. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Heart of Neolithic Orkney”.
60809.m: One of Europe's best-preserved Stone Age villages is on Orkney.

60810.q: Which cave on the Scottish island of Staffa is formed from basalt columns and inspired Felix Mendelssohn?
60810.e: Like the Giant's Causeway, Fingal's Cave is made of basalt columns from the same volcanic province. After his visit in 1829, Mendelssohn composed the overture “The Hebrides”.
60810.m: Fingal's Cave inspired the overture “The Hebrides”.

60811.q: Which islands in the English Channel belong to the British Crown as Crown Dependencies but lie close to the French coast?
60811.e: The Channel Islands of Jersey and Guernsey have their own parliaments, laws and taxes. They lie off the coast of Normandy.
60811.m: Jersey and Guernsey lie closer to France than to England.

60812.q: Which natural disaster directly prompted the building of the Dutch Delta Works?
60812.e: In the night before 1 February 1953, many dykes broke in Zeeland and South Holland. The Delta Commission was set up in the same month.
60812.m: The flood of 1953 triggered the Delta Works.

60813.q: Roughly how many people died in the Netherlands in the storm surge of 1953?
60813.e: In the North Sea flood, 1835 people and over 200,000 animals died. Large parts of Zeeland were flooded.
60813.m: The 1953 storm surge killed over 1800 people in the Netherlands.

60814.q: Why was the Eastern Scheldt not closed off with a solid dam, as originally planned?
a: To keep the tides and the saltwater habitat
Because the seabed could not support a dam
Because Belgium went to court against the dam
Because shipping to Rotterdam would suffer
60814.e: After protests by fishermen and conservationists, a barrier with movable gates was built. That way the Eastern Scheldt stays a tidal water and is only closed during storm surges.
60814.m: The Eastern Scheldt barrier protects against storm surges and normally lets the tides through.

60815.q: Roughly what part of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
60815.e: About a quarter of the country lies below sea level, and even more would be at risk in a flood without dykes and dunes. That is why the Netherlands built the Delta Works after 1953.
60815.m: A quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level.

60816.q: How does the Eastern Scheldt barrier close the opening to the sea during a storm surge?
a: Movable steel gates are lowered between piers
A dam is quickly built up from sand
Huge sandbags are dropped by helicopters
Old ships are sunk across the opening
60816.e: 62 steel gates hang between 65 concrete piers. Normally they are open; during a storm surge they are lowered in about an hour.
60816.m: During a storm surge, the Eastern Scheldt barrier closes movable steel gates.

60817.q: Which barrier protects Rotterdam with two huge gates that swing in from the sides on the Nieuwe Waterweg?
60817.e: The Maeslantkering was built from 1991 to 1997. Its two gates normally lie in docks on the banks and float into the 360-metre-wide waterway when there is danger.
60817.m: The Maeslantkering closes off the Nieuwe Waterweg in front of Rotterdam during storm surges.

60818.q: Why is the Maeslantkering near Rotterdam almost always open?
a: So that ships can reach the port without hindrance
Because it is needed only in summer
Because its gates are too heavy to close
Because there are no tides there
60818.e: The Nieuwe Waterweg is the way into the largest port in Europe. That is why the gates close only during a dangerous storm surge, for real for the first time in December 2023.
60818.m: The Maeslantkering closes only during storm surges so that the port stays reachable.

60819.q: Which Dutch province lies at the centre of the Delta Works and was the worst flooded in 1953?
60819.e: Zeeland consists of islands and peninsulas in the estuary of the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt. Most of the dams and barriers of the Delta Plan were built here.
60819.m: The Delta Works are mainly in the province of Zeeland.

60820.q: What was the main safety advantage of closing off the sea inlets in the delta?
a: The line of dykes to be protected became much shorter
The rivers then carried less water
The land rose behind the dams
The tides disappeared along the whole coast
60820.e: Instead of hundreds of kilometres of dykes along the sea inlets, only a short line of dams and barriers needs to be high enough. This reduces the length of coast that a storm surge can attack.
60820.m: The Delta Works shortened the coastline that has to be defended against storm surges.

60821.q: What is meant by a polder in the Netherlands?
a: Low-lying land enclosed by dykes with an artificially controlled water level
Natural alluvial land in front of the dyke
A bog that has never been drained
60821.e: A polder is surrounded by dykes, and the water from its ditches has to be pumped over the dyke. Many polders lie below sea level.
60821.m: A polder is diked land from which water is pumped out.

60822.q: What happens to a polder below sea level if its pumps fail for a long time?
a: It gradually fills up with water
It slides into the open sea
60822.e: Groundwater and rainwater constantly seep into polders. Without pumps to lift it over the dyke, the land would gradually be flooded.
60822.m: Without pumps, low-lying polders would fill with water.

60823.q: Before steam and motor pumps were introduced, what were Dutch polders mainly drained with?
60823.e: Windmills drove scoop wheels or screws that lifted the water into higher canals. Today electric and diesel pumps do this work.
60823.m: In the past, windmills pumped the water out of the polders.

60824.q: Which group of 19 drainage mills near Rotterdam has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997?
60824.e: The mills of Kinderdijk were built around 1740 to keep the Alblasserwaard dry. They show the traditional water management of the Netherlands.
60824.m: The windmills of Kinderdijk are a World Heritage Site of water management.

60825.q: Which polder in the former Zuiderzee area is regarded as the largest artificial island in the world?
60825.e: The Flevopolder consists of Eastern and Southern Flevoland and covers about 970 square kilometres. It is surrounded by water on all sides, whereas the Noordoostpolder borders the old mainland.
60825.m: The Flevopolder is the largest artificial island in the world.

60826.q: What is special about the Dutch province of Flevoland?
a: It was almost entirely won from the water
It is the most populous province
It lies higher than all other provinces
It used to belong to Belgium
60826.e: Flevoland consists of polders that were drained in the former Zuiderzee in the 20th century. Since 1986 it has been the youngest province of the Netherlands.
60826.m: Flevoland is a province made of drained land.

60827.q: Which reference level are heights in the Netherlands based on, for example for polders below sea level?
60827.e: The Normaal Amsterdams Peil (NAP) goes back to the average high-water level of the IJ near Amsterdam in the 17th century. The Pierre du Niton in Lake Geneva, by contrast, is the starting point for Swiss height measurement.
60827.m: Heights in the Netherlands are based on the NAP.

60828.q: Why does the ground of many drained peat polders keep sinking?
a: Drained peat oxidises in the air and shrinks
The sea washes the ground away from below
The Earth's crust rises after the Ice Age
60828.e: As soon as peat lies above the groundwater, bacteria break down the organic material and the ground sinks. That is why the water level has to be lowered again and again.
60828.m: Drained peat breaks down, and the polder sinks.

60829.q: Which large lake was drained from 1849 to 1852 with steam pumping stations and is now home to Schiphol Airport?
60829.e: The Haarlemmermeer threatened Amsterdam and Leiden with floods. Three steam pumping stations, including Cruquius, drained it in a few years.
60829.m: Schiphol Airport lies in the drained Haarlemmermeer.

60830.q: Why did the Dutch drain inland lakes such as the Beemster in the 17th century?
60830.e: The growing towns needed food, and rich merchants invested in land reclamation. Today the Beemster is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its planned layout.
60830.m: By draining land, the Dutch gained new farmland.

60831.q: Which two Dutch provinces does the Afsluitdijk link?
60831.e: The dam runs from Den Oever in North Holland to Friesland. The A7 motorway runs along it.
60831.m: The Afsluitdijk links North Holland with Friesland.

60832.q: Roughly how long is the Afsluitdijk?
60832.e: The dam is about 32 kilometres long and 90 metres wide. It separates the IJsselmeer from the Wadden Sea.
60832.m: The Afsluitdijk is just over 30 kilometres long.

60833.q: In which period was the Afsluitdijk built in the Netherlands?
a: After the fall of the Berlin Wall
60833.e: Construction began in 1927, and the last gap was closed on 28 May 1932. The official opening followed in 1933.
60833.m: The Afsluitdijk was built between the World Wars.

60834.q: Which two aims did the Netherlands pursue with the Zuiderzee Works and the Afsluitdijk?
a: Protection from storm floods and gaining new land
Building a naval port and an airport
Creating salt pans and fish farms
60834.e: The dam shortened the coastline and protects the land from storm floods. Behind it, large polders were drained, where there are farms and towns today.
60834.m: The Zuiderzee Works brought protection and new land.

60835.q: What did the Afsluitdijk turn the salty Zuiderzee into?
60835.e: Cut off from the sea, the basin gradually became fresh thanks to the inflow of the IJssel. Today the IJsselmeer is an important store of drinking water.
60835.m: The Afsluitdijk turned the Zuiderzee into the IJsselmeer.

60836.q: At the Frisian end of the Afsluitdijk lies a hamlet with the same name as a Swiss city, spelt without the umlaut. Which one?
60836.e: The small hamlet of Zurich lies near Harlingen in the municipality of Súdwest-Fryslân. That is where the Afsluitdijk ends on the Frisian side.
60836.m: At the end of the Afsluitdijk lies the Frisian Zurich.

60837.q: What gave the decisive push in the Netherlands in 1916 to dam the Zuiderzee?
a: A severe storm flood with major flooding
A strong earthquake on the coast
A long drought on the Rhine
60837.e: In January 1916 the Zuiderzee flooded large areas, and there was also a food shortage during the First World War. Two years later the Zuiderzee Act was passed.
60837.m: The storm flood of 1916 paved the way for the Afsluitdijk.

60838.q: Apart from shipping, what job do the Stevin and Lorentz locks in the Afsluitdijk have?
a: At low tide they release surplus water into the Wadden Sea
At high tide they let salt water into the lake
They generate the electricity for all of Friesland
They pump water into the polders
60838.e: At low tide the IJsselmeer lies higher than the Wadden Sea. Then the sluices open and the water of the IJssel flows down into the sea by gravity.
60838.m: The sluices in the Afsluitdijk drain the IJsselmeer at low tide.

60839.q: What was the dam between Enkhuizen and Lelystad in the IJsselmeer, completed in 1975, originally intended for?
a: As the edge of a planned new polder
As a harbour pier for ocean-going ships
As a pipeline to bring salt water into the lake
60839.e: The Houtribdijk was meant to prepare for a Markerwaard polder, which was never drained. Today it separates the Markermeer from the rest of the IJsselmeer.
60839.m: The Houtribdijk separates the Markermeer from the IJsselmeer.

60840.q: Roughly how long is the Sognefjord?
60840.e: The Sognefjord stretches from the coast near Solund to Skjolden. It is the longest and deepest fjord in Norway.
60840.m: At about 205 kilometres, the Sognefjord is Norway's longest fjord.

60841.q: Which glacier, the largest on the European mainland, lies north of the Sognefjord?
60841.e: Jostedalsbreen is a plateau glacier whose tongues reach into side valleys of the Sognefjord. It lies in a national park.
60841.m: Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier on the European mainland.

60842.q: How did a fjord like the Sognefjord form?
a: A glacier carved out a valley that the sea later flooded
A river cut a valley that was later drowned
A tectonic rift sank below sea level
Karst caves collapsed and filled with water
60842.e: Ice Age glaciers deepened existing valleys far below today's sea level. After the ice melted, the sea flowed into these troughs.
60842.m: A fjord is a valley carved by a glacier and flooded by the sea.

60843.q: Which cross-section shape is typical of a fjord valley?
60843.e: Glaciers grind down the valley floor and sides evenly, creating steep walls with a wide floor. Rivers, on the other hand, leave V-shaped valleys.
60843.m: Fjords have the U-shaped cross-section of a glacial trough.

60844.q: Why is a fjord usually much shallower at its mouth than further inland?
a: There is a rock sill there, because the glacier eroded less deeply
The river deposits sand in a delta there
The tides have washed out the inner part
The land has sunk more there
60844.e: Towards the open sea the glacier lost thickness and carving power. It left behind a sill of rock or moraine, behind which the basin is deep.
60844.m: A sill typically lies at the mouth of a fjord.

60845.q: Which narrow branch of the Sognefjord is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “West Norwegian Fjords”?
60845.e: The Nærøyfjord was added to the World Heritage list in 2005 together with the Geirangerfjord. At its narrowest point it is only about 250 metres wide.
60845.m: The Nærøyfjord is a World Heritage branch of the Sognefjord.

60846.q: Which fjord is considered longer than the Sognefjord and therefore the longest in the world?
60846.e: Kangertittivaq on the east coast of Greenland is about 350 kilometres long. At about 205 kilometres, the Sognefjord is clearly shorter.
60846.m: The world's longest fjord is in Greenland.

60847.q: Which Norwegian fylke (county) does the Sognefjord belong to (as of 2025)?
60847.e: Since 2020 the former Sogn og Fjordane and Hordaland have together formed the county of Vestland. Its main town is Bergen.
60847.m: The Sognefjord lies in the county of Vestland.

60848.q: What is the Flåm Railway on the Sognefjord known for?
a: It is one of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world
It is the longest undersea railway in Europe
It is the only railway that runs over a glacier
It is the northernmost railway in the world
60848.e: Between Flåm on the fjord and Myrdal, the Flåm Railway climbs about 860 metres in about 20 kilometres. It is one of the steepest standard-gauge railways and a major tourist attraction.
60848.m: The Flåm Railway climbs steeply from the fjord into the mountains.

60849.q: What characterises the Dalmatian type of coast?
a: Long chains of islands parallel to the coast, separated by sea channels
Deeply cut glacial troughs at right angles to the coast
Flat sand spits in front of calm lagoons
Countless small rocky islands smoothed by ice
60849.e: On the Dalmatian coast, mountain ridges, islands and straits run in the same direction as the coastline. This is called a longitudinal or concordant coast.
60849.m: The Dalmatian coast is a longitudinal coast with parallel islands.

60850.q: Geologically, what are the long, narrow islands off the Dalmatian coast?
a: The ridges of flooded mountain ranges
60850.e: After the last Ice Age, the level of the Adriatic rose. The water filled the long valleys, and only the mountain ridges stick out as islands.
60850.m: The Dalmatian islands are the crests of a drowned mountain range.

60851.q: Which mountain system do the coastal mountains and islands of Dalmatia belong to?
60851.e: The Dinarides run along the eastern coast of the Adriatic from the Slovenian Karst to Albania. Their direction determines the shape of the coast.
60851.m: Dalmatia's coast is shaped by the Dinarides.

60852.q: In which direction do the islands and ridges of Dalmatia run?
60852.e: The islands follow the direction of the Dinarides from north-west to south-east. That is why they lie like barriers parallel to the mainland.
60852.m: The Dalmatian islands are aligned from north-west to south-east.

60853.q: Which bridge, opened in 2022, connects the Croatian mainland with the Pelješac peninsula?
60853.e: The bridge bypasses the short Bosnian stretch of coast near Neum. This links Dubrovnik to the rest of Croatia without crossing a border.
60853.m: The Pelješac Bridge links southern Dalmatia directly with the rest of Croatia.

60854.q: Which rock shapes the mountains and islands of Dalmatia and leads to typical karst landforms?
60854.e: Limestone is dissolved by water containing carbonic acid, which creates sinkholes, caves and underground rivers. The bare, pale slopes are typical of the Dinaric Karst.
60854.m: Limestone forms the karst of Dalmatia.

60855.q: Which river near Šibenik forms limestone terraces and waterfalls in a national park?
60855.e: The Krka flows through the Dalmatian karst and deposits lime on mosses, so that travertine barriers grow. It flows into a bay of the Adriatic near Šibenik.
60855.m: The Krka forms waterfalls made of travertine.

60856.q: Which steep limestone mountain range rises directly behind the Makarska Riviera?
60856.e: Biokovo is a steep limestone range between Makarska and the hinterland. Its highest peak, Sveti Jure, is about 1,760 metres high.
60856.m: Biokovo rises behind the Makarska Riviera.

60857.q: Which town on the Dalmatian coast grew out of the palace of a Roman emperor?
60857.e: Emperor Diocletian had a large retirement residence built around AD 300. In the Middle Ages people settled inside the palace walls, and this became the old town of Split.
60857.m: Split's old town sits inside Diocletian's Palace.

60858.q: How does the western Algarve differ from the eastern Algarve?
a: Cliffs in the west, flat sandy coasts with lagoons in the east
Flat lagoons in the west, high cliffs in the east
Volcanoes in the west, glaciers in the east
Desert in the west, rainforest in the east
60858.e: The western Barlavento between Faro and Cabo de São Vicente is also called the rocky Algarve. East of Faro comes the flat Sotavento with sandy beaches and lagoons.
60858.m: The rocky Algarve lies in the west.

60859.q: Which rocks make up the yellow and reddish-brown cliffs of the rocky Algarve?
60859.e: The waves easily wash out these fairly soft sedimentary rocks. This creates many coves, grottoes and rock towers.
60859.m: The Algarve's cliffs are made of limestone and sandstone.

60860.q: How high are the cliffs of the Barlavento in the Algarve usually?
60860.e: The cliffs between Lagos and Sagres are usually a few dozen metres high, and about 75 metres at Cabo de São Vicente. Below them are small coves with sandy beaches.
60860.m: The Algarve cliffs are usually a few dozen metres high.

60861.q: Which cape in the Algarve is considered the south-westernmost point of mainland Europe?
60861.e: Cabo de São Vicente near Sagres was once thought of as the “end of the world”. Cabo da Roca near Lisbon, on the other hand, is the westernmost point.
60861.m: Cabo de São Vicente is the south-western tip of Europe.

60862.q: What are the rock towers standing freely in the sea, like those at Ponta da Piedade near Lagos, called?
60862.e: Sea stacks are the remains of a cliff that the waves have worn away all around. They are also simply called stacks.
60862.m: Sea stacks are the remains of a cliff that has retreated.

60863.q: In which order do the erosion features typically form on a limestone cliff coast?
60863.e: The waves widen cracks into caves, which join up to form an arch through a headland. If the roof of the arch collapses, a stack is left standing.
60863.m: A cave becomes an arch, and the arch becomes a stack.

60864.q: How does an active cliff like those in the Algarve retreat?
a: The waves hollow out its foot until the overhang breaks off
The rain washes the cliff down evenly from above
The whole cliff slowly sinks into the sea
The wind removes the rock face grain by grain
60864.e: Waves create a wave-cut notch at the foot of the cliff. When the overhang becomes too big, it collapses, and the process starts again.
60864.m: A cliff retreats because the waves undercut its foot.

60865.q: What is the flat rock surface called that forms in the surf zone in front of a retreating cliff?
60865.e: The waves grind the rock in front of the cliff into a surface that slopes gently towards the sea. It often becomes visible at low tide.
60865.m: In front of a cliff lies the wave-cut platform.

60866.q: Which famous sea cave with a hole in its roof is on the rocky Algarve?
60866.e: The Benagil cave lies east of Carvoeiro and can only be reached from the sea. The Höllgrotten near Baar in the canton of Zug, by contrast, are inland caves with stalactites.
60866.m: The Benagil cave is a sea cave on the Algarve.

60867.q: Roughly how long is the Curonian Spit?
60867.e: The spit stretches from Zelenogradsk in the south to opposite Klaipėda in the north. The northern part belongs to Lithuania, the southern part to Russia.
60867.m: The Curonian Spit is almost 100 kilometres long.

60868.q: Roughly how high are the tallest shifting dunes on the Curonian Spit?
60868.e: The large dunes near Nida and Pervalka rise over 50 metres, and the highest reaches almost 70 metres above sea level. They are among the highest shifting dunes in Europe.
60868.m: The shifting dunes of the Curonian Spit are over 50 metres high.

60869.q: Which body of water lies between the Curonian Spit and the mainland?
60869.e: The Curonian Lagoon is a large, shallow lagoon. Near Klaipėda it is connected to the Baltic Sea by a narrow opening.
60869.m: Behind the Curonian Spit lies the Curonian Lagoon.

60870.q: Which process brought the sand for the Curonian Spit?
a: Longshore drift caused by waves arriving at an angle
The uplift of the sea floor
60870.e: Waves that hit the beach at an angle move sand step by step along the coast. Where the coast bends, the sand is deposited as a spit, which keeps growing.
60870.m: Spits form through sand being moved along the coast.

60871.q: In the 19th century, how were the shifting dunes of the Curonian Spit stopped after they had buried several villages?
a: With concrete walls across the dune
By digging them away with excavators
60871.e: After the forests were cut down, the dunes moved inland unhindered. Marram grass, pine trees and a foredune fixed the sand in place again.
60871.m: Plants hold the sand of shifting dunes in place.

60872.q: Which two countries share the Curonian Spit today?
60872.e: The northern part with Nida belongs to Lithuania, the southern part to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The whole spit is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60872.m: The Curonian Spit belongs to Lithuania and Russia.

60873.q: Which institution in the village of Rossitten (today Rybachy) on the Curonian Spit is world-famous?
a: The oldest bird observatory in the world
The largest astronomical observatory in Europe
60873.e: An important migratory bird route crosses the spit. From 1901, birds were ringed systematically in Rossitten, much as was later done at the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach.
60873.m: The world's oldest bird observatory is in Rossitten.

60874.q: Which writer had a summer house built in Nidden (Nida) on the Curonian Spit in 1930?
60874.e: Thomas Mann spent the summers from 1930 to 1932 in Nidden. Today the house is a cultural centre.
60874.m: Thomas Mann had a summer house on the Curonian Spit.

a: A river valley flooded by the sea
A sea valley deepened by a glacier
A strip of sand in front of a lagoon
60875.e: A ria is a former river valley that the sea has flowed into. It is often funnel-shaped and branched.
60875.m: A ria is a drowned river valley.

60876.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a ria from a fjord?
a: It was never carved out by glaciers
It is always deeper than a fjord
It is always in tropical regions
60876.e: Rias are river valleys with a V-shaped cross-section that were flooded only by rising sea levels. Fjords, by contrast, are troughs deepened by glaciers.
60876.m: Rias come from rivers, fjords from glaciers.

60877.q: Which process turned the river valleys of Galicia into rias?
a: The rise in sea level after the last Ice Age
The uplift of the land after the Ice Age
60877.e: When the ice sheets melted, sea level rose worldwide by over 100 metres. The sea pushed far into the lower courses of the rivers.
60877.m: Rias formed through the rise in sea level after the Ice Age.

60878.q: What is the southern group of Galician rias, which includes the Ría de Vigo, called?
60878.e: “Baixas” means “lower” in Galician. The Rías Altas lie in the north, for example near A Coruña and Ferrol.
60878.m: The Ría de Vigo is one of the Rías Baixas.

60879.q: Where does the word “ria” come from?
a: From the Galician word for river
From the Latin word for bay
From the Arabic word for harbour
From the Basque word for sea
60879.e: The Galician “ría” is related to “río” (river). The term was taken into geography from the coast of Galicia.
60879.m: The word ria comes from Galicia and refers to rivers.

60880.q: Which use is especially typical of the calm waters of the Rías Baixas?
a: Tidal power stations in the bays
Sea salt production in salt pans
60880.e: In the sheltered, nutrient-rich rias, mussels hang on ropes under wooden rafts called “bateas”. Galicia is one of the largest mussel producers in the world.
60880.m: The Rías Baixas are a centre of mussel farming.

60881.q: Apart from Galicia, which coast is a well-known example of a ria coast?
a: The North Sea coast of the Netherlands
60881.e: In Brittany, drowned river valleys called “abers” reach deep inland. Norway, by contrast, has fjords, Western Pomerania has bodden lagoons and the Netherlands has a smooth, straightened coast.
60881.m: Brittany also has a ria coast.

60882.q: Why are rias often good natural harbours?
a: They are sheltered, fairly deep and reach far inland
They never freeze because glaciers warm them
They are always filled with fresh water
60882.e: The drowned river valleys offer shelter from waves and enough depth for ships. That is why ports such as Vigo and Ferrol lie in rias.
60882.m: Rias provide sheltered, deep natural harbours.

60883.q: Why are ria coasts counted as transverse (discordant) coasts?
a: Because the valleys reach inland at right angles to the coastline
Because the islands lie parallel to the coast
Because the coast runs at right angles to the wind
Because glaciers flowed across the valley
60883.e: On a transverse coast, valleys and ridges meet the sea roughly at right angles. This creates bays reaching deep inland with peninsulas in between.
60883.m: Ria coasts are transverse coasts with deep bays.

a: Small rocky islands smoothed by ice
Sandbanks that disappear at high tide
Long chains of dunes off the coast
60884.e: Skerries are mostly flat, rounded humps of granite or gneiss. Huge numbers of them lie off the coasts of Sweden and Finland.
60884.m: Skerries are rocky islands smoothed by glaciers.

60885.q: Which glacial landform, when flooded by the sea, makes a typical skerry?
60885.e: Glaciers ground the rock smooth on the side facing the ice flow and plucked it away on the sheltered side. After the ice melted, these roches moutonnées stick out of the water as islands.
60885.m: A skerry is a roche moutonnée in the sea.

60886.q: Roughly how many islands make up the Stockholm archipelago?
60886.e: The archipelago stretches about 60 kilometres east of Stockholm. It is the largest group of islands in Sweden.
60886.m: The Stockholm archipelago has about 24,000 islands.

60887.q: Why do new islands keep appearing on Sweden's skerry coasts?
a: The land is rising after the ice melted
The Baltic Sea is evaporating more and more
60887.e: The heavy ice sheet had pressed the Earth's crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly springing back, which is called isostatic uplift.
60887.m: Post-glacial uplift creates new skerries in Sweden.

60888.q: By how much has the land on the High Coast (Höga Kusten) in Sweden risen since the last Ice Age?
60888.e: At about 285 metres, the High Coast shows the greatest post-glacial uplift in the world. It has been a World Natural Heritage Site since 2000.
60888.m: The High Coast has risen by about 285 metres since the Ice Age.

60889.q: Roughly how fast is the land on the High Coast rising today?
60889.e: The uplift today is about 8 millimetres per year. In a hundred years that adds up to almost a metre.
60889.m: The High Coast rises by about eight millimetres a year.

60890.q: Which island group in the Baltic Sea is even larger than the Stockholm archipelago?
60890.e: The Archipelago Sea between Turku and Åland is considered the largest archipelago in the Baltic. The Stockholm archipelago comes second.
60890.m: The largest skerry archipelago in the Baltic lies off Finland.

60891.q: In which Swedish province on the west coast do reddish granite skerries shape the coastline?
60891.e: Bohuslän lies north of Gothenburg on the Skagerrak. The ice ground the reddish Bohus granite into smooth skerries.
60891.m: The skerries of Bohuslän are made of reddish granite.

60892.q: How many chemical elements are named after the village of Ytterby in the Stockholm archipelago?
60892.e: The names yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium come from minerals found in the Ytterby mine on Resarö. No other place has given its name to so many elements.
60892.m: Four chemical elements are named after Ytterby.

60893.q: What does the name “Côte d'Azur” refer to?
a: The blue in the French flag
60893.e: Azur means sky blue. The poet Stéphen Liégeard coined the name in 1887 with his book “La Côte d'Azur”.
60893.m: The name Côte d'Azur means “sky-blue coast”.

60894.q: At which border does the Côte d'Azur end in the east?
a: At the border with Italy near Menton
At the border with Spain near Cerbère
At the mouth of the Rhône near Marseille
At the border with Monaco near Nice
60894.e: Menton is the last French town before Ventimiglia. In the west, the coast is counted as far as Toulon or Cassis, depending on the source.
60894.m: In the east, the Côte d'Azur reaches Menton on the Italian border.

60895.q: What is the origin of the red rocks of the Esterel massif on the Côte d'Azur?
a: They are made of present-day desert sand
60895.e: The rocks are made of rhyolite, a volcanic rock from the Palaeozoic era. Iron compounds colour it red.
60895.m: The red rocks of the Esterel are volcanic in origin.

60896.q: Why are winters on the Côte d'Azur especially mild?
a: The Maritime Alps shelter it from cold north winds
The Gulf Stream flows right along the coast
The sun is directly overhead there in winter
Warm springs heat the coastal water
60896.e: The mountains behind hold back cold air masses, and the Mediterranean stores heat. That is why the coast became a winter destination for wealthy travellers in the 19th century.
60896.m: The Alps behind it make the Côte d'Azur mild in winter.

60897.q: Which independent microstate lies on the Côte d'Azur?
60897.e: The Principality of Monaco is surrounded by French territory on all sides except the sea. After the Vatican, it is the second smallest country in the world.
60897.m: Monaco lies in the middle of the Côte d'Azur.

60898.q: Who is the Promenade des Anglais in Nice named after?
a: English winter visitors who started its construction
An English king who lived there
60898.e: In the 19th century, many English people spent the winter in Nice. In the 1820s they paid for a first path along the shore, which was later turned into a grand boulevard.
60898.m: The Promenade des Anglais recalls the English winter visitors in Nice.

60899.q: Which seafront promenade is the landmark of Cannes?
60899.e: The Boulevard de la Croisette runs along the bay of Cannes. The Festival Palace of the film festival stands on it.
60899.m: La Croisette is the famous seafront road of Cannes.

60900.q: Apart from the island itself, what does the Port-Cros National Park off Hyères protect?
a: The surrounding sea with its seagrass meadows
The castles of the Maritime Alps
A glacier in the Maritime Alps
The marshes of the Rhône delta
60900.e: Port-Cros was founded in 1963 and was one of the first national parks in Europe to include a marine area. The seagrass meadows are a nursery for many fish.
60900.m: Port-Cros is a marine national park on the Côte d'Azur.

60901.q: In which French department are Nice, Cannes and Antibes?
60901.e: The Alpes-Maritimes department stretches from the Maritime Alps to the sea, and its main town is Nice. Saint-Tropez, by contrast, is in the Var department.
60901.m: Nice, Cannes and Antibes are in the Alpes-Maritimes.

60902.q: What happens on a cliff coast when the waves hollow out the foot of the cliff?
a: The cliff collapses and the coast retreats
The coast grows out towards the sea
A delta forms in front of the cliff
The salt hardens the cliff permanently
60902.e: The waves cut a notch into the foot of the cliff. When the overhang becomes too heavy, it breaks off, and the coast moves back inland. On the Holderness coast in England this is up to 2 metres per year.
60902.m: Waves undercut cliffs until they collapse.

60903.q: Why is the Holderness coast eroding so quickly?
a: It is made of soft glacial till
It is made of hard but cracked granite
A volcano is pushing the coast down
60903.e: The cliffs are made of loose boulder clay, which glaciers deposited in the last Ice Age. Waves and rain wear it away easily.
60903.m: Soft glacial material makes Holderness vulnerable to erosion.

60904.q: What is the “Sand Engine” (Zandmotor) on the Dutch coast near The Hague?
a: An artificial sand peninsula whose sand is spread by nature
A pumping station that removes sand from polders
A machine that shapes dunes with wind
A power station that makes electricity from sand
60904.e: In 2011 a hook-shaped area of sand was pumped up off Ter Heijde. Currents and wind gradually spread the sand onto the neighbouring beaches.
60904.m: With the Sand Engine, nature spreads deposited sand along the coast.

60905.q: What is the biggest advantage of the Sand Engine near The Hague compared with yearly beach nourishment?
a: Sand only has to be pumped once instead of every year
The sand stays in the same place for ever
It needs no sand from the sea at all
It keeps the wind away from the dunes
60905.e: In 2011 about 21.5 million cubic metres of sand were pumped up in one go. Waves and currents spread it along the coast over about 20 years, so fewer operations are needed and nature on the beach is disturbed less often.
60905.m: The Sand Engine replaces many small nourishments with one big one.

60906.q: What are groynes, built into the sea at right angles to the beach, for?
a: They slow down the movement of sand along the coast
They break the waves far out at sea
They carry river water into the sea
They stop salt water getting in
60906.e: Groynes trap the sand that the current carries parallel to the beach. On the side facing away from the current, however, more sand may be lost.
60906.m: Groynes hold sand on the beach.

60907.q: Which method has mainly been used since the 1970s to make up for sand loss on the west coast of Sylt?
60907.e: Special ships pump about one million cubic metres of sand onto the beach every year. This soft coastal protection replaces the sand that storms carry away.
60907.m: Sylt is protected by beach nourishment.

60908.q: What is the free-standing red rock tower on Heligoland, threatened by the waves, called?
60908.e: Lange Anna (“Tall Anna”) is a sea stack about 47 metres high made of red sandstone. Without protective structures, its foot would quickly wear away further.
60908.m: Lange Anna is the landmark of Heligoland.

60909.q: Why do rocks keep breaking off the chalk coast of Rügen?
a: Frost, rain and waves undermine the soft chalk
The level of the Baltic Sea is falling fast
Glaciers push the rocks into the sea
60909.e: Chalk is a soft rock. Freezing water forces cracks open, rain softens the slope and the waves gnaw at the foot. In 2005 the well-known Wissower Klinken mostly fell into the sea in this way.
60909.m: Frost, rain and waves wear away the chalk cliffs of Rügen.

60910.q: Why can a sea wall even increase erosion on neighbouring stretches of coast?
a: It cuts off the supply of sand along the coast
It attracts the tides more strongly
It warms the water off the coast
It makes the sea level rise locally
60910.e: Behind the wall, no more material is worn away that the current could carry onwards. The neighbouring beaches lack this sand and are eroded more strongly.
60910.m: Hard coastal defences can starve neighbouring beaches.

60911.q: In countries with low mortality, roughly how high must the total fertility rate be for a population to stay the same size in the long run without immigration?
60911.e: This so-called replacement level is about 2.1, because on average each woman has to replace herself and a partner. The value is slightly above 2 because not all girls reach childbearing age and slightly more boys are born.
60911.m: Without immigration, a stable population needs about 2.1 children per woman.

60912.q: What effect does a permanently low birth rate have on pension systems such as the AHV (old-age insurance)?
a: Fewer workers have to pay for more pensioners
60912.e: If few children are born over decades, there will later be fewer people in work. At the same time, people live longer. As a result, there are fewer and fewer contributors for each person of retirement age.
60912.m: Few births put a strain on pensions later on.

60913.q: According to Eurostat, how many children did a woman in Spain have on average in 2023?
60913.e: In 2023 Spain had a total fertility rate of about 1.12, making it one of the countries with the lowest figures in the EU.
60913.m: With about 1.1 children per woman, Spain is one of Europe's countries with the fewest births.

60914.q: What does a fertility rate of about 1.2 children per woman mean for a population without immigration?
a: Each generation is much smaller than the one before
The population stays the same size in the long run
60914.e: A stable population needs about 2.1 children per woman. With about 1.2 children, each new generation is almost half the size of the parents' generation. Countries such as Spain and Italy are close to such figures.
60914.m: At about 1.2 children per woman, each new generation shrinks sharply.

60915.q: Which factor is considered an important cause of the falling birth rate in southern Europe?
a: Young adults move out of home late
There are a great many nurseries
60915.e: In Italy, Spain and Greece, young people leave their parents' home at around 30 on average. Insecure jobs, high youth unemployment and expensive housing delay starting a family.
60915.m: People who move out late and have insecure work often start a family late.

60916.q: How does the shape of the population pyramid change when births fall sharply over decades?
a: It becomes narrower at the bottom and looks like an urn
It becomes wider at the bottom like a triangle
It becomes narrower at the top like a tower
It stays unchanged like a bell
60916.e: When fewer children are born, the lower age groups become narrower than the middle ones. This creates the typical urn shape of ageing societies.
60916.m: An urn-shaped population pyramid shows a shrinking, ageing population.

60917.q: How did the number of births in the EU in 2023 compare with the year before?
a: It fell more sharply than ever since 1961
It rose to a new record
It stayed practically exactly the same
It rose clearly because of immigration
60917.e: In 2023 about 3.67 million children were born in the EU, around 5 per cent fewer than the year before. According to Eurostat, that was the biggest drop since records began in 1961.
60917.m: In 2023 births in the EU fell more sharply than at any time since 1961.

60918.q: According to Eurostat, what was the total fertility rate of the whole EU in 2023?
60918.e: In 2023 the EU reached a figure of 1.38 children per woman. That is well below the replacement level that would keep a population stable without immigration.
60918.m: At about 1.4 children per woman, the EU is clearly below replacement level.

60919.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
a: The number of children a woman would have at current age-specific birth rates
The number of births per 1,000 inhabitants
The number of children per household
The share of children in the population
60919.e: The figure adds up the birth rates of all ages from about 15 to 49. It shows how many children a woman would have if today's rates applied throughout her life.
60919.m: The total fertility rate gives the average number of children per woman.

60920.q: According to Eurostat, which EU country had the highest median age of its population in 2024?
60920.e: Italy's median age in 2024 was about 48.7 years, well above the EU figure of about 44.7 years. Ireland had the youngest population.
60920.m: Italy has the oldest population in the EU.

60921.q: How has the number of births in Italy changed since the 1960s?
a: It has fallen to about a third
It has stayed about the same
It has fallen to about a hundredth
60921.e: In the 1960s about one million children were born each year; in 2024, according to ISTAT, it was just under 370,000. That is a historic low.
60921.m: Only about a third as many children are born in Italy today as in the 1960s.

60922.q: According to ISTAT, what was Italy's total fertility rate in 2024?
60922.e: ISTAT reported about 1.18 children per woman for 2024, one of the lowest figures ever recorded in the country.
60922.m: Italian women have only about 1.2 children on average.

60923.q: What does it mean that Italy has had a negative natural balance for years?
a: More people die than are born
More boys than girls are born
60923.e: The natural balance is the difference between births and deaths. In Italy deaths clearly outnumber births, so without immigration the population shrinks.
60923.m: A negative natural balance means deaths outnumber births.

60924.q: Which problem caused by Italy's ageing population is especially serious for the state budget?
a: Rising pension spending with fewer people in work
60924.e: Italy spends one of the largest shares of its economic output in the EU on pensions. At the same time, fewer and fewer workers are paying for pensions in a pay-as-you-go system.
60924.m: When fewer young people pay for more old people, the pension system comes under pressure.

60925.q: Which figure compares the number of people over 64 with the number of people of working age?
60925.e: The old-age dependency ratio shows how many older people there are for every 100 people of working age. Italy has one of the highest old-age dependency ratios in the EU.
60925.m: The old-age dependency ratio measures the burden of the older generation on people in work.

60926.q: Which measure do some depopulated villages in Italy use to attract new residents?
a: Selling empty houses for a symbolic one euro
Banning people from moving to the cities
Abolishing all local taxes for pensioners
Building new motorways through the villages
60926.e: Municipalities such as Salemi and Sambuca in Sicily offered empty houses for 1 euro. Buyers must promise to renovate the buildings within a few years.
60926.m: Italian villages fight depopulation with one-euro houses.

60927.q: Which region of Italy is considered a “Blue Zone” because of its many centenarians?
60927.e: In the mountains of Sardinia, especially in the province of Ogliastra, an unusually large number of very old people live, above all men. Researchers study their diet, exercise and social ties there.
60927.m: Sardinia is one of the well-known Blue Zones with many centenarians.

60928.q: What does “fuga dei cervelli” mean in Italy?
a: The emigration of well-educated young people
The arrival of pensioners from northern Europe
The flight from the countryside to the cities in the 19th century
The return of emigrants from America
60928.e: The expression means “brain drain” (literally “flight of brains”). Many young graduates go abroad, which makes the ageing of the country even worse.
60928.m: In Italy the emigration of young skilled people is called “fuga dei cervelli”.

60929.q: How many inhabitants did Bulgaria have in the 2021 census?
60929.e: The 2021 census counted about 6.52 million inhabitants. That was around 840,000 fewer than in the 2011 census.
60929.m: In 2021 Bulgaria had only about 6.5 million inhabitants.

60930.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Bulgaria have at its peak at the end of the 1980s?
60930.e: At the end of the 1980s almost 9 million people lived in Bulgaria. Since then the country has lost about a quarter of its population.
60930.m: Bulgaria has lost about a quarter of its population since the end of communism.

60931.q: Which two causes mainly explain Bulgaria's sharp population decline?
a: Emigration and more deaths than births
Border changes and loss of territory
60931.e: Since 1989, hundreds of thousands of mostly young people have moved abroad. In addition, far more people have died in Bulgaria than have been born for years.
60931.m: Emigration and more deaths than births are shrinking Bulgaria's population.

60932.q: According to Eurostat, which region of Bulgaria was long considered the poorest region in the EU?
60932.e: The North-West region around towns such as Vidin and Vratsa has the lowest income per head in the EU. It is losing especially many inhabitants through emigration.
60932.m: North-western Bulgaria is one of the poorest and fastest-shrinking regions in the EU.

60933.q: Which event of 1989 is known as the “Big Excursion”?
a: The departure of about 360,000 Bulgarian Turks to Turkey
The opening of the border with Greece for tourists
The mass departure of students to West Germany
The resettlement of farmers to Sofia
60933.e: After forced measures against the Turkish minority, about 360,000 people left Bulgaria for Turkey in 1989. Some of them later returned.
60933.m: The “Big Excursion” of 1989 was the emigration of many Bulgarian Turks.

60934.q: According to Eurostat, which EU country had the highest total fertility rate in 2023 despite a shrinking population?
60934.e: With about 1.81 children per woman, Bulgaria was top of the EU in 2023, ahead of France. The population loss comes mainly from emigration and high mortality.
60934.m: High fertility rates alone do not stop a population falling if many people emigrate.

60935.q: Which sector in Bulgaria suffers especially from the emigration of skilled workers?
a: Tourism on the Black Sea coast
Rose oil production in the Rose Valley
60935.e: Many Bulgarian doctors and nurses work in Germany or other EU countries, where wages are much higher. Rural hospitals struggle to fill posts.
60935.m: The emigration of medical staff weakens Bulgarian healthcare.

60936.q: Within Bulgaria, where do especially many people from rural areas move to?
60936.e: Sofia is the economic centre and one of the few regions with a growing population. Many villages, by contrast, are ageing or almost abandoned.
60936.m: While villages empty, it is mainly Sofia that is growing in Bulgaria.

60937.q: What increased emigration from Bulgaria to other European countries from 2007 onwards?
a: Joining the EU, with access to the European labour market
60937.e: When Bulgaria joined the EU, its citizens gradually gained the right to work in other EU countries. The last transitional restrictions ended in 2014 at the latest.
60937.m: Joining the EU made labour migration from Bulgaria much easier.

60938.q: Which four fundamental freedoms of the EU single market include the free movement of workers?
60938.e: The single market is based on the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. The free movement of workers is part of the free movement of persons.
60938.m: The EU single market rests on four fundamental freedoms.

60939.q: Since when has the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons between Switzerland and the EU been in force?
60939.e: The agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements I, which were signed in 1999. It came into force on 1 June 2002.
60939.m: Free movement of persons with the EU has applied in Switzerland since 2002.

60940.q: What does the so-called guillotine clause of the Bilateral Agreements I do?
a: If one agreement is terminated, all seven lapse
New EU members are automatically included
Switzerland must adopt EU law immediately
Cross-border commuters must pay a tax
60940.e: The seven agreements of the Bilaterals I are legally linked. If Switzerland terminated free movement of persons, for example, the other six agreements would also cease to apply.
60940.m: Because of the guillotine clause, the Bilaterals I hang together.

60941.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the limitation initiative in September 2020?
a: They rejected it with about 62 per cent voting no
They narrowly accepted it with 50.3 per cent
They rejected it with over 80 per cent
They accepted it with about 58 per cent
60941.e: The initiative wanted to end free movement of persons with the EU. On 27 September 2020 about 61.7 per cent of voters said no.
60941.m: The limitation initiative was clearly rejected in 2020.

60942.q: What are Switzerland's measures against wage and social dumping in connection with the free movement of persons called?
60942.e: Since 2004 the cantons and the social partners have checked whether foreign companies and posted workers comply with Swiss wage and working conditions. This is meant to stop wages coming under pressure.
60942.m: The accompanying measures protect wages in Switzerland from dumping.

60943.q: Which group of foreign nationals is the largest in Switzerland (as of 2024)?
60943.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, people with Italian nationality form the largest foreign group, just ahead of Germans and Portuguese. Many came as guest workers after the Second World War.
60943.m: Italians are the largest foreign population group in Switzerland.

60944.q: What were the old EU member states allowed to do for a few years after the eastern enlargement of 2004?
a: Restrict access to their labour market
Charge customs duties on goods from the new states
Deny the new states the right to vote
60944.e: Transitional rules allowed them to restrict the free movement of workers for up to seven years. Germany and Austria used the full period until 2011.
60944.m: After the eastern enlargement, old EU states could protect their labour markets for a while.

60945.q: Which permit do cross-border commuters from EU countries receive in Switzerland?
60945.e: The G cross-border commuter permit is for people who live abroad and work in Switzerland. As a rule they must return to their place of residence at least once a week.
60945.m: Cross-border commuters work in Switzerland with a G permit.

60946.q: Which country ended free movement of persons with the EU at the end of 2020?
60946.e: With Brexit and the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020, free movement between the United Kingdom and the EU ended. Since then a points-based immigration system has applied.
60946.m: Brexit ended free movement of persons between the UK and the EU.

60947.q: On which body of water near Schengen was the first Schengen Agreement signed?
a: On a boat on the Moselle
On a boat on the Rhine
On a ferry on the Saar
On a boat on the Meuse
60947.e: Representatives of five countries signed it on the pleasure boat “Princesse Marie-Astrid” on the Moselle. Luxembourg, Germany and France meet there.
60947.m: The Schengen Agreement was signed on a boat on the Moselle.

60948.q: Which five countries signed the first Schengen Agreement?
a: Germany, France and the three Benelux countries
France, Italy and the three Benelux countries
60948.e: The Federal Republic of Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg began removing border controls. Other countries joined later.
60948.m: Five founding states laid the foundations of the Schengen Area.

60949.q: What does the abbreviation SIS stand for in the Schengen Area?
60949.e: The SIS is a shared search database in which police and border authorities post alerts for wanted people and stolen objects. It makes up for the removal of internal border controls.
60949.m: The Schengen Information System links the member states' police searches.

60950.q: How did Switzerland vote on joining Schengen and Dublin in June 2005?
60950.e: On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent of voters accepted the association agreements. The agreements are part of the Bilateral Agreements II.
60950.m: In 2005 Switzerland narrowly said yes to Schengen and Dublin.

60951.q: What changed for travellers at Swiss airports when Schengen was introduced?
a: Passport checks no longer apply on flights within the Schengen Area
All flights now need a visa
60951.e: Since 2009 flights within the Schengen Area have been treated like domestic flights, with no passport control. Customs checks remain, however, because Switzerland is not in the EU customs union.
60951.m: Schengen flights from Switzerland no longer have passport control.

60952.q: Which non-EU country joined the Schengen Area in 2011 as the last of today's associated states?
60952.e: Liechtenstein brought Schengen into force in December 2011. Together with Switzerland, Norway and Iceland, it is an associated state.
60952.m: Liechtenstein has been part of the Schengen Area since 2011.

60953.q: Which EU member does not yet fully apply the Schengen rules because the island is divided (as of 2025)?
60953.e: Cyprus is obliged to introduce Schengen, but the unresolved division of the island makes it hard to control the external border. That is why there are still passport checks.
60953.m: Cyprus is an EU member but not yet a full Schengen member.

60954.q: Since when has Croatia been fully part of the Schengen Area?
60954.e: Croatia joined the EU in 2013. On 1 January 2023 the checks at its borders with Slovenia and Hungary ended, and at the same time it introduced the euro.
60954.m: Croatia has been a member of the Schengen Area since 2023.

60955.q: What may Schengen countries do in exceptional cases despite open internal borders?
a: Permanently expel citizens of other Schengen countries
Require their own visas for EU citizens
Charge customs duties on goods at the border
60955.e: The Schengen Borders Code allows temporary internal border controls if there is a serious threat to public order. Several countries did this, for example during the 2015 migration crisis and the Covid pandemic.
60955.m: In emergencies, Schengen countries may carry out checks at internal borders for a limited time.

60956.q: Which EU agency helps member states monitor the Schengen external borders?
60956.e: Frontex is the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, based in Warsaw. As a Schengen country, Switzerland takes part in it.
60956.m: Frontex helps protect the Schengen external borders.

60957.q: Which language family does Hungarian belong to?
60957.e: Like Finnish and Estonian, Hungarian is a Uralic language. The ancestors of the Hungarians came from the east into the Carpathian Basin in the 9th century.
60957.m: Hungarian is distantly related to Finnish.

60958.q: Which ancient language of India turned out to be closely related to Greek and Latin?
60958.e: At the end of the 18th century, scholars realised that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin go back to a common ancestor language. This is how the Indo-European language family was discovered, which German and English also belong to.
60958.m: Like English and German, Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-European language family.

60959.q: Which language of Europe belongs to the Turkic languages?
60959.e: Turkish is the most widely spoken Turkic language and is spoken in the European part of Turkey and parts of the Balkans. It is not Indo-European.
60959.m: Turkish belongs to the Turkic language family.

60960.q: Which language is a North Germanic language?
60960.e: Icelandic, Faroese, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish make up the North Germanic languages. Icelandic has changed particularly little since Old Norse.
60960.m: Icelandic is the closest to Old Norse.

60961.q: Which language with its own script belongs to the Kartvelian language family?
60961.e: Georgian is the most important Kartvelian language and is written in its own script. This small language family is found almost only in the South Caucasus.
60961.m: Georgian is one of the Kartvelian languages of the Caucasus.

60962.q: How many official languages does the European Union have (as of 2025)?
60962.e: The EU has 24 official languages for 27 member states, because some countries share the same language. Irish has had full equal status since 2022.
60962.m: The EU works with 24 official languages.

60963.q: According to estimates, which European language has the most native speakers in Europe?
60963.e: If the European part of Russia is included, Russian is the native language of the most people in Europe. Within the EU, German has the most native speakers.
60963.m: Russian has the most native speakers in Europe.

60964.q: Which sound shift describes the change from Indo-European to Germanic, for example from Latin “pater” to English “father”?
a: Second or High German sound shift
60964.e: In the first sound shift, p became f, t became th and k became h, among other changes. It was described by Rasmus Rask and Jacob Grimm and is therefore also called Grimm's law.
60964.m: The first sound shift separates Germanic from the rest of Indo-European.

60965.q: In which Russian republic in Europe is a Mongolic language widely spoken?
60965.e: The Kalmyks speak a Mongolic language and are mostly Buddhists. Their republic lies on the lower Volga, north-west of the Caspian Sea.
60965.m: Kalmykia is the only region of Europe with a mainly Buddhist tradition.

60966.q: Which language family provides three of Switzerland's four national languages?
60966.e: French, Italian and Romansh are Romance languages that developed from Latin. Only German belongs to the Germanic languages.
60966.m: Three of Switzerland's four national languages are Romance languages.

60967.q: What do the Basques call their own language?
60967.e: The Basques call their language Euskara and their country Euskal Herria. The language is spoken on both sides of the western Pyrenees.
60967.m: In Basque, the Basque language is called Euskara.

60968.q: Which Basque town was bombed by German and Italian aircraft on 26 April 1937 during the Spanish Civil War?
60968.e: The Condor Legion largely destroyed the symbolic town. Pablo Picasso portrayed the attack in his famous painting “Guernica”.
60968.m: The bombing of Gernika became world-famous through Picasso's painting.

60969.q: Which city is the seat of the government and parliament of the Basque Autonomous Community?
60969.e: Bilbao is the largest city, but the government and parliament are based in Vitoria-Gasteiz in the province of Álava.
60969.m: Vitoria-Gasteiz is the seat of the Basque government.

60970.q: In which year did the Basque underground organisation ETA announce its dissolution?
60970.e: ETA had declared a definitive end to violence in 2011. In 2018 it announced its complete dissolution.

60971.q: What is special about the finances of the Spanish Basque Country?
a: It pays no taxes to Spain
It receives its money directly from the EU
60971.e: Thanks to the historic economic agreement (“Concierto Económico”), the Basque provinces collect most taxes themselves. They pay Spain a contribution for shared tasks.
60971.m: The Basque Country has extensive powers over taxation.

60972.q: On which day did the disputed independence referendum take place in Catalonia?
60972.e: The Spanish Constitutional Court had banned the vote. It went ahead despite police operations, after which Madrid temporarily took control of the regional government.
60972.m: The Catalan independence referendum took place on 1 October 2017.

60973.q: Which event does the Diada, Catalonia's national day on 11 September, commemorate?
a: The fall of Barcelona in 1714 in the War of the Spanish Succession
