a: GDP per head below 75 per cent of the EU average
GDP per head below 50 per cent of the EU average
61205.e: Regions below 75 per cent of average GDP per head receive the highest funding rates. GDP is measured in purchasing power standards.
61205.m: Below 75 per cent of the EU average, a region counts as less developed.

61206.q: What is the EU's NUTS classification used for?
a: To divide regions comparably for statistics and funding
To set customs duties at the external borders
To count the official languages of the regions
To create constituencies for the European Parliament
61206.e: The NUTS classification divides Europe into areas of different sizes. Decisions on which regions receive how much funding are usually made at the NUTS 2 level.
61206.m: NUTS divides Europe into comparable regions.

61207.q: Which EU country received the most money from cohesion policy in the funding periods from 2014?
61207.e: As a large country with many eligible regions, Poland is the largest recipient. The money was used, for example, to modernise motorways and railway lines.
61207.m: Poland is the largest recipient of EU cohesion policy.

61208.q: What do EU countries usually have to contribute themselves for projects funded by regional policy?
a: The entire cost, paid back later
61208.e: The EU usually pays only part of a project, and the rest is borne by the state, region or municipality. EU money is meant to add to their own spending, not replace it.
61208.m: EU funding requires the country to make its own contribution.

61209.q: What is the EU programme for cross-border cooperation called, in which Switzerland also takes part?
61209.e: Interreg supports projects across national borders, for example on the Upper Rhine or around Lake Geneva. Switzerland takes part as part of its New Regional Policy.
61209.m: Interreg links border regions, including with Switzerland.

61210.q: What was Switzerland's first contribution to reducing economic inequalities in the new EU member states from 2004 called?
61210.e: With the enlargement contribution, Switzerland supported projects in the countries that joined the EU in 2004 and later. Voters accepted it in 2006, and it amounted to about 1.3 billion francs.
61210.m: With the enlargement contribution, Switzerland supported new EU member states.

61211.q: Which oil field in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea was discovered in 1969 and began Norway's oil age?
61211.e: Ekofisk was discovered by Phillips Petroleum at the end of 1969 and produced oil from 1971. It was the first large find in Norwegian waters.
61211.m: Norway's oil age began with the discovery of Ekofisk in 1969.

61212.q: Which important crude oil benchmark is named after a British North Sea oil field?
61212.e: Brent is named after the Brent field east of the Shetland Islands, discovered in 1971. It serves worldwide as a price benchmark for crude oil.
61212.m: The Brent oil price is named after a North Sea oil field.

61213.q: Which disaster on a platform in the British North Sea claimed 167 lives in 1988?
61213.e: On 6 July 1988 the Piper Alpha platform exploded and burned out, and 167 people died. It is still the worst disaster in offshore oil production.
61213.m: Piper Alpha is the worst disaster in the offshore oil industry.

61214.q: On which principle was the North Sea floor divided between the neighbouring countries for oil production?
a: Proportional principle by length of coastline
61214.e: Based on the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf, the sea floor was divided along median lines between the coasts. That is why Norway and Great Britain received large shares.
61214.m: The North Sea floor is divided along median lines between the coastal states.

61215.q: What is the Norwegian, majority state-owned oil company called that was named Statoil until 2018?
61215.e: Statoil was founded in 1972 as a state oil company and renamed Equinor in 2018. The Norwegian state holds the majority of the shares.
61215.m: The former oil company Statoil is now called Equinor.

61216.q: Which term describes the weakening of a country's industry through sudden wealth from raw materials and a strong currency?
61216.e: The term was coined in 1977 in “The Economist”, looking at the Netherlands after the natural gas discoveries near Groningen. High raw material exports pushed up the currency and harmed other export industries.
61216.m: Dutch disease describes the damage done by one-sided wealth from raw materials.

61217.q: Over which disused oil installation was there a big conflict between Shell and Greenpeace in 1995?
61217.e: Shell wanted to sink the Brent Spar oil storage buoy in the Atlantic. After protests and boycotts it was dismantled on land, and in 1998 the OSPAR states banned the sinking of such installations.
61217.m: The dispute over Brent Spar led to a ban on sinking oil platforms at sea.

61218.q: How has British oil production in the North Sea developed since about 2000?
a: It has stayed exactly the same
61218.e: British production reached its peak around 1999 and has fallen considerably since then. Since the mid-2000s Great Britain has once again had to import more oil than it produces.
61218.m: The British North Sea is past its production peak.

61219.q: What does Norway invest a large part of its North Sea oil income in?
a: A state fund for future generations
61219.e: Norway invests its oil income in the Government Pension Fund, one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world. This is meant to preserve the wealth even after the oil runs out.
61219.m: Norway saves its oil money in a huge state fund.

61220.q: Where does the money in Norway's sovereign wealth fund mainly come from?
61220.e: The state's income from oil and gas production flows into the fund. That is why it is often called the “oil fund”.
61220.m: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is fed by oil and gas income.

61221.q: Which institution manages Norway's sovereign wealth fund on behalf of the Ministry of Finance?
61221.e: It is managed by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), part of the Norwegian central bank. The owner is the state, through the Ministry of Finance.
61221.m: The Norwegian central bank manages the sovereign wealth fund.

61222.q: Under the fiscal rule in force since 2017, what percentage of the fund's value may Norway use in the state budget each year?
61222.e: The fiscal rule allows roughly the expected real return to be spent each year, about 3 per cent since 2017. This preserves the capital for future generations.
61222.m: Norway spends only about 3 per cent of its oil fund each year.

61223.q: Why does Norway save its oil income in a fund instead of spending it straight away?
a: So that future generations also benefit from the oil
Because the constitution forbids state spending
Because the EU requires Norway to
So that the oil stays in the ground
61223.e: Oil and gas will run out one day. The fund invests the money, and the state uses only a small part of it each year. This preserves the wealth for later generations.
61223.m: The oil fund spreads Norway's oil wealth over many generations.

61224.q: Where does the Government Pension Fund Global invest its money?
61224.e: The fund invests its money only abroad, in shares, bonds, property and renewable energy infrastructure. This is to stop the domestic economy from overheating.
61224.m: The oil fund deliberately invests only outside Norway.

61225.q: Roughly what share of the value of all the world's listed companies does Norway's sovereign wealth fund hold (as of 2025)?
61225.e: The fund has stakes in about 8,500 companies and owns about 1.5 per cent of all listed shares worldwide (as of 2025). This makes it one of the largest investors in the world.
61225.m: The oil fund owns about one and a half per cent of all the world's shares.

61226.q: Which body has checked since 2004 whether companies should be excluded from Norway's sovereign wealth fund for ethical reasons?
61226.e: The Council on Ethics (Etikkrådet) was set up in 2004. It recommends, for example, excluding makers of certain weapons or companies that cause serious environmental damage.
61226.m: A Council on Ethics helps decide which companies the oil fund should avoid.

61227.q: Measured by its assets, what is Norway's sovereign wealth fund?
a: One of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world
A small fund only for fishermen's pensions
The largest fund in Scandinavia, but unimportant worldwide
A fund that only stores gold
61227.e: The fund was set up in 1990 and has grown through oil and gas income to well over 20,000 billion kroner. It is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.
61227.m: Norway's oil fund is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.

61228.q: Roughly what was the value of Norway's sovereign wealth fund in 2026?
61228.e: In mid-2026 its value was well over 20,000 billion Norwegian kroner, equivalent to about 2.3 trillion US dollars. It is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.
61228.m: The oil fund is worth over 20,000 billion kroner (as of 2026).

61229.q: Roughly what share of Norway's sovereign wealth fund was invested in shares in 2026?
61229.e: The largest part of the fund, about 70 per cent, is in shares. The rest is invested mainly in bonds and in property and renewable energy infrastructure.
61229.m: The oil fund invests most of its money in shares.

61230.q: In which German state do the Nord Stream pipelines come ashore?
61230.e: Both pipeline systems end at Lubmin near Greifswald in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. From there the gas was passed on into the European network.
61230.m: The Nord Stream pipelines come ashore in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

61231.q: In which Swiss canton did the operating company Nord Stream AG have its headquarters?
61231.e: Both Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2 AG were based in Zug. The majority owner was the Russian company Gazprom.
61231.m: The operators of the Nord Stream pipelines were based in Zug.

61232.q: What happened to the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022?
a: They were badly damaged by explosions
61232.e: On 26 September 2022, explosions in the Baltic Sea near Bornholm ripped open three of the four pipeline strings. The investigation into who did it went on for a long time.
61232.m: In 2022 the Nord Stream pipelines were damaged by explosions.

61233.q: When did the first string of Nord Stream 1 go into operation?
61233.e: The first string started operating in November 2011, the second in October 2012. This meant Russian gas flowed directly to Germany without transit countries.

61434.q: Which city is the largest in Jutland and the second largest in Denmark?
61434.e: Aarhus lies on the east coast of Jutland and has a large university and an important port. Odense, on the other hand, is on the island of Funen.
61434.m: Aarhus is Denmark’s second largest city.

61435.q: How were the sandy soils in western Jutland mainly formed?
a: By outwash plains from Ice Age meltwater
By coral reefs from the Cretaceous period
61435.e: Meltwater rivers in front of the ice margin laid down large areas of sand and gravel in the west. Heathland used to spread across these nutrient-poor soils.
61435.m: Western Jutland consists of Ice Age outwash plains.

61436.q: Which landscape in County Clare is known for its bare limestone pavements?
61436.e: In the Burren the limestone lies exposed with almost no soil, and rainwater has dissolved cracks and grooves in it. Even so, Arctic, Alpine and Mediterranean plants grow side by side there.
61436.m: The Burren is a karst landscape in the west of Ireland.

61437.q: What is Ireland’s strong economic boom of the 1990s often called?
61437.e: Low corporate taxes, a well-trained workforce and EU funding attracted many international companies. The term is based on the Asian Tiger economies.
61437.m: Ireland’s boom of the 1990s is called the Celtic Tiger.

61438.q: Which type of wetland covers large parts of central and western Ireland and was dug for fuel for a long time?
61438.e: Peat has built up in Ireland’s raised bogs over thousands of years. It was cut and burned; today many bogs are being restored to protect the climate.
61438.m: Irish bogs supply peat and store a lot of carbon.

61439.q: What are the hexagonal columns of the Giant’s Causeway in the north of the island of Ireland made of?
61439.e: Around 60 million years ago, basalt lava cooled slowly there and contracted. This created the regular columns.
61439.m: The Giant’s Causeway is made of basalt columns.

61440.q: Which Ice Age landform, whose name comes from Irish, shapes large parts of northern and central Ireland?
61440.e: Drumlins are long, streamlined hills of moraine material that formed beneath the glacier. The word comes from the Irish “droim” meaning back or ridge.
61440.m: Drumlins are hills shaped by ice.

61441.q: According to the Irish constitution, which language is the country’s first official language?
61441.e: The 1937 constitution names Irish as the national language and first official language, with English as the second. In everyday life, however, most people speak English.
61441.m: Irish is Ireland’s first official language.

61442.q: Which 1998 agreement largely ended the conflict in Northern Ireland?
61442.e: The Good Friday Agreement created a shared government of both communities in Northern Ireland. That is why, after Brexit, people wanted to avoid checks at the border on the island of Ireland.
61442.m: The Good Friday Agreement brought peace to Northern Ireland in 1998.

61443.q: What happens every year at the winter solstice in the passage tomb of Newgrange?
a: The morning sun lights up the inner chamber
A fire is lit inside it
61443.e: The tomb in the Boyne Valley, about 5000 years old, has a roof box above the entrance. Only around 21 December does sunlight shine down the passage into the chamber.
61443.m: At Newgrange the winter sunlight reaches the burial chamber.

61444.q: What was the standard rate of corporation tax with which Ireland attracted international companies for decades?
61444.e: The 12.5% rate was among the lowest in Europe. Since 2024, a minimum rate of 15% has applied to very large international companies because of an OECD agreement.
61444.m: Ireland attracted firms for a long time with 12.5% corporation tax.

61445.q: At 1345 m, which mountain is the highest in the United Kingdom?
61445.e: Ben Nevis lies near Fort William in the western Highlands. It is the remains of an ancient volcano.
61445.m: Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Great Britain.

61446.q: Along which major fault does Loch Ness lie?
61446.e: The Great Glen Fault runs diagonally across Scotland from Inverness to Fort William. Several long, deep lochs lie along this fault zone.
61446.m: Loch Ness lies in the Great Glen fault zone.

61447.q: What was the result of the 2014 Scottish independence referendum?
a: About 55% voted to stay in the United Kingdom
61447.e: On 18 September 2014, 55.3% voted No to independence. Scotland therefore remained part of the United Kingdom.

61448.q: With which law did Scotland and England join to form the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707?
61448.e: The Acts of Union united the parliaments of both countries in London. Only in 1999 did Scotland once again get its own parliament in Edinburgh.
61448.m: The Act of Union of 1707 united Scotland and England.

61449.q: What are the evictions of small farmers from the Scottish Highlands in the 18th and 19th centuries called?
61449.e: Landowners drove out tenants so they could use the land for profitable sheep farming. Many of those affected emigrated to Canada, Australia or the USA.
61449.m: The Highland Clearances emptied the Scottish Highlands.

61450.q: Which well-preserved Stone Age village lies on the Orkney Islands?
61450.e: Skara Brae was lived in around 3100 BC. In 1850 a storm uncovered the houses buried under sand, complete with stone furniture.
61450.m: Skara Brae is a Stone Age village on Orkney.

61451.q: Which realm did the Orkney and Shetland Islands belong to before they were pledged to Scotland in 1468/69?
61451.e: King Christian I pledged the islands as a dowry for his daughter. The pledge was never redeemed, and the Nordic influence can still be seen today.
61451.m: Orkney and Shetland used to be Nordic.

61452.q: In Scotland, what does a “firth”, as in the Firth of Forth, mean?
a: A wide sea inlet or estuary
A mountain lake in the Highlands
61452.e: A firth is a wide arm of the sea, often the funnel-shaped mouth of a river. The capital, Edinburgh, lies on the Firth of Forth.
61452.m: In Scotland a firth is a wide sea inlet.

61453.q: According to the 2021 census, what share of the population of Wales could speak Welsh?
61453.e: The 2021 census found that 17.8% of people aged three and over spoke Welsh. The Welsh Government aims to reach one million speakers by 2050.
61453.m: Just under a fifth of people in Wales speak Welsh.

61454.q: Which raw material shaped the valleys of South Wales, such as the Rhondda Valley, in the 19th century?
61454.e: South Wales was one of the most important coalfields in the world. As a result, Cardiff became one of the largest coal ports.
61454.m: The valleys of South Wales lived from coal mining.

61455.q: Which landscape in North Wales became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 because of the stone that used to be quarried there?
61455.e: In the 19th century North Wales supplied roofing slate to the whole world. The quarries, railways and villages of this industry are now World Heritage.
61455.m: North Wales was a world centre of slate quarrying.

61456.q: Since when has Cardiff officially been the capital of Wales?
61456.e: Cardiff was only officially declared the capital in 1955. Before that, Wales had no recognised capital.
61456.m: Cardiff has been the capital of Wales since 1955.

61457.q: Which national park in south-west Wales is protected mainly because of its coast?
61457.e: The national park was founded in 1952 and consists almost entirely of coastal landscape. A coast path about 300 km long runs through it.
61457.m: The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park protects a coastline.

61458.q: What is the 8th-century earthwork called that roughly follows the border between England and Wales?
61458.e: King Offa of Mercia had the earthwork built against the Welsh kingdoms. Today a long footpath follows it.
61458.m: Offa’s Dyke marks the old border with Wales.

61459.q: Which English king had Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech castles built in North Wales in the 13th century?
61459.e: After conquering Wales in 1283, Edward I secured his rule with a ring of mighty castles. Several of them are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
61459.m: Edward I built the great castles in North Wales.

61460.q: Which river, the longest in Great Britain, rises in the mountains of Wales?
61460.e: The Severn rises on Plynlimon and flows through Wales and England into the Bristol Channel. It is about 350 km long.
61460.m: The Severn is Great Britain’s longest river.

61461.q: What cooperation did the governments in exile of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg agree on in London in 1944?
61461.e: The London Customs Convention came into force in 1948 and created the Benelux customs union. It is seen as a model for later European integration.
61461.m: The Benelux countries founded a customs union after the Second World War.

61462.q: How many regions does the federal state of Belgium have?
61462.e: Belgium is divided into the regions of Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital. In addition, there are three language communities.

61463.q: Roughly what share of the area of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
61463.e: About 26% of the country lies below mean sea level. These areas are protected by dykes, dunes and pumping stations.
61463.m: A quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level.

61464.q: What is the urban area with Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht called?
61464.e: The Randstad forms a ring of cities around a green, farmed heart. Almost half of the Dutch population lives there.
61464.m: The Randstad is the urban centre of the Netherlands.

61465.q: Where is Belgium’s highest point, the Signal de Botrange?
61465.e: The Signal de Botrange is 694 m high and lies on the raised bog plateau of the High Fens. It is part of the foothills of the Ardennes.
61465.m: Belgium’s highest point lies in the High Fens.

61466.q: Which languages are official languages in Belgium?
61466.e: A legal language border separates Dutch-speaking Flanders from French-speaking Wallonia. In the east there is also a small German-speaking community.

61467.q: Via which river is the port of Antwerp connected to the North Sea, with its mouth in the Netherlands?
61467.e: The Western Scheldt lies on Dutch territory. Deepening it for large ships therefore had to be settled in treaties between the two countries.
61467.m: Antwerp reaches the sea via the Scheldt.

61468.q: Why was the Eastern Scheldt not fully dammed but protected by a storm surge barrier with movable gates?
a: To keep the tides and the saltwater habitat
Because a dam would have been too expensive
Because the ground could not support a dam
To save ships from passing through
61468.e: After protests from fishermen and conservationists, an open barrier was chosen in 1976. The gates only close during storm surges; otherwise the sea flows freely in and out.
61468.m: The Eastern Scheldt barrier only closes during storm surges.

61469.q: Which sandy landscape in north-east Belgium was a coalfield in the 20th century?
61469.e: In the Kempen (Campine) in the province of Limburg, coal was mined at great depth from 1917. The last mine closed in 1992.
61469.m: The Kempen in north-east Belgium was a coalfield.

61470.q: In which area is Luxembourg the largest financial centre in Europe?
61470.e: Funds with assets of several thousand billion euros are managed in Luxembourg. After the USA, it is the second largest fund centre in the world.
61470.m: Luxembourg is Europe’s largest fund centre.

61471.q: Which European bank has its headquarters in Luxembourg?
a: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
61471.e: The European Investment Bank (EIB) grants long-term loans for projects in the interest of the EU. The ECB is based in Frankfurt, the BIS in Basel.
61471.m: The European Investment Bank is based in Luxembourg.

61472.q: Why can funds authorised in Luxembourg be sold throughout the EU?
a: Thanks to an EU passport for authorised funds
Because Luxembourg is the capital of the EU
Because Luxembourg has no fund supervision
Because all EU funds must be based in Luxembourg
61472.e: Under the EU rules for funds (UCITS), a fund authorised in one EU country may be sold in all other member states. The fund centre of Luxembourg benefits greatly from this.
61472.m: An EU passport allows funds to be sold throughout the EU.

61473.q: Which type of bond was first issued by the European Investment Bank in 2007 and listed in Luxembourg?
61473.e: The EIB’s “Climate Awareness Bond” is considered the world’s first green bond. The Luxembourg Stock Exchange now runs its own platform for sustainable bonds.
61473.m: The first green bond was listed in Luxembourg.

61474.q: From 2015, Luxembourg automatically exchanged account information with other EU countries. What was largely given up as a result?
a: Banking secrecy towards foreign tax authorities
61474.e: Under international pressure, Luxembourg took part in the automatic exchange of information. Switzerland also adopted this standard from 2017.
61474.m: With the automatic exchange of information, banking secrecy ended for foreign tax authorities.

61475.q: Where do almost half of the people working in Luxembourg come from?
a: From neighbouring countries as cross-border commuters
61475.e: Every day over 200,000 people commute to Luxembourg from France, Belgium and Germany. This makes GDP per head particularly high, because the commuters work there but are not counted as residents.
61475.m: Many workers in Luxembourg are cross-border commuters.

61476.q: With which country did Luxembourg form an economic and currency union from 1921?
61476.e: The Belgium-Luxembourg Economic Union firmly linked the two currencies. The Belgian franc was also valid in Luxembourg until the euro arrived in 2002.
61476.m: From 1921 Luxembourg was closely linked economically with Belgium.

61477.q: Which institution of the euro countries, which gives loans to countries in financial difficulty, is based in Luxembourg?
61477.e: The ESM was founded in 2012 as the permanent rescue fund of the eurozone. It grants loans in return for reforms.
61477.m: The euro rescue fund ESM is based in Luxembourg.

61478.q: Which tax do most residents of Monaco not pay?
61478.e: Monaco does not charge income tax on individuals. French citizens are an exception because of an agreement from 1963.
61478.m: In Monaco most people pay no income tax.

61479.q: How has Monaco increased its area in recent decades?
a: By reclaiming land from the sea
61479.e: The district of Fontvieille was built on land reclaimed from the sea from the 1970s. Most recently, the Mareterra district was added.
61479.m: Monaco gains new land from the sea.

61480.q: Who may vote for Monaco’s parliament, the National Council?
a: Only members of the princely family
61480.e: The Conseil national has 24 members and is elected every five years. Because only about a quarter of residents are Monégasques, the majority cannot vote.
61480.m: In Monaco only Monégasques elect the parliament.

61481.q: Why did Monaco rely on the Monte Carlo Casino in the 19th century?
a: It needed new income after losing territory
61481.e: Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848 and were handed over to France in 1861. Monaco lost about four fifths of its territory and much tax income. Prince Charles III therefore relied on a casino and tourism.
61481.m: After losing Menton and Roquebrune, Monaco relied on the casino.

61482.q: Who is not allowed to enter the gaming rooms of the Monte Carlo Casino as a player?
61482.e: Prince Charles III banned his own citizens from gambling in the casino. The casino was meant to bring in money from visitors, not to ruin the locals.
61482.m: Monégasques may not gamble in their own casino.

61483.q: With which country does Monaco form a customs union?
61483.e: Because of the customs union, there are no customs checks at the border with France. Through France, Monaco is also linked to the EU customs area.
61483.m: Monaco and France form a customs union.

61484.q: Roughly what share of Monaco’s residents hold Monégasque citizenship?
61484.e: In the 2016 census, about 9300 of just over 37,000 residents were Monégasques. The largest of the other groups are French and Italian.
61484.m: Only about a quarter of people in Monaco are Monégasques.

61485.q: What is the district on the rock where the Prince’s Palace stands called?
61485.e: Monaco-Ville sits on a rocky headland above the sea and is called “Le Rocher”. The cathedral and the town hall also stand there.
61485.m: The Prince’s Palace stands in Monaco-Ville on the rock.

61486.q: What is special about the capital Andorra la Vella?
a: It is the highest capital in Europe
It is the oldest capital in Europe
It is the southernmost capital in Europe
It is the smallest capital in Europe
61486.e: Andorra la Vella lies at about 1000 m above sea level in a Pyrenean valley. No other capital in Europe is higher.
61486.m: Andorra la Vella is Europe’s highest capital.

61487.q: Who are the two heads of state (co-princes) of Andorra today?
a: The Bishop of Urgell and the President of France
The King of Spain and the Pope
The President of France and the King of Spain
Two presidents elected by the people
61487.e: The joint rule goes back to a treaty from 1278. The rights of the Count of Foix later passed to the French kings and today to the French president.
61487.m: Andorra has two co-princes: a bishop and the President of France.

61488.q: What does Andorra’s economy mainly live on?
a: Tourism, such as winter sports and shopping
61488.e: Andorra attracts millions of visitors who ski in the Pyrenees or shop cheaply because of low taxes. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror valley is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

61489.q: What is the parliament of Andorra called?
61489.e: The Consell General has 28 members. Half are elected nationwide and the other half in the parishes.
61489.m: Andorra’s parliament is called the Consell General.

61490.q: Which language is Andorra’s only official language?
61490.e: Although Andorra lies between Spain and France, Catalan is the only official language. Spanish and French are also widely spoken in daily life.
61490.m: Catalan is the official language of Andorra.

61491.q: Into which large Spanish river does the water of the Gran Valira from Andorra finally flow?
61491.e: The Gran Valira flows into the Segre near La Seu d’Urgell. The Segre continues into the Ebro and so into the Mediterranean.
61491.m: Andorra’s water flows via the Segre into the Ebro.

61492.q: Which tax did Andorra only introduce for individuals in 2015?
61492.e: For a long time Andorra was seen as a country with almost no direct taxes. Under pressure from the EU, it introduced an income tax in 2015 with a top rate of 10%.
61492.m: Andorra has only had an income tax since 2015.

61493.q: What arrangement has Andorra had with the European Community since 1991?
a: A customs union for industrial goods
61493.e: There are no customs duties on industrial goods between Andorra and the EU. However, Andorra is neither an EU member nor part of the Schengen Area.
61493.m: Andorra forms a customs union with the EU for industrial goods.

61494.q: Roughly how large is the area of San Marino?
61494.e: At about 61 km², San Marino is the fifth smallest country in the world. Only Vatican City, Monaco, Nauru and Tuvalu are smaller.
61494.m: San Marino covers about 61 square kilometres.

61495.q: What are the nine municipalities that San Marino is divided into called?
61495.e: San Marino is divided into nine castelli, including the capital, the City of San Marino. Each castello has its own council.
61495.m: San Marino consists of nine castelli.

61496.q: According to its own tradition, what is San Marino known for?
a: It is considered the oldest surviving republic in the world
It is the smallest country in the world
It has no government of its own
It is a member of the EU
61496.e: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in the year 301. Vatican City and Monaco, for example, are smaller, and it does not belong to the EU.
61496.m: San Marino is considered the oldest republic in the world.

61497.q: Which offer is San Marino said to have turned down from Napoleon in 1797?
a: A seaport of its own as a gift
61497.e: Napoleon offered to expand the country’s territory. San Marino declined so as not to put its independence and neutrality at risk.
61497.m: San Marino turned down Napoleon’s offer of more land.

61498.q: How long is the term of office of San Marino’s two Captains Regent?
61498.e: The regents take office on 1 April and 1 October. The short term is meant to stop anyone from gathering too much power, similar to the Swiss Federal Presidency that changes every year.
61498.m: San Marino’s regents change every six months.

61499.q: Which US president became an honorary citizen of San Marino in 1861?
61499.e: San Marino offered Lincoln honorary citizenship. He thanked them in a letter and praised the small republic.
61499.m: Abraham Lincoln was an honorary citizen of San Marino.

61500.q: What can be seen from far away on Monte Titano and is also shown on San Marino’s coat of arms?
61500.e: The three towers Guaita, Cesta and Montale stand on the peaks of Monte Titano. They are the country’s landmark and appear on its flag and coat of arms.
61500.m: Three towers are San Marino’s landmark.

61501.q: How has San Marino traditionally earned money from collectors around the world?
61501.e: San Marino issues its own stamps and its own euro coins in small numbers. Many of them are not used in everyday life but collected.
61501.m: Stamps and coins from San Marino are popular with collectors.

61502.q: Which three inhabited islands make up the country of Malta?
61502.e: Gozo is the second largest and Comino the smallest inhabited island. Lampedusa, Linosa and Pantelleria belong to Italy.
61502.m: Malta consists of Malta, Gozo and Comino.

61503.q: Which order of knights founded the capital Valletta in 1566?
61503.e: Grand Master Jean de la Valette gave the city its name. The Knights of St John ruled Malta from 1530 to 1798.
61503.m: The Knights of St John founded Valletta.

61504.q: Against whom did the knights on Malta defend themselves in the Great Siege of 1565?
61504.e: A large Ottoman fleet besieged the island for months without success. The victory made Malta famous throughout Europe.
61504.m: Malta withstood the Ottoman siege in 1565.

61505.q: How does Malta meet a large part of its drinking water needs?
61505.e: Malta has no rivers and hardly any rain in summer. Reverse osmosis plants therefore supply a large part of the tap water.
61505.m: Malta gets drinking water from the sea.

61506.q: Which award did the whole island of Malta receive in 1942 for its resistance in the Second World War?
61506.e: King George VI awarded the George Cross to the people, who endured heavy air raids. The cross appears on Malta’s flag today.
61506.m: The George Cross on Malta’s flag recalls the Second World War.

61507.q: What is the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum on Malta?
a: A tunnel of the Knights of St John
61507.e: The chambers cut into the rock were made around 4000 BC. The remains of about 7000 people were found inside.
61507.m: The Hypogeum is a Stone Age burial site cut into the rock.

61508.q: Since which year have people in Malta paid with the euro?
61508.e: On 1 January 2008, Malta replaced the Maltese lira with the euro. Cyprus switched at the same time as Malta.
61508.m: Malta has had the euro since 2008.

61509.q: Who drove the Knights of St John out of Malta in 1798?
61509.e: On his way to Egypt, Napoleon captured the island almost without a fight. By 1800 the British had taken control.
61509.m: Napoleon ended the rule of the Knights of St John on Malta in 1798.

61510.q: After Malta’s independence in 1964, who was still head of state at first?
a: The Grand Master of the Knights of St John
61510.e: After 1964 Malta remained a monarchy with Elizabeth II as queen. Only in 1974 did the country become a republic with its own president.
61510.m: Malta has been a republic since 1974.

61511.q: In the geography of Spain, what is the “Meseta”?
a: The central plateau of the Iberian Peninsula
The coastal plain on the Mediterranean
The mountain range on the border with France
61511.e: The Meseta is the vast high plateau in the interior of Spain. The name means something like “little table” and refers to its flat, raised shape.
61511.m: The Meseta is the high plateau at the heart of Spain.

61512.q: Which river drains most of the northern Meseta?
61512.e: The Douro (Duero in Spanish) collects the water of the northern plateau and flows into the Atlantic at Porto.
61512.m: The Douro is the river of the northern Meseta.

61513.q: Which type of land use has traditionally shaped large parts of the Meseta?
a: Dry farming of cereals and sheep keeping
61513.e: Because of the low rainfall, mainly cereals were grown without irrigation (secano). Sheep farming was also important, for example with Merino sheep.
61513.m: On the Meseta cereals grow and sheep graze.

61514.q: What is the moving of herds between summer and winter pastures, as was common on the Meseta, called?
61514.e: In the Middle Ages, the Mesta association drove huge herds of Merino sheep along fixed routes between the mountains in the north and the plains in the south. This seasonal grazing is called transhumance.
61514.m: Transhumance is the seasonal moving of herds.

61515.q: What geological base forms the core of the Meseta?
a: Glacial moraines from the last Ice Age
61515.e: The Meseta rests on the Iberian Massif, a remnant of the Variscan mountains. These were worn down over millions of years and later uplifted.
61515.m: The Meseta is an ancient, levelled mountain base.

61516.q: Which region of the southern Meseta is famous for the windmills in the novel “Don Quixote”?
61516.e: Cervantes had his hero fight windmills in La Mancha. The region is a wide, dry plain in Castilla-La Mancha.
61516.m: Don Quixote fought windmills in La Mancha.

61517.q: Which mountain range forms the southern edge of the Meseta towards the Guadalquivir basin?
61517.e: The Sierra Morena is more of a fault scarp than a high mountain range. South of it, the land drops down to the Andalusian lowland.
61517.m: The Sierra Morena separates the Meseta from Andalusia.

61518.q: Why do the Douro, Tagus and Guadiana flow from the Meseta into the Atlantic and not into the Mediterranean?
a: Because the plateau slopes towards the west
Because there is desert in the east
Because they are channelled west underground
Because the wind pushes the water west
61518.e: The Meseta is higher in the east than in the west. That is why the big rivers drain towards Portugal and the Atlantic; only the Ebro flows into the Mediterranean.
61518.m: The Meseta tilts west, and its rivers flow into the Atlantic.

61519.q: Which former royal city lies on the southern Meseta in a tight bend of the Tagus?
61519.e: Toledo sits on a rock that the Tagus flows almost all the way around. The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and was for a long time the centre of Castile.
61519.m: Toledo sits above a bend in the Tagus.

61520.q: What is Gibraltar’s constitutional status today?
61520.e: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with its own government. The United Kingdom is responsible for foreign policy and defence.
61520.m: Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

61521.q: How did Gibraltar’s voters decide on shared sovereignty with Spain in 2002?
61521.e: In the 2002 referendum, about 99 per cent voted against shared British-Spanish sovereignty. In 1967 a large majority had already voted for Britain.
61521.m: Gibraltar clearly rejected shared sovereignty in 2002.

61522.q: What measure did Spain take in 1969 in the dispute over Gibraltar?
a: It closed the land border completely
It declared Gibraltar a free trade zone
61522.e: Under Franco the border was closed in 1969. Pedestrians were allowed through again from 1982, and it was fully reopened in 1985.
61522.m: Spain closed the border with Gibraltar from 1969 until the 1980s.

61523.q: What was Gibraltar Airport known for for a long time?
a: A main road crossed the runway
It was on a floating platform
It was inside a cave in the rock
61523.e: Winston Churchill Avenue crossed the runway and was closed when planes took off or landed. Since 31 March 2023 a tunnel has taken road traffic under the runway.
61523.m: In Gibraltar a road crossed the runway.

61524.q: How did Gibraltar vote in the 2016 Brexit referendum?
a: About 96 per cent to remain in the EU
Gibraltar was not allowed to vote
61524.e: Gibraltar took part in the vote as part of the South West England region. Over 95 per cent wanted to stay in the EU because the open border with Spain is important for the economy.
61524.m: Gibraltar voted almost unanimously against Brexit in 2016.

61525.q: Which two powers besieged Gibraltar without success from 1779 to 1783?
61525.e: During the American War of Independence, Spain and France tried to win back Gibraltar. The Great Siege lasted almost four years and failed.
61525.m: The Great Siege of Gibraltar failed in 1783.

61526.q: Which currency is issued in Gibraltar?
a: Gibraltar pound, pegged to the British pound
British pound with no notes of its own
61526.e: The Government of Gibraltar issues its own banknotes and coins. The Gibraltar pound is pegged one to one to the pound sterling.
61526.m: Gibraltar has its own pound, equal in value to the British one.

61527.q: Which Spanish town borders Gibraltar directly by land?
61527.e: A narrow isthmus connects Gibraltar with the mainland. La Línea lies just beyond the border, and many of its residents commute to Gibraltar every day.
61527.m: La Línea lies right on the border with Gibraltar.

61528.q: In which direction does the surface water flow through the Strait of Gibraltar?
a: From the Atlantic into the Mediterranean
From the Mediterranean into the Atlantic
It changes completely every day with the tides
61528.e: More water evaporates from the Mediterranean than rivers and rain supply. So Atlantic water flows in at the top, while heavier, saltier Mediterranean water flows out at depth.
61528.m: At the surface, Atlantic water flows into the Mediterranean.

61529.q: Which statesman led the rebuilding of Lisbon’s lower town, the Baixa, after 1755?
61529.e: The minister Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, later the Marquis of Pombal, had the Baixa laid out again with straight streets. The houses were given an earthquake-proof wooden frame (gaiola).
61529.m: Pombal rebuilt the Baixa to a plan after the earthquake.

61530.q: For which occasion was the Vasco da Gama Bridge in Lisbon opened in 1998?
61530.e: The bridge over the Tagus was finished in time for Expo 98. The world fair marked 500 years of the sea route to India.
61530.m: The Vasco da Gama Bridge was built for Expo 98.

61531.q: Which old quarter of Lisbon largely survived the great earthquake thanks to its rocky ground?
61531.e: The Alfama, with its narrow lanes, lies on solid rock below São Jorge Castle. That is why its medieval street plan has survived.
61531.m: The Alfama is Lisbon’s oldest quarter.

61532.q: In which building in Lisbon is the tomb of the navigator Vasco da Gama?
a: In the Jerónimos Monastery in Belém
61532.e: The Mosteiro dos Jerónimos was founded by King Manuel I from 1501. Vasco da Gama and the poet Luís de Camões rest in its church.
61532.m: Vasco da Gama is buried in the Jerónimos Monastery.

61533.q: Whose 500th death anniversary in 1960 was the reason for building the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos)?
61533.e: The monument on the bank of the Tagus in Belém is shaped like a ship’s bow. Henry the Navigator stands at the front, followed by other figures from the Age of Discovery.
61533.m: The Monument to the Discoveries honours Henry the Navigator.

61534.q: Where did the Portuguese royal court move in 1807/08 when French troops advanced on Lisbon?
61534.e: Fleeing Napoleon’s army, the court escaped to Brazil under British protection. Until 1821 Rio de Janeiro was in effect the capital of the Portuguese empire.
61534.m: In 1808 Rio de Janeiro became the seat of the Portuguese court.

61535.q: Which large square on the bank of the Tagus was built on the site of the royal palace destroyed in 1755?
61535.e: The square used to be called Terreiro do Paço, meaning palace square. It is surrounded by arcades on three sides and opens onto the river.
61535.m: The Praça do Comércio replaced the old royal palace.

61536.q: Which large statue of Christ looks over Lisbon from the south bank of the Tagus?
61536.e: Cristo Rei stands in Almada and was inaugurated in 1959. It was modelled on the statue of Christ in Rio de Janeiro.

61537.q: Which Enlightenment philosopher wrote about the Lisbon earthquake in a poem and in the novel “Candide”?
61537.e: In view of the disaster, Voltaire doubted that we live in the “best of all possible worlds”. In this way he attacked the philosophy of Leibniz.
61537.m: In Candide, Voltaire mocked the belief in the best of all worlds.

61538.q: Which ancient people does the name Tuscany go back to?
61538.e: The Romans called the land of the Etruscans “Tuscia”. The name Toscana developed from this.
61538.m: The name Tuscany recalls the Etruscans.

61539.q: Why is the Tuscan dialect regarded as the basis of standard Italian?
a: Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio wrote in the everyday language of Florence
It was the official language of the Roman Empire
The popes wrote their bulls in Tuscan
61539.e: The great poets of the 14th century made Florentine a respected literary language. After the unification of Italy it became established as the standard language.
61539.m: Standard Italian has its roots in Florentine.

61540.q: What is the Tuscan town of Carrara world famous for?
61540.e: Marble has been quarried in the Apuan Alps above Carrara since Roman times. Michelangelo also chose blocks for his sculptures here.
61540.m: Famous white marble comes from Carrara.

61541.q: What was tried out for the first time at Larderello in Tuscany in 1904?
a: A hydroelectric power station in the mountains
61541.e: At Larderello, hot steam comes out of the ground. In 1904 it was used to light light bulbs for the first time, and later the world’s first geothermal power station was built there.
61541.m: Larderello is the birthplace of geothermal electricity.

61542.q: Which horse race takes place twice every year on the Piazza del Campo?
61542.e: At the Palio on 2 July and 16 August, riders representing the city districts (contrade) race bareback around the square. The race lasts only about one and a half minutes.
61542.m: The Palio is Siena’s famous horse race.

61543.q: Which cultural landscape in southern Tuscany, with cypresses and gentle hills, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
61543.e: The Val d’Orcia south of Siena became World Heritage in 2004. Its landscape was deliberately shaped during the Renaissance and has inspired paintings and photos.
61543.m: The Val d’Orcia shows the typical Tuscan hill landscape.

61544.q: Where was Napoleon first sent into exile in 1814?
a: To the Tuscan island of Elba
61544.e: After he abdicated, Napoleon was given Elba as a principality. In 1815 he returned, was defeated at Waterloo and taken to Saint Helena.
61544.m: Napoleon’s first exile took him to Elba.

61545.q: Which coastal area of Tuscany was for a long time a marshland full of malaria and was then drained?
61545.e: Because of malaria, few people lived in the Maremma. Drainage in the 19th and 20th centuries turned it into farmland.
61545.m: The Maremma changed from marsh to farmland.

61546.q: Which small Tuscan town is known for its medieval tower houses?
61546.e: In the Middle Ages, rich families built residential towers as high as possible as a sign of their power. Of around 70 towers, about 15 still survive in San Gimignano today.
61546.m: San Gimignano is the town of tower houses.

61547.q: Which bridge has connected the north-west of the Peloponnese to the mainland since 2004?
61547.e: The cable-stayed bridge over the Gulf of Corinth is about 2.9 km long. It was opened shortly before the 2004 Olympic Games.
61547.m: The Rio-Antirrio Bridge spans the Gulf of Corinth.

61548.q: Which mountain range rises between Sparta and Kalamata?
61548.e: At over 2400 m, the Taygetus is the highest mountain range in the Peloponnese. It separates Laconia from Messenia and stretches far to the south.
61548.m: The Taygetus is the highest mountain range of the Peloponnese.

61549.q: Which canal has separated the Peloponnese from the rest of the Greek mainland since 1893?
61549.e: The Corinth Canal, about 6 kilometres long, cuts through the narrow isthmus between the Aegean and the Ionian Sea. Strictly speaking, the Peloponnese has been an island ever since.
61549.m: The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnese from the mainland.

61550.q: Which ancient city in the Peloponnese was famous for its tough upbringing and its warriors?
61550.e: In Sparta, boys from the age of seven were raised as warriors in strict groups. To this day, “spartan” means simple and harsh.
61550.m: Sparta was known for its strict warrior training.

61551.q: Which Bronze Age citadel in the Peloponnese is known for its Lion Gate?
61551.e: Mycenae was the centre of the culture named after it. The Lion Gate from the 13th century BC is its landmark.
61551.m: The Lion Gate is the landmark of Mycenae.

61552.q: Which late Byzantine ruined city near Sparta is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
61552.e: In the 14th and 15th centuries Mystras was a cultural centre of Byzantium. Churches with frescoes and palaces climb up a hillside.
61552.m: Mystras is a Byzantine ruined city near Sparta.

61553.q: Which barren peninsula in the south of the Peloponnese is known for its tower houses and old family feuds?
61553.e: The people of the Mani built fortified stone towers and stayed largely independent for a long time. Blood feuds were common there until the 19th century.
61553.m: The Mani is the land of tower houses.

61554.q: Which city is the largest in the Peloponnese and an important ferry port for Italy?
61554.e: Patras lies in the north-west on the gulf of the same name. Ferries sail from here to Ancona, Bari and Venice.
61554.m: Patras is the largest city of the Peloponnese.

61555.q: Which naval battle off the Peloponnese in 1827 helped decide the Greek struggle for independence?
61555.e: In the Bay of Navarino near Pylos, a British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet. This paved the way for Greek independence.
61555.m: The Battle of Navarino helped Greece to independence.

61556.q: Which event in July 1974 led to the division of Cyprus?
a: A coup by Greek nationalists and the Turkish military intervention
The Republic of Cyprus joining the EU
61556.e: The military junta in Athens backed a coup aimed at union with Greece. Turkey then intervened militarily and has occupied the north ever since.
61556.m: Since 1974 Cyprus has in effect been divided.

61557.q: Which country is the only one to recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, declared in 1983?
61557.e: The UN Security Council declared the 1983 declaration invalid. Internationally, the north is regarded as part of the Republic of Cyprus.
61557.m: Only Turkey recognises Northern Cyprus as a state.

61558.q: How did the communities vote on the Annan Plan for reunification in 2004?
a: The Greek Cypriots rejected it, the Turkish Cypriots approved it
The Turkish Cypriots rejected it, the Greek Cypriots approved it
61558.e: About 76 per cent of Greek Cypriots rejected the UN plan, while about 65 per cent of Turkish Cypriots approved it. As both had to agree, it failed.
61558.m: The Annan Plan failed in 2004 because the Greek Cypriots voted no.

61559.q: What does the term “Enosis” mean in the history of Cyprus?
61559.e: In the 20th century many Greek Cypriots demanded enosis, meaning union with Greece. Turkish Cypriots countered with the demand for partition (taksim).
61559.m: Enosis means the union of Cyprus with Greece.

61560.q: Which areas of Cyprus still belong to the United Kingdom today?
a: The military bases of Akrotiri and Dhekelia
61560.e: At independence in 1960, Britain kept two military bases as sovereign areas. They lie in the south of the island.
61560.m: Akrotiri and Dhekelia are British military bases on Cyprus.

61561.q: Since Cyprus joined the EU in 2004, what applies to the north of the island?
a: It is a separate EU member
It is part of the Schengen Area
It has used the euro ever since
61561.e: Legally, the whole island joined the EU. Because the government does not control the north, EU law is suspended there.
61561.m: EU law does not apply in northern Cyprus for now.

61562.q: Which ghost town near Famagusta has been a closed military zone since 1974?
61562.e: The hotel district of Varosha was abandoned in a rush in 1974 and sealed off. Since 2020, parts of it have been open to visitors again, which has been criticised internationally.
61562.m: Varosha is the ghost town of Famagusta.

61563.q: What has divided the capital Nicosia into a northern and a southern part since 1974?
a: A buffer zone monitored by the UN
61563.e: The buffer zone, also called the Green Line, is monitored by UN troops. Since 2008 it has been possible to cross it on foot in Ledra Street, a shopping street.
61563.m: Nicosia is divided by the UN buffer zone.

61564.q: Which three countries became guarantor powers for the order of the Republic of Cyprus in 1960?
61564.e: The Treaty of Guarantee was meant to secure the constitution and independence of Cyprus. Turkey justified its intervention in 1974 with this treaty.
61564.m: Greece, Turkey and Britain are the guarantor powers of Cyprus.

61565.q: In which city was Albania’s independence declared in 1912?
61565.e: Ismail Qemali proclaimed independence on 28 November 1912 in the port city of Vlorë. Tirana only became the capital in 1920.
61565.m: Albania became independent in Vlorë in 1912.

61566.q: What triggered serious unrest in Albania in 1997?
a: The death of the head of state
61566.e: Many Albanians had put their savings into fraudulent pyramid schemes. Their collapse led to uprisings and the breakdown of state order.
61566.m: In 1997 pyramid schemes plunged Albania into crisis.

61567.q: Which river in Albania was protected in 2023 as one of Europe’s first wild river national parks?
61567.e: The Vjosa flows for a long stretch without any dams. The national park is meant to keep it as a free-flowing river.
61567.m: The Vjosa is a protected wild river in Albania.

61568.q: Since which year has Albania been a member of NATO?
61568.e: Albania joined NATO on 1 April 2009 together with Croatia. Before that, it had cut itself off from all alliances for decades.
61568.m: Albania has been in NATO since 2009.

61569.q: What is Albania’s status in relation to the EU (as of 2025)?
a: It is a candidate country negotiating membership
It has been an EU member since 2004
Like Norway, it is only in the EEA
It rejected membership in a referendum
61569.e: The European Council granted Albania candidate status in 2014. Accession negotiations were formally opened in 2022.
61569.m: Albania is an EU candidate country.

61570.q: Which language family does Albanian belong to?
a: To the Indo-European languages, as its own branch
To the Slavic languages, like Serbian
To the Romance languages, like Italian
To the Turkic languages, like Turkish
61570.e: Albanian is an Indo-European language but forms its own branch with no close relatives. There are two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south.
61570.m: Albanian is a separate branch of the Indo-European languages.

61571.q: What mostly shapes the landscape of Albania?
a: Mountains, with a narrow coastal plain
Bogs and lakes as in Finland
61571.e: A large part of Albania is mountainous. The highest mountain is Korab on the border with North Macedonia, at about 2760 m above sea level. The flat land is mainly along the Adriatic coast.
61571.m: Albania is a mountainous country with a narrow coastal plain.

61572.q: Which Roman long-distance road began on the Albanian coast at Dyrrachium, today’s Durrës?
61572.e: The Via Egnatia led across the Balkans to Byzantium. It extended the Via Appia, which ended at Brindisi on the other side of the Adriatic.
61572.m: The Via Egnatia began at Durrës.

61573.q: To which Italian port did the freighter “Vlora” bring about 20,000 Albanian refugees in August 1991?
61573.e: After the end of the dictatorship, many Albanians fled across the Adriatic. Pictures of the hopelessly overcrowded ship went around the world; most were sent back.
61573.m: In 1991 tens of thousands of Albanians reached Bari by ship.

61574.q: When did Croatia join the European Union?
61574.e: Croatia became the 28th member of the EU on 1 July 2013. After Slovenia, it was the second successor state of Yugoslavia in the Union.
61574.m: Croatia has been in the EU since 2013.

61575.q: Which Roman emperor had a palace built in Split that now forms the old town?
61575.e: Diocletian retired to his palace on the Adriatic around 305. Later, the inhabitants built their houses into its walls.
61575.m: Split’s old town lies inside Diocletian’s Palace.

61576.q: When did Croatia declare its independence from Yugoslavia?
61576.e: On 25 June 1991 Croatia declared itself independent. A war followed that lasted until 1995.

61577.q: Which largest peninsula in the Adriatic does Croatia share with Slovenia and Italy?
61577.e: Most of Istria belongs to Croatia, a small part to Slovenia and a tiny tip to Italy. Well-known places are Pula and Rovinj.
61577.m: Istria is the largest peninsula in the Adriatic.

61578.q: Which national park near Šibenik is known for the travertine falls of Skradinski buk?
61578.e: The River Krka flows through a karst gorge and forms several waterfalls. At Skradinski buk the water tumbles down over many steps.
61578.m: Krka National Park lies near Šibenik.

61579.q: Which town on the Danube became a symbol of the Croatian War after a siege lasting months in 1991?
61579.e: Vukovar was almost completely destroyed by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian units. After the town fell, war crimes were committed.
61579.m: Vukovar is a symbol of the Croatian War.

61580.q: Which item of clothing owes its name to Croatian soldiers in the 17th century?
61580.e: Croatian horsemen serving France wore knotted neckcloths. The French named these “cravate” after them.
61580.m: The cravat is named after the Croats.

61581.q: Which old Slavic script was used in Croatia for church texts into modern times?
61581.e: The Glagolitic script goes back to Cyril and Methodius, the apostles to the Slavs. It survived particularly long in Croatia, for example on the Baška tablet.
61581.m: Croatia kept the Glagolitic script particularly long.

61582.q: Which river delta in southern Croatia is known for growing mandarins?
61582.e: The mouth of the Neretva was drained in the 19th and 20th centuries. Today citrus fruit grows there, especially mandarins.
61582.m: Mandarins grow in the Neretva Delta.

61583.q: Which group of islands in the Aegean was under Italian rule from 1912 to 1947?
61583.e: Italy occupied the Dodecanese in 1912 during its war against the Ottoman Empire. Only the peace treaty of 1947 gave the islands to Greece.
61583.m: The Dodecanese only became Greek after the Second World War.

61584.q: How was the caldera of Santorini formed?
a: By a huge volcanic eruption in the Bronze Age
61584.e: The Minoan eruption in the 2nd millennium BC made the magma chamber collapse. The sea filled the crater, and today’s island forms a ring around the caldera.
61584.m: Santorini is the rim of a collapsed volcano.

61585.q: Which largest island of the Dodecanese was the seat of the Knights of St John?
61585.e: The Knights of St John ruled Rhodes from 1309 to 1522. Their fortified old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
61585.m: Rhodes was the fortress of the Knights of St John.

61586.q: Which Aegean island became a focal point of refugee movements to Europe from 2015?
61586.e: Lesbos lies only a few kilometres off the Turkish coast. Hundreds of thousands of refugees reached the island in boats, and the Moria camp burned down in 2020.
61586.m: Lesbos lies close to the Turkish coast and became the arrival island for many refugees.

61587.q: Which treaty set the borders of the new Turkey in 1923, including for the Aegean islands?
61587.e: The Treaty of Lausanne replaced the Treaty of Sèvres, which was never carried out. The islands of Imbros (Gökçeada) and Tenedos off the Dardanelles went to Turkey; most other Aegean islands stayed Greek.
61587.m: The Treaty of Lausanne set Turkey’s borders in 1923, including in the Aegean.

61588.q: Which resin is produced only in the south of the island of Chios?
61588.e: The mastic shrub only gives a usable resin in southern Chios. The mastic villages were therefore wealthy for centuries.
61588.m: Mastic is the resin of Chios.

61589.q: On which Dodecanese island was the famous physician Hippocrates born?
61589.e: Hippocrates lived in the 5th century BC and is regarded as the father of medicine. Kos also has a sanctuary of Asclepius, the god of healing.
61589.m: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos.

61590.q: Which Aegean island is regarded as a “Blue Zone”, where a strikingly large number of people live to a very old age?
61590.e: On Ikaria, an above-average number of people live to over 90. Researchers suspect causes such as diet, exercise and close communities.
61590.m: On Ikaria many people live to a very old age.

61591.q: On which island in the northern Aegean was the goddess of victory found in 1863 that now stands in the Louvre?
61591.e: The Winged Victory of Samothrace once stood in a sanctuary on the island. Today it stands at the top of a great staircase in the Louvre.
61591.m: The Winged Victory of Samothrace comes from the island of Samothrace.

61592.q: Which EU member state lies geographically entirely in Asia?
61592.e: The island of Cyprus lies in the eastern Mediterranean off the coast of Anatolia and geographically belongs to Asia. Politically and culturally it is closely linked with Europe.
61592.m: Cyprus is geographically Asian and politically European.

61593.q: Which country in the South Caucasus is partly counted as part of Europe, depending on where the border is drawn?
61593.e: Depending on the definition, the border runs through the Caucasus or north of it. Georgia also sees itself politically as a European country and is an EU candidate.
61593.m: Georgia lies on the border between Europe and Asia.

61594.q: According to the common definition today, what forms the border between Europe and Asia in the north?
a: The Ural Mountains and the Ural River
The River Ob and the Altai Mountains
61594.e: The border usually runs along the eastern edge of the Ural Mountains and along the Ural River to the Caspian Sea. The Swedish officer Philip Johan von Strahlenberg suggested the Urals as the border in the 18th century.
61594.m: In the north the Ural Mountains and Ural River separate Europe from Asia.

61595.q: Roughly what share of Russia’s area lies in Europe?
61595.e: European Russia covers just under 4 million km² out of about 17 million km². Most of the country lies in Siberia and the Far East.
61595.m: Only about a quarter of Russia lies in Europe.

61596.q: Where does the majority of Russia’s population live?
a: In the European part west of the Urals
61596.e: About three quarters of the people in Russia live in the European part. Moscow and Saint Petersburg are also there.

61597.q: What is the European part of Turkey called?
61597.e: East Thrace lies west of the Bosporus and Dardanelles and borders Greece and Bulgaria. Edirne is an important city in this region.
61597.m: East Thrace is the European part of Turkey.

61598.q: Which strait lies on the border line if the border is drawn through the Kuma-Manych Depression and the Sea of Azov?
61598.e: In this definition, the border runs from the Caspian Sea through the lowland to the Sea of Azov. From there, the Strait of Kerch connects to the Black Sea.
61598.m: The Strait of Kerch connects the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

61599.q: Which sea lies entirely within Turkish territory between two straits of the Europe-Asia border?
61599.e: The Sea of Marmara is a small inland sea. In the north-east and the south-west it is connected to the neighbouring seas by narrow straits.
61599.m: The Sea of Marmara lies entirely in Turkey.

61600.q: Which country in the South Caucasus has its capital right on the Caspian Sea and is partly counted as European?
61600.e: Baku lies on the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian Sea. Depending on where the border is drawn, a small part of Azerbaijan north of the main Caucasus ridge lies in Europe.
61600.m: Azerbaijan, with Baku, lies on the Caspian Sea.

61601.q: What does the Italian word “Mezzogiorno” literally mean?
61601.e: At midday the sun is in the south. That is why Mezzogiorno also means the south of Italy.
61601.m: Mezzogiorno means midday and refers to southern Italy.

61602.q: Apart from the southern mainland, which regions are usually also part of the Mezzogiorno?
61602.e: The Mezzogiorno includes Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Apulia, Basilicata and Calabria, as well as the large islands of Sicily and Sardinia.
61602.m: Sicily and Sardinia also belong to the Mezzogiorno.

61603.q: What is meant by the “Questione meridionale”?
a: The economic and social backwardness of the south since unification
The dispute over the status of Rome
The question of South Tyrolean autonomy
The conflict over the Adriatic border
61603.e: After unification in 1861, a big gap between north and south became clear. The debate about its causes and solutions is called the Southern Question.
61603.m: The Southern Question describes the gap between northern and southern Italy.

61604.q: Which state institution supported the development of southern Italy from 1950 into the 1980s?
61604.e: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno financed roads, irrigation and industry. It was dissolved in 1984 because its effects fell short of expectations.
61604.m: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno was meant to develop the south.

61605.q: What did critics call large, isolated industrial plants in the south that attracted hardly any suppliers?
61605.e: Examples are the steelworks in Taranto and chemical plants in Sicily. They created jobs but hardly triggered broad development.
61605.m: Isolated large industry in the south was mockingly called cathedrals in the desert.

61606.q: Which farming structure held back the development of the Mezzogiorno for a long time?
61606.e: A few large landowners owned a lot of land, which was farmed extensively by day labourers. The land reform of 1950 redistributed part of it.
61606.m: Latifundia shaped farming in the south.

61607.q: Which criminal organisation has its origins in Calabria?
61607.e: The ’Ndrangheta comes from Calabria and is now seen as one of the most powerful mafia organisations, including in the international cocaine trade.

61608.q: Which kingdom covered most of the Mezzogiorno until 1860/61?
61608.e: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, with its capital Naples, was conquered by Garibaldi’s Expedition of the Thousand and became part of the Kingdom of Italy.
61608.m: Before unification the south belonged to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

61609.q: What effect did the economic situation in the Mezzogiorno have on the population in the 20th century?
a: Heavy emigration to northern Italy and abroad
City dwellers returning to the countryside
61609.e: Millions of people moved to Turin, Milan, the USA or Switzerland. In the 1950s and 1960s many southern Italians worked in Swiss factories and on building sites.
61609.m: Many people from the Mezzogiorno emigrated, including to Switzerland.

61610.q: Which organisation with roots in Naples and Campania is a typical example of organised crime in the south?
61610.e: The Camorra is not a single organisation but a network of clans in and around Naples. It is active in the waste business and drug trafficking, among other things.
61610.m: The Camorra is the clan network of Campania.

61611.q: In Alpine geology, what is meant by a “nappe”?
a: A slab of rock pushed far over other rocks
A horizontal layer of lake clay
A thin layer of soil over the bedrock
A solidified lava layer from a volcano
61611.e: Nappes are large packages of rock that were detached from their place of origin during mountain building and pushed many kilometres over other rocks.
61611.m: A nappe is a package of rock moved a long way.

61612.q: Which two continental plates or continental margins collided when the Alps were formed?
a: Europe and the North American Plate
The Indian and the Eurasian Plate
61612.e: The Alps were formed when the Adriatic (Apulian) Plate, a spur of Africa, collided with the European continental margin and the ocean in between disappeared.
61612.m: The Alps formed from the collision of Adria and Europe.

61613.q: What is the order of the major nappe systems in the Swiss Alps from bottom to top?
61613.e: At the bottom lie the nappes from the European shelf, above them those from the ocean area, and at the top the Austroalpine nappes that come from the Adriatic margin.
61613.m: The Austroalpine nappes lie at the top of the nappe stack.

61614.q: What is an isolated remnant of a nappe, cut off by erosion and lying on younger ground, called?
61614.e: A klippe is a detached remnant of a nappe that lies on other rocks like a foreign body.
61614.m: A klippe is an isolated remnant of a nappe.

a: A place where erosion has cut through the nappe and deeper units can be seen
A cave formed by limestone dissolving
A gap in a glacial moraine
A natural rock arch in a ridge
61615.e: In a window the upper nappe has been worn away, so you look through it at the rocks below, for example in the Tauern Window in Austria.
61615.m: In a tectonic window you look through a nappe at deeper rocks.

61616.q: Which geologist from western Switzerland brought together the nappe structure of the Alps into a complete theory around 1902?
61616.e: The Lausanne geologist Maurice Lugeon presented a complete nappe theory of the Alps in 1902. Albert Heim accepted it in the same year.
61616.m: Maurice Lugeon founded the nappe theory of the Alps in 1902.

61617.q: Which line separates the Southern Alps from the rest of the Alps in Switzerland?
61617.e: The Insubric Line is part of the Periadriatic Seam. South of it lie the Southern Alps, which were hardly thrust northwards.
61617.m: The Insubric Line separates the Southern Alps from the main body of the Alps to the north.

61618.q: Which nappe unit forms the summit of the Matterhorn?
a: The Molasse of the Swiss Plateau
The granite of the Aar Massif
61618.e: The summit pyramid consists of gneisses of the Dent Blanche nappe, which comes from the Adriatic continental margin. That is why people speak of the “African” summit of the Matterhorn.
61618.m: The Matterhorn summit comes from the Adriatic continental margin.

61619.q: Which sequence of rocks typically formed in the sea in front of the growing Alps and was later overridden itself?
61619.e: Flysch consists of alternating layers of sandstone, marl and clay deposited in deep water in front of the advancing nappes.
61619.m: Flysch is a marine rock from the early phase of Alpine formation.

61620.q: Where were the rocks of the Helvetic zone originally deposited?
a: On the shelf at the southern edge of Europe
On the floor of a deep ocean
On the edge of the Adriatic Plate
In freshwater lakes of the Swiss Plateau
61620.e: The Helvetic sediments come from the shallow European continental shelf. Towards the south the layers become thicker and richer in limestone.
61620.m: The Helvetic zone comes from the European shelf.

61621.q: Where does the Helvetic zone get its name from?
a: From Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland
From the Helvetic Confession of the Reformed Church
61621.e: The system was first described in Switzerland and named after Helvetia. Many of its type localities are here.
61621.m: The Helvetic zone is named after Helvetia.

61622.q: Which type of rock mainly makes up the Helvetic nappes?
61622.e: The Helvetic nappes consist mainly of sedimentary rocks from the Jurassic, the Cretaceous and the early Tertiary, especially limestones and marls.
61622.m: Helvetic nappes consist mainly of limestone and marl.

61623.q: What happened to the Helvetic sediments during mountain building?
a: They were sheared off the crystalline basement and pushed north
They sank completely into the Earth’s mantle
They stayed flat and undisturbed in place
61623.e: The sediments came loose from their basement along soft layers and were thrust over as the northernmost part of the nappe stack.
61623.m: The Helvetic sediments were sheared off their basement.

61624.q: Which mountain in eastern Switzerland is a textbook example of folded Helvetic limestone layers?
61624.e: On the Säntis, the folds of the Helvetic Säntis nappe are superbly exposed.
61624.m: The Säntis impressively shows folded Helvetic limestones.

61625.q: Which pale, karst-forming Lower Cretaceous limestone forms many striking rock faces in the Helvetic zone, for example on the Schrattenfluh?
61625.e: Schrattenkalk is a pale, massive limestone from the Lower Cretaceous. It tends to form karst and creates limestone pavements (Schratten).
61625.m: Schrattenkalk is a typical limestone of the Helvetic nappes.

61626.q: What are the Helvetic units called that were deposited on the southernmost edge of the shelf and mark the transition to the ocean?
61626.e: The Ultrahelvetic comes from the very southern edge of the European shelf, right at the transition to the Penninic ocean.
61626.m: The Ultrahelvetic is the southernmost part of the Helvetic zone.

61627.q: Which mountain chain by Lake Walen is made of Helvetic limestone layers and shows striking layer edges?
61627.e: The Churfirsten consist of Helvetic Cretaceous limestones tilted to the north, whose layer edges drop steeply to Lake Walen.
61627.m: The Churfirsten are built of Helvetic limestones.

61628.q: Where does the name Penninic come from?
a: From the Pennine Alps in Valais
61628.e: The name comes from the Pennine Alps (Valais Alps), in Latin Mons Poeninus. Deriving it from Hannibal is considered wrong.
61628.m: The Penninic is named after the Pennine Alps.

61629.q: From which area of deposition does a large part of the Penninic rocks come?
a: From the Tethys, an ocean between Europe and Adria
From the Molasse sea on the Swiss Plateau
From the ancient valley of the Rhine
From an inland lake in the Jura
61629.e: The Penninic nappes come from the ocean area of the Tethys, including the Piedmont-Liguria Ocean, and from the continental Briançonnais in between.
61629.m: Penninic rocks mostly come from the Tethys.

a: Remains of oceanic crust and mantle
Fossilised coral reefs of a shallow sea
Pebbles from an old river delta
Sandstones turned to glass by heat
61630.e: Ophiolites are rock sequences of serpentinite, gabbro and basalt. They prove that an ocean once lay between Europe and Adria.
61630.m: Ophiolites are remains of a former ocean floor.

61631.q: Which grey, finely layered rock from the Penninic zone is named after a Swiss canton?
61631.e: Bündner schists are limy, clayey deep-sea sediments of the Tethys that are widespread in the Grisons.
61631.m: Bündner schists are typical rocks of the Penninic zone.

61632.q: The Penninic zone consists of several nappes. What is a nappe in Alpine geology?
a: A package of rock pushed far over other rocks
A thin layer of glacier ice
A flat lava layer from a volcano
61632.e: When the Alps formed, huge packages of rock were sheared off and pushed over each other, some more than a hundred kilometres. Such packages are called nappes.
61632.m: The Alps are built of nappes pushed over each other.

61633.q: In which canton do deep Penninic gneiss nappes lie at the surface over large areas?
61633.e: In Ticino the Penninic zone was strongly uplifted and worn away. That is why deep gneiss nappes such as the Maggia or the Leventina nappe appear there.
61633.m: In Ticino deep Penninic gneisses lie at the surface.

61634.q: Which nappe unit do the Mythen near Schwyz form?
61634.e: The Mythen belong to the Penninic klippe nappe, which, like the Préalpes, lies on younger Helvetic rocks and flysch.
61634.m: The Mythen are a Penninic klippe on younger ground.

61635.q: In which Swiss valley is there a large tectonic window where Penninic rocks appear from under Austroalpine nappes?
61635.e: In the Lower Engadine Window, the River Inn has cut through the Austroalpine nappes, so the Penninic rocks below can be seen. It reaches as far as Prutz in Tyrol.
61635.m: In the Lower Engadine you see Penninic rocks through a window.

61636.q: What is special about the Glarus Thrust?
a: Older rocks lie on much younger ones
Younger rocks lie on older ones
61636.e: Along a sharp line, Verrucano about 260 to 300 million years old was pushed onto flysch that is only 35 to 50 million years old.
61636.m: At the Glarus Thrust old lies on young.

61637.q: What is the reddish Permian rock above the Glarus Thrust called?
61637.e: Verrucano is a reddish, coarse rock made of fragments from the Permian period. It forms the older, upper part of the thrust.
61637.m: Red Verrucano lies above the Glarus Thrust.

61638.q: Which rock lies below the Glarus thrust plane?
a: Moraine from the last Ice Age
61638.e: Under the thrust lies slaty flysch that was deposited about 35 to 50 million years ago.
61638.m: Young flysch lies under the Glarus Thrust.

61639.q: Roughly how far north were the rocks at the Glarus Thrust pushed?
61639.e: The upper mass of rock was moved about 40 kilometres north over the younger layers.
61639.m: The Glarus Thrust has a displacement of about 40 kilometres.

61640.q: Under which name did the area of the Glarus Thrust become a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008?
61640.e: In July 2008 UNESCO added the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona as a World Natural Heritage Site.
61640.m: The Tectonic Arena Sardona has been World Natural Heritage since 2008.

61641.q: What is the hole through the rock of the Tschingelhörner called, through which the sun shines on the church of Elm twice a year?
61641.e: The Martinsloch is a natural hole in the ridge of the Tschingelhörner. Twice a year sunbeams fall through it onto Elm.
61641.m: The sun shines on Elm through the Martinsloch.

61642.q: What is the outcrop near Sool in the lower Sernf Valley called, where you can see the thrust plane up close?
61642.e: At the Lochsite (Lochseite) near Sool, the sharp boundary surface with a pale layer of limestone is easy to reach on the valley floor.
61642.m: At the Lochsite you can touch the thrust.

61643.q: How did Albert Heim first explain the rock layers in Glarus before he accepted the nappe theory in 1902?
61643.e: For a long time Heim supported the “Glarus double fold”, meaning two folds facing each other. Only in 1902 did he accept the thrust, in a letter to Lugeon.
61643.m: Albert Heim first believed in a Glarus double fold.

61644.q: Which explanation for the rock layers in Glarus finally won through around 1900?
a: A single great thrust of rock nappes
A double fold made of two folds
61644.e: For a long time Albert Heim’s double fold was accepted. Around 1900 the nappe theory won through: older rocks had been pushed far over younger ones as a nappe.
61644.m: The rock layers in Glarus are a great thrust.

61645.q: On which soft rock layers did the pile of sediments slide when the Folded Jura was formed?
a: On Triassic layers of salt and anhydrite
61645.e: The Jura layers were sheared off over Triassic layers of salt and anhydrite. These acted like a lubricant.
61645.m: The Folded Jura slid on Triassic salts.

61646.q: What does “distant push” mean in the formation of the Folded Jura?
a: The push of the Alps was passed across the Swiss Plateau into the Jura
The Jura was lifted from below by volcanoes
Glaciers pushed the Jura folds together
The Rhine Graben pulled the Jura north
61646.e: The pressure from the formation of the Alps was passed beneath the Molasse basin to the sediments of the Jura, which folded into ridges there.
61646.m: The Folded Jura was formed by a distant push from the Alps.

61647.q: What is a narrow gorge cut by a river right across a Jura ridge called?
61647.e: A cluse cuts across a ridge, as at Balsthal or Moutier. Cluses are important transport routes.
61647.m: A cluse is a gorge cutting across a Jura ridge.

61648.q: What is a long valley carved out by erosion along the crest of a Jura fold called?
61648.e: In a combe, erosion has broken through the hard limestone cover of an arch and cleared out the softer layers in the core.
61648.m: A combe lies hollowed out along the crest of an arch.

61649.q: In Jura tectonics, what is an upward-arched fold called?
61649.e: An anticline (arch, saddle) is arched upwards.
61649.m: A Jura arch is an anticline.

61650.q: Which part of the Jura do the high plateaus of the Franches-Montagnes belong to?
a: To the Plateau Jura, as part of the Folded Jura
